beginner.question: Which MATLAB window shows the variables currently held in memory during your session?
beginner.explanation: The Workspace browser lists every variable currently in memory, along with its size, class, and value.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — the Command Window is where you type and run commands interactively; it doesn’t list variables.
Correct — the Workspace panel shows all variables currently in memory.
Incorrect — the Editor is where you write and edit script (.m) files.
Incorrect — the Command History logs commands you’ve previously executed, not current variables.

beginner.question: The Command Window is where you write and save reusable MATLAB scripts.
beginner.explanation: False. The Command Window executes statements immediately and doesn’t save them as a file — reusable code belongs in a script written in the Editor and saved as a .m file.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — nothing typed directly into the Command Window is saved as a script.
Correct — script files are written and saved in the Editor, not the Command Window.
commonMistakes: Typing multi-line analyses directly into the Command Window and losing the work when MATLAB closes.

beginner.question: What file extension is used for a MATLAB script file?
beginner.explanation: MATLAB script and function files use the .m extension.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB code files (scripts and functions) are saved as .m files.
Incorrect — .mat is the extension for saved MATLAB *data* (Workspace variables), not code.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB file extension.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB file extension.

beginner.question: Which action is performed in the Editor rather than the Command Window?
options: Writing and saving a multi-line script
Running a single command immediately and seeing its result
Browsing the values of variables currently in memory
Viewing a list of previously executed commands
beginner.explanation: The Editor is where you compose and save reusable code as a script (.m) file. Running one-off commands, browsing variables, and viewing command history are the jobs of the Command Window, Workspace, and Command History respectively.
optionExplanations: Correct — the Editor is for writing and saving multi-line scripts.
Incorrect — that describes the Command Window.
Incorrect — that describes the Workspace browser.
Incorrect — that describes the Command History panel.

beginner.question: Every MATLAB script must begin with the keyword "function".
beginner.explanation: False. Scripts are simply a sequence of statements with no required header. Only function files must begin with a "function" definition line.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — the "function" keyword is only required to start a function file, not a plain script.
Correct — scripts have no required starting keyword.

beginner.question: If you type "3 + 4" into the Command Window without assigning it to a variable, where does MATLAB store the result?
beginner.explanation: MATLAB automatically stores the result of any unassigned expression in a special variable called ans, which you can reuse in the next command.
optionExplanations: Correct — ans automatically holds the most recent unassigned result.
Incorrect — temp is not a special MATLAB variable.
Incorrect — result is not a special MATLAB variable.
Incorrect — the result is kept, not discarded, in ans.

beginner.question: Pressing the up-arrow key in the Command Window recalls previously typed commands.
beginner.explanation: True. The up-arrow (and down-arrow) key cycles through your command history right in the Command Window, without needing to open the Command History panel.
optionExplanations: Correct — the up-arrow key recalls prior commands.
Incorrect — this is a standard, commonly used MATLAB shortcut.

beginner.question: Which panel shows the files located in the folder MATLAB is currently using?
beginner.explanation: The Current Folder browser lists the files and subfolders in whatever folder MATLAB is currently pointed at.
optionExplanations: Correct — Current Folder lists the files in the active folder.
Incorrect — Workspace shows variables, not files.
Incorrect — Command History shows past commands, not files.
Incorrect — the Editor shows the contents of one open file, not a folder listing.

beginner.question: Double-clicking a variable in the Workspace panel opens:
options: The Variable Editor — a spreadsheet-like view of its data
beginner.explanation: Double-clicking a Workspace variable opens the Variable Editor, letting you view (and edit) its values in a spreadsheet-like grid.
optionExplanations: Correct — this opens the Variable Editor.
Incorrect — the Command Window is always open; double-clicking a variable doesn’t affect it.
Incorrect — this doesn’t create a new script.
Incorrect — this doesn’t open documentation.
beginner.concept: Inspecting variables with the Variable Editor

beginner.question: What mainly distinguishes a Live Script (.mlx) from a plain script (.m)?
options: Live Scripts combine code, formatted text, and inline output/plots in one document, while a plain script is just code
Live Scripts cannot contain any MATLAB code at all
There is no real difference between them
beginner.explanation: Live Scripts interleave narrative text, code, and the resulting output (including plots) directly in the document — useful for reports and tutorials — whereas a .m script is plain code with no built-in formatting or inline output.
optionExplanations: Correct — Live Scripts blend narrative, code, and inline results.
Incorrect — execution speed is not meaningfully different.
Incorrect — Live Scripts absolutely contain MATLAB code; that’s their core purpose.
Incorrect — the file format and capabilities genuinely differ.

beginner.question: Comments (starting with %) in a script are ignored by MATLAB and have no effect on how the code runs.
beginner.explanation: True. Comments exist purely for human readers; MATLAB skips over anything after a % on a line.
optionExplanations: Correct — comments never affect execution.
Incorrect — comments are exactly the part of a line MATLAB ignores.

beginner.question: What does clicking the "Run" (▶) button in the Editor normally do?
options: Runs the entire script from the beginning
Only runs the line the cursor is currently on
Opens the script inside the Command Window
Saves the script without running it
beginner.explanation: The Run button executes the whole script (or function) from top to bottom, saving the file first if needed.
optionExplanations: Correct — Run executes the entire file.
Incorrect — running just the current line uses a different feature (Evaluate Selection).
Incorrect — the script stays in the Editor; only its output appears in the Command Window.
Incorrect — Run also executes the code, not just saves it.

beginner.question: Which panel would you check to see a list of commands you typed earlier in the session, even several minutes ago?
beginner.explanation: The Command History panel keeps a running log of everything typed into the Command Window, across the whole session (and often beyond).
optionExplanations: Correct — Command History logs past commands.
Incorrect — Workspace shows variables, not typed commands.
Incorrect — Current Folder shows files, not commands.
Incorrect — the Editor shows script files, not typed command history.

beginner.question: You can type more than one statement on the same line in the Command Window by separating them with commas or semicolons.
beginner.explanation: True. For example, "a = 1, b = 2" runs both assignments and displays both results; using semicolons instead would run both but suppress their output.
optionExplanations: Correct — commas or semicolons can separate multiple statements on one line.
Incorrect — this is valid, commonly used MATLAB syntax.

beginner.question: After running this in the Command Window, what does the second line display?
beginner.explanation: The first line (unassigned) sets ans to 7 and echoes it; typing ans again on the next line simply re-displays its current value.
optionExplanations: Correct — ans holds 7 from the first line.
Incorrect — ans was just set by the previous line, so it is defined.
Incorrect — 3 alone is never displayed here.
Incorrect — 4 alone is never displayed here.

beginner.question: Which command changes MATLAB’s current folder from within the Command Window?
beginner.explanation: cd (short for "change directory") changes MATLAB’s current folder, e.g. cd('myfolder').
optionExplanations: Correct — cd changes the current folder.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB function.

beginner.question: A function file must be named exactly the same as the function it defines (e.g., a function named computeStats must be saved as computeStats.m).
beginner.explanation: True. MATLAB primarily resolves a top-level function call by looking for a file with that exact name — the file name and the function name should match.
optionExplanations: Correct — the file name is how MATLAB primarily finds a top-level function.
Incorrect — a mismatched file name is a common, genuine source of "undefined function" errors.

beginner.question: What does the small red dot that appears in the margin next to a line number in the Editor represent, after you click there?
options: A breakpoint set on that line
That line has been saved separately
beginner.explanation: Clicking in the line-number margin toggles a breakpoint on that line, shown as a red dot — execution will pause there when you run the script.
optionExplanations: Correct — the red dot marks a breakpoint.
Incorrect — the line is still fully present.
Incorrect — comments are shown differently (as green text), not by a red dot.
Incorrect — this has nothing to do with saving.

beginner.question: Which key runs a script currently open in the Editor, in addition to clicking the Run button?
beginner.explanation: F5 is the default keyboard shortcut for running the current file in the MATLAB Editor.
optionExplanations: Correct — F5 runs the current script.
Incorrect — F1 typically opens help, not run.
Incorrect — Ctrl+Z is Undo.
Incorrect — Esc does not run anything.
beginner.concept: Running a script via keyboard shortcut

beginner.question: Undo (Ctrl+Z) in the Editor can only undo the single most recent change, not multiple steps back.
beginner.explanation: False. Like most text editors, the MATLAB Editor supports multiple levels of undo — pressing Ctrl+Z repeatedly steps back further through your edit history.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — multiple undo steps are supported.
Correct — Ctrl+Z can be pressed repeatedly to undo several changes.

beginner.question: A wavy red or orange underline beneath a line of code in the Editor most likely indicates:
options: A potential problem flagged by MATLAB’s Code Analyzer
beginner.explanation: The Editor continuously runs the Code Analyzer in the background, underlining lines with likely issues (like an unused variable or a suspicious pattern) even before you run the code.
optionExplanations: Correct — this marks a Code Analyzer warning or suggestion.
Incorrect — running lines aren’t shown with underlines.
Incorrect — comments are shown in green text, not underlined.
Incorrect — breakpoints show as a red dot in the margin, not an underline.

beginner.question: Match each action to its default MATLAB Editor keyboard shortcut.
matchOptions: Ctrl+S
Ctrl+Z
F5
Ctrl+R
beginner.explanation: These are the default MATLAB Editor shortcuts on Windows: Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Z undoes, F5 runs the file, and Ctrl+R comments out the selected lines (Ctrl+T uncomments them).

beginner.question: Pressing Ctrl+S while a script is open in the Editor writes your changes to the .m file on disk.
beginner.explanation: True. Ctrl+S is the standard save shortcut, and it writes the Editor’s current contents to the file.
optionExplanations: Correct — Ctrl+S saves the file to disk.
Incorrect — Ctrl+S does perform a real save.

beginner.question: If you’re unsure what a MATLAB function does, which command prints its documentation directly in the Command Window?
beginner.explanation: help functionName (e.g., help plot) prints that function’s documentation as plain text right in the Command Window.
optionExplanations: Correct — help prints documentation text.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB function.

beginner.question: Put these steps in order for writing and running your very first MATLAB script.
options: Open a new file in the Editor
Save the file with a .m extension
beginner.explanation: You open a new file, write the code, save it as a .m file, and only then run it — MATLAB needs a saved file on disk to execute.

intermediate.question: You type "x = 5;" directly into the Command Window, then close MATLAB without saving anything. The next time you open MATLAB, what happens to x?
options: x is still 5, because the Workspace is saved automatically
x no longer exists, because the Workspace is cleared when MATLAB closes
x is automatically written to a .m file called x.m
x becomes a permanent global variable available in every future session
intermediate.explanation: The Workspace only exists for the current session. Closing MATLAB clears it, so any variables created only in the Command Window are gone unless you explicitly saved them (e.g., with save).
optionExplanations: Incorrect — MATLAB does not auto-save the Workspace between sessions.
Correct — the Workspace is session-only memory; it is cleared when MATLAB closes.
Incorrect — MATLAB never auto-converts variables into script files.
Incorrect — there is no such thing as an automatically-persisted global variable across sessions.
commonMistakes: Assuming variables typed into the Command Window persist like a saved file.

intermediate.question: A colleague sends you a script "analysis.m" that calls a custom function "computeStats.m". For the script to run without error, what is required?
options: Both files must be in the same folder, or computeStats.m must be on the MATLAB path
computeStats.m must be pasted directly into analysis.m
MATLAB automatically searches the entire computer for any function name
computeStats.m must be renamed to match analysis.m
intermediate.explanation: MATLAB can only call a function if it can find it — either in the current folder or in a folder on the search path (via addpath or the Set Path dialog).
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB resolves function calls by looking in the current folder and the search path.
Incorrect — functions do not need to be inlined; that defeats the purpose of a separate function file.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not search your entire filesystem; it only checks the current folder and the path.
Incorrect — function files are matched by the function name inside them, not by matching the calling script’s filename.
intermediate.concept: MATLAB search path and file organization
intermediate.hint: Think about how MATLAB decides where to look when you type a function name it doesn’t already know.

intermediate.question: A semicolon at the end of a line suppresses the Command Window output but does not affect whether the assignment itself occurs.
intermediate.explanation: True. The semicolon only controls whether MATLAB echoes the result — the statement still executes and the variable is still assigned either way.
optionExplanations: Correct — the assignment happens regardless; the semicolon only hides the printed confirmation.
Incorrect — the semicolon has no effect on execution, only on display.
commonMistakes: Believing a missing semicolon means the code “didn’t run,” rather than that it simply printed its result.

intermediate.question: Match each MATLAB desktop tool to its primary purpose.
matchOptions: Executes commands interactively, one at a time
Shows variables currently held in memory
Where you write and save reusable script/function files
Lists commands you have previously executed
intermediate.explanation: Each tool has a distinct role: the Command Window runs commands immediately, the Workspace tracks live variables, the Editor is for saved code, and the Command History logs what you’ve already run.

intermediate.question: You edit a script in the Editor but haven’t saved it yet, then click Run. In MATLAB’s default configuration, what happens?
options: MATLAB prompts you to save the file before it will run
MATLAB refuses to run and shows a permanent error
MATLAB runs the version currently in memory and ignores your unsaved edits
MATLAB automatically discards your edits and reloads the last saved version
intermediate.explanation: By default, MATLAB needs a saved file to run, so it prompts you to save your changes first — it won’t silently run stale or discarded code.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB prompts for a save before running unsaved changes.
Incorrect — it prompts to save rather than refusing outright.
Incorrect — MATLAB runs from the file on disk, not an in-memory version of your edits.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not discard unsaved edits automatically.

intermediate.question: You want to run just one highlighted portion of your script to test it, without running the whole file. Which Editor feature does this?
options: Highlight the code and press F9 (Evaluate Selection)
Delete all the other code temporarily
Save the file under a different name
There is no way to do this in MATLAB
intermediate.explanation: F9 (Evaluate Selection) runs only the currently highlighted code in the context of the Command Window, without running the rest of the file.
optionExplanations: Correct — F9 evaluates just the selected code.
Incorrect — that’s destructive and unnecessary.
Incorrect — saving under a new name doesn’t select what runs.
Incorrect — MATLAB does support this.

intermediate.question: You divide a long script into labeled blocks using %% markers. What is this feature, and what does it let you do?
options: Code Sections — lets you run one section at a time (e.g., with Ctrl+Enter) instead of the whole script
They are just comments with no special behavior at all
They mark the physical end of the file
They are required at the very top of every script
intermediate.explanation: %% creates a Code Section. The Editor highlights the current section and lets you run just that section, which is useful for testing one part of a long script at a time.
optionExplanations: Correct — %% defines runnable Code Sections.
Incorrect — sections do have special Editor behavior beyond being a comment.
Incorrect — a file can have %% markers anywhere, not just at the end.
Incorrect — %% is optional, not required.

intermediate.question: What does the second line display?
intermediate.explanation: The semicolon on the first line only suppresses the printed confirmation — ans is still set to 7 behind the scenes. Typing ans on the next line (unsuppressed) then displays "ans = 7".
optionExplanations: Correct — ans was silently set to 7, then displayed.
Incorrect — the second line has no semicolon, so it does display.
Incorrect — ans was set by the first line even though it wasn’t printed.
Incorrect — MATLAB always echoes the variable name along with the value.
commonMistakes: Assuming a semicolon prevents ans from being set at all, rather than just suppressing the printed output.

intermediate.question: Which of the following will set (overwrite) the value stored in ans? Select all that apply.
options: Typing an unassigned arithmetic expression, e.g. 5 + 2
Calling a function that returns a value without assigning it, e.g. sqrt(4)
Calling disp(5+2), which has no output to capture
intermediate.explanation: Any unassigned expression that produces a value — a bare arithmetic expression or an unassigned function call that returns something — sets ans. An explicit assignment (x = ...) does not touch ans, and disp() has no output argument to capture, so it doesn’t set ans either.

intermediate.question: You run a script that processes patient files, but MATLAB can’t find the data even though the files exist on your computer. What should you check first?
options: The Current Folder, to confirm MATLAB is pointed at the folder containing your data files
intermediate.explanation: "File not found" errors are very often caused by MATLAB’s current folder not matching where the data actually lives — checking (and fixing) the Current Folder is the first thing to try.
optionExplanations: Correct — the current folder controls where bare filenames are looked for.
Incorrect — command history doesn’t affect file lookup.
Incorrect — the Workspace holds variables, not file locations.
Incorrect — font size is unrelated to file access.

intermediate.question: If a script or function file in your current folder happens to be named the same as a built-in function (e.g., a file called mean.m), calling that name could invoke your file instead of the built-in, potentially producing wrong results silently.
intermediate.explanation: True. MATLAB’s name resolution can favor a file on your current folder/path over certain built-ins, so an accidental same-named file is a real and silent risk.
optionExplanations: Correct — a same-named file can silently take priority.
Incorrect — this genuinely can happen and is a known gotcha.
commonMistakes: Naming a personal script the same as a common built-in function.

intermediate.question: This script errors when a user types their name (e.g., Ana) without quotes. Why?
intermediate.code:
n = input('Enter your name: ');
disp(['Hello, ' n])
options: input() by default evaluates typed text as a MATLAB expression, so an unquoted name causes an "undefined variable" error — use input(prompt, 's') to read plain text instead
n must be a number, not text
Nothing is wrong; this works exactly as written
intermediate.explanation: By default, input() treats whatever the user types as a MATLAB expression to evaluate. Typing Ana with no quotes makes MATLAB look for a variable named Ana, which doesn’t exist. Using input(prompt, 's') reads the typed text as a plain string instead.
optionExplanations: Correct — unquoted text is evaluated as an expression by default.
Incorrect — disp() concatenating strings inside [] is standard and works fine.
Incorrect — the whole point here is to read text, not a number.
Incorrect — this genuinely errors for unquoted text input.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the 's' option when input() should read plain text rather than evaluate an expression.

intermediate.question: A colleague wants a path change to persist across future MATLAB sessions, not just the current one. Which approach achieves that?
options: Use the Set Path dialog (or savepath) to save the change, not addpath alone
Restarting the computer makes any path change permanent
This is not possible in MATLAB
intermediate.explanation: A plain addpath() call only affects the current session. Saving the path (via the Set Path dialog or savepath) is what makes the change available in future sessions too.
optionExplanations: Correct — saving the path is what makes it persist.
Incorrect — addpath alone is session-only unless saved.
Incorrect — restarting the computer has nothing to do with MATLAB’s saved path.
Incorrect — MATLAB does support a persistent, saved path.

intermediate.question: Which of the following are true about running an unsaved script by clicking Run? Select all that apply.
options: MATLAB prompts you to save unsaved changes before running
Once saved, the statements execute from top to bottom
Unsaved edits are silently discarded with no prompt
The script can reference variables that already exist in the Workspace from earlier commands
intermediate.explanation: MATLAB prompts for a save (never silently discards), then runs the file top to bottom. Because a plain script shares the base Workspace, it can see and use variables that already exist there from earlier commands.
intermediate.concept: Running a script and the shared Workspace

intermediate.question: Unlike a script, a function file has its own private workspace — variables created inside a function do not appear in the base Workspace after it finishes, unless explicitly returned as an output.
intermediate.explanation: True. A function’s internal variables are local to that function call and disappear when it returns, except for whatever it explicitly passes back as an output argument — unlike a script, which shares the base Workspace directly.
optionExplanations: Correct — functions have their own private scope.
Incorrect — this local-scope behavior is a defining feature of functions.

intermediate.question: You wrote a function with no output argument in its definition, then try bmi = computeBMI(70, 1.75);. What happens?
options: MATLAB raises an error because the function doesn’t produce any output to assign to bmi
MATLAB automatically uses the last value computed inside the function as the output
bmi becomes a string describing the error
intermediate.explanation: If a function’s signature has no output variable (e.g., function computeBMI(weight, height) with nothing before the name), trying to capture a return value with = errors, since there’s nothing defined to assign.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB errors when you try to capture output a function doesn’t provide.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not silently substitute 0.
Incorrect — MATLAB never auto-selects "the last computed value" as an implicit output.
Incorrect — the error is a real MATLAB error, not a string value.

intermediate.question: Which line correctly completes this function so that bmi = computeBMI(70, 1.75) returns a value?
intermediate.explanation: The function’s declared output variable is bmi (from the function bmi = ... signature). The function body must actually assign a value to that exact variable name for it to be returned.
optionExplanations: Correct — this assigns the declared output variable bmi.
Incorrect — this computes a value but never assigns it to bmi, so nothing is returned.
Incorrect — "return bmi = ..." is not valid MATLAB syntax.
Incorrect — print is not a MATLAB function.
intermediate.concept: Assigning a function’s declared output variable
commonMistakes: Computing a result inside a function but never assigning it to the exact output variable name declared in the function signature.

intermediate.question: A single .m file can contain additional local functions below the main function or script, but only the file’s own code can call them — they are not visible from outside that file.
intermediate.explanation: True. Local functions defined at the bottom of a script or function file are private helpers usable only within that same file — other files cannot call them directly.
optionExplanations: Correct — local functions are private to their containing file.
Incorrect — local functions are specifically NOT callable from other files.

intermediate.question: Which debugging control executes the current line and pauses on the next line, without diving into any function calls on that line?
intermediate.explanation: Step (F10) runs the current line as a single unit and pauses on the next line — if that line calls a function, Step treats the call as a black box rather than entering it.
optionExplanations: Correct — Step (F10) runs one line at a time without entering function calls.
Incorrect — Step In (F11) is what dives into a function call.
Incorrect — Continue runs until the next breakpoint or the end.
Incorrect — Stop halts execution entirely, not a single-step control.

intermediate.question: Which debugging control jumps INTO a function being called on the current line, so you can step through its internals?
intermediate.explanation: Step In (F11) descends into the function called on the current line, letting you step through its own lines one at a time.
optionExplanations: Correct — Step In enters the called function.
Incorrect — Step (F10) treats the function call as a single black-box step.
Incorrect — Continue resumes normal execution until the next breakpoint.
Incorrect — Run to Cursor runs to a chosen line, not into a function call specifically.

intermediate.question: You set a breakpoint inside a function called 500 times inside a loop, but only want execution to pause on the 250th call. What MATLAB feature is designed for exactly this?
options: A conditional breakpoint (pauses only when a specified condition, e.g. a counter, is true)
A regular breakpoint (pauses on the 1st call only)
There is no way to do this
intermediate.explanation: A conditional breakpoint only pauses execution when its attached logical condition (e.g., callCount == 250) evaluates to true, letting you skip straight to the case you care about.
optionExplanations: Correct — conditional breakpoints pause only when a condition is met.
Incorrect — a plain breakpoint pauses every single time that line is reached.
Incorrect — font size is unrelated to debugging logic.
Incorrect — MATLAB directly supports this via conditional breakpoints.

intermediate.question: Which of the following are valid ways to view a MATLAB function’s documentation? Select all that apply.
options: help functionName (text in the Command Window)
Hovering over the function name in the Editor to see a quick tooltip
Deleting the function and seeing what error appears
intermediate.explanation: help and doc both display real documentation, and the Editor also offers a quick-help tooltip on hover. Deleting a function tells you nothing about what it does.

intermediate.question: Put these steps in order for a typical breakpoint-based debugging session.
options: Click in the line-number margin to set a breakpoint
Run the script (execution pauses at the breakpoint)
Inspect variable values in the Workspace while paused
Click Continue (F5) or Step (F10) to resume execution
intermediate.explanation: You set the breakpoint first, then run the script so execution pauses there, inspect state while paused, and finally resume with Continue or Step.

intermediate.question: Write the exact MATLAB command to change the current folder to a subfolder named "labdata" (relative to where you currently are).
intermediate.explanation: cd labdata (or cd('labdata')) changes MATLAB’s current folder to the labdata subfolder of wherever you currently are.

intermediate.question: Which best distinguishes help plot from doc plot?
options: help prints plain text directly in the Command Window; doc opens a formatted, searchable window with examples and links
They are identical in every way
help only works for built-in functions; doc only works for user-written ones
doc is faster because it doesn’t show any content
intermediate.explanation: Both show documentation, but help is quick plain text in the Command Window, while doc opens a richer, browsable window — often with runnable examples.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is the key practical difference between the two.
Incorrect — they present the same underlying information very differently.
Incorrect — both work on built-in and appropriately documented user functions alike.
Incorrect — doc opens a full documentation page, not nothing.

advanced.question: You are debugging a script and want to inspect a variable’s value at the exact moment an error occurs, without littering the code with disp statements. Which environment feature should you use?
options: A breakpoint set in the Editor
The Workspace browser, checked after the script finishes running
Increasing the Command Window font size
advanced.explanation: Breakpoints pause execution at a specific line so you can inspect (and even modify) variables in the Workspace at that exact point — far more targeted than adding and removing disp calls.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — Command History only shows past commands, not live variable state.
Correct — a breakpoint halts execution exactly where you need to inspect state.
Incorrect — if the script errors out, the variables at the moment of failure may not survive to be checked afterward, and this doesn’t let you step through line by line.
Incorrect — a cosmetic change with no debugging value.
commonMistakes: Relying only on disp() statements sprinkled through the code instead of using the built-in debugger.

advanced.question: Your script calls a function that lives in a folder MATLAB doesn’t currently search. Which action resolves this?
options: Add the folder to the search path with addpath (or the Set Path dialog)
Rename the script to match the function name
Restart MATLAB and try again with no other changes
Save the script as a .mat file instead of a .m file
advanced.explanation: addpath (or Set Path) tells MATLAB to also look in that folder when resolving function calls — restarting or renaming files does nothing to fix a path problem.
optionExplanations: Correct — this directly adds the folder to MATLAB’s search locations.
Incorrect — the filename of the caller is irrelevant to whether the callee can be found.
Incorrect — restarting doesn’t change which folders are on the path.
Incorrect — .mat files store data, not code, and this would break the script entirely.

advanced.question: Running "clear" to empty the Workspace also deletes the .m script files stored on disk.
advanced.explanation: False. clear only removes variables from memory (the Workspace); it has no effect on files saved on disk.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — clear never touches files on disk.
Correct — clear only affects in-memory variables, not saved script or function files.
commonMistakes: Confusing “clearing memory” with “deleting files” — these are unrelated operations in MATLAB.

advanced.question: Two students both define a variable named "mean" in their Workspace, shadowing the built-in mean function. What is the main risk?
options: Later calls to mean(x) in their script use their variable instead of the built-in function, silently producing wrong results
MATLAB throws an error immediately when a variable named mean is created
Nothing — MATLAB always distinguishes variables and functions automatically, regardless of naming
The built-in mean function is permanently overwritten for all future MATLAB sessions
advanced.explanation: MATLAB resolves a name by checking variables in the current Workspace before built-in functions. If a variable named mean exists, mean(x) attempts to index into that variable instead of calling the built-in function — a common, silent source of bugs.
optionExplanations: Correct — the variable shadows the function for the rest of that Workspace’s life.
Incorrect — MATLAB allows this assignment with no error or warning.
Incorrect — this is exactly the ambiguity that causes the bug.
Incorrect — the shadowing only affects the current Workspace/session, not MATLAB itself.
commonMistakes: Naming a variable after a common built-in function (mean, sum, size, etc.) and being surprised when that function stops working later in the same script.

advanced.question: A script runs fine from your Editor but throws "Undefined function" when a colleague runs it on their computer. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A function it depends on isn’t on the colleague’s MATLAB search path
MATLAB licenses are computer-specific, so functions vary machine to machine
The colleague’s MATLAB version doesn’t support user-defined functions at all
Scripts are never allowed to call functions defined in separate files
advanced.explanation: A very common cause of "Undefined function" errors when sharing code is that a helper function file wasn’t shared along with the script, or the folder it’s in isn’t on the colleague’s path — MATLAB simply can’t find it.
optionExplanations: Correct — a missing file or missing path entry is the most common cause.
Incorrect — MATLAB licensing doesn’t control which user-written functions exist.
Incorrect — user-defined functions are a core, universally supported MATLAB feature.
Incorrect — calling functions defined in other files is completely normal and expected.
advanced.concept: Sharing code that depends on custom functions
commonMistakes: Sharing only the main script and forgetting to include the helper function files it depends on.

advanced.question: A student writes a function starting with "function y = myFunc(x)" but saves the file as my_function.m. What happens when they call myFunc(5) from the Command Window (the folder is on the path)?
options: MATLAB errors because it looks for a file named myFunc.m, not my_function.m — the file name must match the function name
MATLAB still finds and runs it correctly, because it reads the function keyword inside the file
MATLAB renames the file automatically to match
MATLAB runs whichever function happens to be defined first, regardless of file name
advanced.explanation: MATLAB primarily resolves a top-level function call by file name — calling myFunc looks specifically for myFunc.m. A mismatched file name like my_function.m means that call fails to find it.
optionExplanations: Correct — the file name, not the internal declaration, is what MATLAB searches for.
Incorrect — the internal function keyword line does not override file-name-based resolution for this call.
Incorrect — MATLAB never renames files automatically.
Incorrect — there’s no other same-named function here to fall back to.
advanced.concept: File name vs. declared function name
commonMistakes: Saving a function file under a different name than the function it declares.

advanced.question: You have loadECG.m in your current folder and ecg_patient01.csv inside a subfolder called data. Running the script gives "file not found" even though the file exists. What’s most likely wrong?
options: The script references the file by name only, and MATLAB’s current folder doesn’t include the data subfolder in that reference
CSV files cannot be read by MATLAB at all
The script must be renamed to match the data file
ECG data requires a special toolbox just to be found on disk
advanced.explanation: If the script tries to open a bare filename like "ecg_patient01.csv" rather than "data/ecg_patient01.csv" (or the equivalent full path), MATLAB looks in the current folder, not the data subfolder, and won’t find it.
optionExplanations: Correct — a missing subfolder in the referenced path is the classic cause.
Incorrect — MATLAB reads CSV files natively (e.g., with readtable or csvread).
Incorrect — script and data file names don’t need to match.
Incorrect — finding a file on disk doesn’t require a special toolbox.
advanced.concept: Relative file paths and the current folder

advanced.question: A user expects this to return a BMI value, but x = computeBMI(70, 1.75) throws an error about an unassigned output. What’s the bug?
options: The declared output variable is "bmi" (lowercase), but the calculation assigns to "BMI" (capitalized) — MATLAB is case-sensitive, so bmi itself is never actually assigned
weight and height must be swapped
The function is simply missing a semicolon
advanced.explanation: MATLAB is case-sensitive, so BMI and bmi are two entirely different variables. The function declares bmi as its output but only ever assigns BMI, so bmi is left unassigned and MATLAB errors when the function tries to return it.
optionExplanations: Correct — the case mismatch means the declared output is never actually assigned.
Incorrect — the argument order is irrelevant to this particular error.
Incorrect — height^2 is perfectly valid MATLAB syntax.
Incorrect — a missing semicolon would cause unwanted printing, not this specific "unassigned output" error.
advanced.concept: Case sensitivity in function output variables
commonMistakes: Assigning a result to a variable whose capitalization doesn’t exactly match the function’s declared output name.

advanced.question: A teammate’s script works for them, but fails for you with "Undefined function or variable applesToOranges" — a name that appears nowhere in the code they showed you. What’s a likely explanation?
options: Their script calls a local/helper function defined lower in their actual file that wasn’t included when they shared just a snippet with you
MATLAB has a bug that randomly invents function names
The function only exists on certain days of the week
advanced.explanation: If you were only shown part of a file (or a different file than the one actually being run), a helper function it depends on may simply be missing from what you have — not evidence of a MATLAB bug.
optionExplanations: Correct — an incomplete copy of the code is the most realistic explanation.
Incorrect — MATLAB doesn’t invent function names.
Incorrect — function availability has nothing to do with the day.
Incorrect — reinstalling MATLAB wouldn’t create a missing helper function.
advanced.concept: Diagnosing missing dependencies from shared code

advanced.question: A script behaves differently depending on which computer it runs on. Which of the following are legitimate causes to investigate? Select all that apply.
options: Different current folders, so relative file paths resolve differently
Different items on the MATLAB search path — a required helper function present on one machine, missing on another
Leftover variables in the Workspace from a previous session on one machine
MATLAB always produces identical results everywhere, so this cannot be MATLAB-related
advanced.explanation: Differing current folders, differing paths, and leftover Workspace state are all real, common causes of machine-to-machine differences in behavior.

advanced.question: If two functions with the exact same name are both on the path (in different folders), MATLAB will only ever use one of them and does not raise an error about the conflict by default.
advanced.explanation: True. MATLAB silently resolves to whichever same-named function it finds first in its search order, without warning about the duplicate by default.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB resolves silently to one of them, with no automatic conflict warning.
Incorrect — this genuinely happens silently, which is exactly why it can be a confusing bug.
advanced.concept: Silent name conflicts on the path

advanced.question: Given two same-named functions both on the path, what is the safest way to find out which one currently takes priority, without deleting either file?
options: Use which functionName to see exactly which file MATLAB currently resolves to
Guess based on which folder is alphabetically first
Rename both files to something random
Assume MATLAB always uses the one in the current folder
advanced.explanation: which functionName reports the exact file path MATLAB will use for that call — the direct way to resolve the ambiguity instead of guessing.
optionExplanations: Correct — which directly answers the question.
Incorrect — alphabetical order has nothing to do with MATLAB’s resolution order.
Incorrect — renaming risks breaking other code that depends on the original names.
Incorrect — the current folder is usually checked first, but this isn’t guaranteed in every configuration — which is what actually confirms it.
advanced.concept: Using which to resolve name conflicts

advanced.question: A loop analyzing 20 patients works but a code reviewer flags it as inefficient. What tool would quantify exactly how much time it costs relative to the rest of the script?
options: The MATLAB Profiler (profile on / profile viewer)
advanced.explanation: The Profiler measures exactly how much time is spent in each line and function call, replacing guesswork with data when deciding what’s worth optimizing.
optionExplanations: Correct — the Profiler is built specifically for this purpose.
Incorrect — Command History doesn’t measure execution time.
Incorrect — the Workspace shows variable values, not timing.
Incorrect — font size has no effect on performance measurement.

advanced.question: You want to compare two versions of a script side by side to see exactly which lines differ, before merging changes with a labmate’s copy. What’s the most appropriate approach?
options: Use the Editor’s built-in Compare feature (select both files → Compare)
Manually read both files character by character
Delete one version and hope you picked the right one
advanced.explanation: The MATLAB Editor includes a built-in file Compare tool that highlights exactly which lines differ between two files, far more reliable than manual comparison.
optionExplanations: Correct — Compare is built specifically for this.
Incorrect — manual comparison is slow and error-prone.
Incorrect — deleting a version without comparing risks losing real work.
Incorrect — renaming doesn’t reveal any actual differences.

advanced.question: Closing an Editor tab for a script with unsaved changes will prompt you to save before those changes are discarded.
advanced.explanation: True. MATLAB prompts you to save unsaved changes when you try to close a modified file, rather than silently discarding your work.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB prompts before discarding unsaved changes.
Incorrect — this safety prompt is standard MATLAB Editor behavior.

advanced.question: Which of these are genuine advantages of a breakpoint over scattering disp() statements throughout a script while debugging? Select all that apply.
options: You can inspect any variable’s current value interactively, not just the ones you remembered to disp
You don’t have to remember to remove temporary disp() calls afterward
disp() statements always run measurably faster than breakpoints
Breakpoints let you step through execution one line at a time
advanced.explanation: Breakpoints offer interactive, on-demand inspection and step-through control, and don’t leave leftover debug code behind. Relative execution speed of disp() vs. breakpoints isn’t a meaningful reason to prefer one debugging approach over the other.

advanced.question: A drug-trial analysis script errors on a colleague’s laptop: "Undefined function readTrialData". On your machine, that function lives in a Utilities folder you added to the path months ago and forgot about. What’s the most likely fix?
options: Share the Utilities folder with your colleague (or include it in the same project folder) so they can add it to their path too
Tell your colleague to reinstall MATLAB
There is no fix; the script must be rewritten from scratch
advanced.explanation: The function simply isn’t available to your colleague because its folder was never shared. Sharing the folder (and adding it to their path, or bundling it with the project) resolves it directly.
optionExplanations: Correct — sharing the missing folder/function directly addresses the cause.
Incorrect — reinstalling MATLAB does not add a missing personal helper function.
Incorrect — renaming would just break the function-file-name match.
Incorrect — rewriting from scratch isn’t necessary; the fix is straightforward.

advanced.question: Which line correctly completes this function so it returns the mean of the input vector readings?
advanced.explanation: The declared output is avgBP, so the body must assign the computed mean to that exact variable for it to be returned to the caller.
optionExplanations: Correct — this assigns the declared output variable.
Incorrect — computing the mean without assigning it to avgBP means nothing is returned.
Incorrect — "return mean(...)" is not valid MATLAB syntax.
Incorrect — disp() only prints the value; it doesn’t return it as the function’s output.
advanced.concept: Assigning a function’s declared output variable

advanced.question: A conditional breakpoint’s condition is written as a normal MATLAB logical expression (e.g., i == 250), evaluated fresh every time execution reaches that line.
advanced.explanation: True. Each time execution reaches the breakpointed line, MATLAB evaluates the attached condition and only pauses if it’s currently true.
optionExplanations: Correct — the condition is a standard logical expression re-checked every time.
Incorrect — this is exactly how conditional breakpoints work.

advanced.question: You’re stepping through a loop with the debugger and want to skip ahead to right before its 50th iteration, without manually pressing Step 50 times. What’s the most efficient approach?
options: Set a conditional breakpoint on the loop line with a condition like i == 50, then Continue (F5)
Press Step (F10) exactly 50 times, counting carefully
There is no way to do this
advanced.explanation: A conditional breakpoint lets you jump directly to the iteration you care about, instead of manually stepping through every prior iteration.
optionExplanations: Correct — this reaches iteration 50 in one Continue, not 50 manual steps.
Incorrect — this works but is slow and error-prone compared to a conditional breakpoint.
Incorrect — restarting MATLAB has nothing to do with loop iteration.
Incorrect — MATLAB directly supports this via conditional breakpoints.

advanced.question: Which of the following statements about MATLAB’s current folder are true? Select all that apply.
options: Scripts and files are found more easily when the current folder matches (or is on the path with) the folder they live in
Changing the current folder changes which files MATLAB can reference by a bare filename (without a full path)
The current folder is fixed at MATLAB’s installation location and can never be changed
Files in the current folder do not need to be explicitly added to the path to be run directly
advanced.explanation: The current folder directly affects bare-filename resolution and access, and files in it are usable without an explicit addpath. It is absolutely changeable at any time — it has nothing to do with the fixed installation location.

advanced.question: This function is missing something a careful MATLAB programmer would add. What, and why does it matter here?
options: A semicolon after the calculation — without it, every call to celsiusToF also prints "out = ..." to the Command Window as an unwanted side effect
The function needs an explicit return statement
c must be converted to a string first
9/5 should be written as 1.8, or the function won’t work
advanced.explanation: A missing semicolon inside a function has the same suppression effect as in a script — without it, every single call echoes the result, which is almost always undesirable inside a function meant to just quietly return a value.
optionExplanations: Correct — the missing semicolon causes unwanted output on every call.
Incorrect — MATLAB functions don’t use an explicit return statement; assigning the output variable is enough.
Incorrect — c is used numerically here and doesn’t need string conversion.
Incorrect — 9/5 and 1.8 are numerically identical in MATLAB; both work.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a missing semicolon inside a function causes output on every single call, not just once.

advanced.question: Two labmates each keep their own slightly different copy of a shared analysis script, with no shared folder or version control. Months later, no one can tell which version is "correct." What practice would have prevented this?
options: Keeping a single shared copy of the script (e.g., in a shared folder or version-controlled repository) instead of independent local copies
Using more comments in each copy
advanced.explanation: The root problem is divergent, uncoordinated copies — a single shared source of truth (a shared folder or version control) avoids this entirely.
optionExplanations: Correct — a single shared source avoids divergence in the first place.
Incorrect — comments don’t prevent copies from silently diverging.
Incorrect — renaming doesn’t address the underlying duplication problem.
Incorrect — unrelated to the actual issue.

advanced.question: MATLAB’s Code Analyzer (the tool behind the wavy underlines in the Editor) can flag likely problems — like an unused variable or a missing semicolon leading to unintended output — before you even run the script.
advanced.explanation: True. The Code Analyzer runs continuously in the background as you type, flagging likely issues statically, without needing to actually execute the code.
optionExplanations: Correct — Code Analyzer checks statically, before execution.
Incorrect — this static analysis is a real, always-on Editor feature.

advanced.question: A script processing 50 patient files works fine for files 1–30, then errors on file 31, halting the run and losing the already-computed results. What tool would help find exactly which line in file 31’s processing fails?
options: A breakpoint (or dbstop if error) to pause execution right at the point of failure and inspect the Workspace
Guessing based on the file number alone
Deleting file 31 and never examining it
Increasing the Command Window font size
advanced.explanation: Pausing execution exactly where the failure occurs (via a breakpoint, or the dbstop if error command that automatically stops at any uncaught error) lets you inspect real variable values at the moment things went wrong, rather than guessing.
optionExplanations: Correct — this directly reveals the failing line and its live variable state.
Incorrect — guessing isn’t a reliable diagnostic method.
Incorrect — deleting the file loses the chance to actually understand or fix the problem.
Incorrect — font size has no diagnostic value.

expert.question: A script runs correctly the first time, but running it again immediately afterward (with no input changed) produces different output. What is the most likely root cause?
options: A leftover variable from the previous run is still in the Workspace and is being reused instead of being freshly (re)initialized inside the script
MATLAB scripts are designed to produce randomized output on every run
The Command Window must be fully restarted between every script run
MATLAB caches and reuses the results of the previous run automatically
expert.explanation: If a script assumes a variable starts out undefined or reset (e.g., an accumulator) but a stale value is left over from a previous run, results can silently depend on run history. A defensive habit is to start scripts with clear (or explicitly initialize every variable the script uses) so behavior doesn’t depend on the Workspace’s prior state.
optionExplanations: Correct — reused Workspace state is the classic cause of this kind of non-reproducibility.
Incorrect — MATLAB code is deterministic unless it explicitly calls a random-number function.
Incorrect — restarting the Command Window isn’t required; the real fix is not depending on leftover state.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not silently cache and reuse results between separate runs.
expert.concept: Reproducibility and Workspace state
commonMistakes: Relying on Workspace state carrying over between runs instead of explicitly initializing every variable a script needs.

expert.question: A folder contains both "analysis.m" and an old copy "analysis_OLD.m", and both happen to define a function called processData. Calling processData(x) uses whichever one MATLAB finds first on the path — silently. Which command tells you exactly which file will actually run?
expert.explanation: which reports the full file path of the function MATLAB will actually call, which is exactly what’s needed to resolve this kind of shadowing/duplicate-name ambiguity.
optionExplanations: Correct — which resolves and reports exactly which file will run.
Incorrect — help shows documentation for whichever file which would resolve to, but doesn’t itself tell you which one that is.
Incorrect — type displays a file’s source code, again for whichever one is resolved — it doesn’t reveal the resolution itself.
Incorrect — whos lists variables in the Workspace, not information about functions.
expert.concept: Resolving function name ambiguity

expert.question: A teammate says a script "isn’t working." Which of the following are appropriate first debugging steps using MATLAB’s built-in tools, before rewriting any code? Select all that apply.
options: Set a breakpoint near where the problem is suspected and step through execution
Read the exact error message and line number reported in the Command Window
Immediately rewrite the entire script from scratch
Use which to confirm the correct version of any custom function is actually being called
expert.explanation: Breakpoints, reading the actual error message/line, and confirming which file a function resolves to are all targeted, low-cost diagnostic steps. Rewriting from scratch skips diagnosis entirely and risks losing whatever in the code was actually working.
expert.concept: Systematic debugging workflow

expert.question: You’re preparing a MATLAB script that a lab partner will run days later, on a shared lab computer, to analyze patient heart-rate data. Which practice most reduces the chance it silently fails or gives wrong results in that future session?
options: Start the script with clear, clc, and explicit initialization of every variable it uses, rather than relying on whatever happens to already be in the Workspace
Never use semicolons, so every intermediate result is printed
Give every variable the same name for simplicity
Avoid writing comments so the script loads faster
expert.explanation: A script that starts from a known, clean state (no leftover variables, nothing assumed to already exist) behaves the same way regardless of what a previous user left in the Workspace — critical for a script meant to be reused by someone else later.
optionExplanations: Correct — starting from a clean, explicit state is what makes a script reliably reproducible for someone else.
Incorrect — this only affects what gets printed, not correctness or reliability.
Incorrect — reusing one variable name for everything guarantees bugs, not simplicity.
Incorrect — comments don’t meaningfully affect load time and remove important context for future users.
expert.concept: Writing reproducible, shareable scripts

expert.question: Because MATLAB manages memory automatically, it is never necessary to use clear at the start of a script, even in a shared, long-running MATLAB session.
expert.explanation: False. Automatic memory management has nothing to do with this risk — stale variables left in the Workspace from earlier work can still silently affect a script that assumes a clean starting state. Starting with clear (or explicitly initializing what you’re about to use) is a common defensive habit, especially in shared or long-running sessions.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — this conflates memory management with Workspace state correctness, which are unrelated concerns.
Correct — clear (or explicit initialization) remains a useful defensive habit regardless of automatic memory management.
expert.concept: Workspace hygiene vs. memory management

expert.question: You inherit a legacy pipeline: 40 .m files, no README, deeply nested function calls, and several duplicate function names in different subfolders. Where should you start to build a reliable mental model of what actually runs?
options: Use which (or which -all) on key function names to resolve exactly which file each call reaches, then trace forward from the main script
Delete all subfolders except one and hope nothing breaks
expert.explanation: Before changing anything, confirming exactly which file each ambiguous call currently resolves to gives you an accurate starting map — guessing or deleting risks destroying a working (if messy) system.
optionExplanations: Correct — resolving ambiguity first is the systematic starting point.
Incorrect — rewriting blind, without understanding what currently works, is extremely risky.
Incorrect — deleting subfolders without understanding dependencies risks breaking the pipeline.
Incorrect — renaming everything first, before understanding the structure, adds risk without benefit.
expert.concept: Auditing an unfamiliar legacy codebase

expert.question: A collaborator’s script fails only when run twice in a row in the same session, never after a fresh restart. What’s the most systematic way to isolate the cause, without guessing?
options: Add clear at the top of the script and see whether the failure still reproduces on a fresh MATLAB session — if it does, the bug is in the script’s own logic; if not, it depends on leftover Workspace state
Restart the entire computer every time before running
Rename the script and hope the problem goes away
expert.explanation: This is a controlled experiment: forcing a clean state at the start isolates whether the bug lives in the script’s own logic or depends on accumulated Workspace state from repeated runs.
optionExplanations: Correct — this directly isolates the two possible root causes.
Incorrect — restarting the whole computer is unnecessary overhead that doesn’t isolate anything additional.
Incorrect — renaming the file has no effect on the underlying logic or state issue.
Incorrect — an intermittent bug will eventually cause a real, hard-to-trace failure; it shouldn’t be ignored.
expert.concept: Isolating state-dependent bugs

expert.question: You’re preparing a pipeline a future student (who has never seen your code) will run unsupervised on new patient data. Which practices genuinely reduce the risk of silently wrong results? Select all that apply.
options: Starting the main script with clear and clc
Adding comments explaining non-obvious assumptions (units, expected file format, etc.)
Hardcoding your personal file paths (e.g., C:\Users\YourName\...) so it "just works" the exact way you had it
Checking inputs with assert() or clear error messages when a file or format doesn’t match expectations
expert.explanation: A clean starting state, documented assumptions, and explicit input validation all genuinely reduce silent-failure risk. Hardcoding personal file paths is the opposite of portable — it will break the moment anyone else runs it.
expert.concept: Writing pipelines for unsupervised future use

expert.question: Your lab’s shared folder has both computeStats.m (from last year) and a newer computeStats_v2.m. A script still calls computeStats, and you’re unsure whether it runs the old logic. How do you verify EXACTLY what code is running, without modifying any files?
options: Use type computeStats (or open the file resolved by which) to read the exact source code currently being used for that call
Assume it’s the newer one, since that’s usually intended
Run the whole pipeline and hope the output looks reasonable
expert.explanation: type (or which followed by opening the resolved file) shows you the exact source code MATLAB is actually using — the only way to be certain rather than assuming.
optionExplanations: Correct — this directly confirms the actual code being executed.
Incorrect — assuming intent isn’t the same as verifying actual behavior.
Incorrect — guessing provides no real certainty.
Incorrect — "looking reasonable" doesn’t confirm which logic actually ran.
expert.concept: Verifying which version of code is executing

expert.question: Renaming a function’s .m file on disk does NOT automatically update the function declaration line inside the file — you must edit that line yourself, or the file name and the declared function name will no longer match.
expert.explanation: True. Renaming a file is purely a file-system operation; MATLAB never reaches into the file to update its contents for you.
optionExplanations: Correct — renaming a file never edits its contents.
Incorrect — file renaming and file content are entirely separate operations in any file system, MATLAB included.
expert.concept: File renaming does not update file contents

expert.question: You inherit a script that takes 40 minutes, and you’re told a colleague’s "equivalent" version takes 90 seconds. Before touching a single line of code, what is the professionally correct first step?
options: Profile the slow script (profile on / profile viewer) to find out exactly where the 40 minutes is actually being spent
Immediately start rewriting the entire script line by line
Assume it’s a loop and vectorize everything without checking
Ask MATLAB support to fix it for you
expert.explanation: Optimizing based on assumptions often targets the wrong code entirely. Profiling first tells you exactly where the time is going, so effort goes where it actually matters.
optionExplanations: Correct — measure before optimizing.
Incorrect — rewriting blind risks wasted effort on code that wasn’t actually the bottleneck.
Incorrect — assuming the cause without data is exactly the mistake profiling avoids.
Incorrect — this is a workflow decision you should make yourself, informed by data.
expert.concept: Profile before optimizing

expert.question: compute_BMI (shown below) has no logic bug, but calling it inside "for p = 1:500, bmiResults(p) = compute_BMI(w(p), h(p)); end" floods the Command Window with 500 lines of output and runs noticeably slower. Why?
options: The line inside compute_BMI has no semicolon, so MATLAB echoes the result on every single one of the 500 calls
for loops always print output regardless of what they contain
bmiResults must be preallocated for the output to be silent
expert.explanation: A missing semicolon inside a frequently-called function has a compounding cost: it prints on every single call, not just once — here, 500 unwanted print statements plus the real (if modest) overhead of that extra printing.
optionExplanations: Correct — the missing semicolon inside the function is echoed on every call.
Incorrect — for loops don’t inherently print anything; only unsuppressed statements inside them do.
Incorrect — preallocation affects performance, not whether output prints.
Incorrect — height ^ 2 is valid MATLAB syntax.
expert.concept: Compounding cost of missing semicolons in frequently-called functions
commonMistakes: Not noticing that a small oversight (a missing semicolon) inside a helper function scales into a real problem when that function is called hundreds of times.

expert.question: Because scripts share the base Workspace, calling a script 500 times inside a loop can behave very differently from calling an equivalent function 500 times, since the script’s internal variables persist and accumulate across the whole loop, unlike a function’s private workspace which resets on every call.
expert.explanation: True. A script has no private scope of its own — it operates directly in the base Workspace, so variables it sets stick around and can leak into the next iteration, unlike a function whose local variables are discarded when it returns.
optionExplanations: Correct — this state-persistence distinction is a real practical difference.
Incorrect — this behavioral difference between scripts and functions is real and matters in loops.
expert.concept: Practical consequences of script vs. function scope

expert.question: A senior researcher advises wrapping risky file-loading code in try/catch so one missing patient file doesn’t crash an entire 500-file batch analysis. From a workflow (not syntax) perspective, which are genuine benefits? Select all that apply.
options: The rest of the batch can continue even if one file is missing or malformed
You can log which specific files failed and revisit them later, instead of losing all progress
It completely eliminates the need to ever test your code
It converts what would be a hard stop (an uncaught error killing the whole run) into a recoverable, reportable event
expert.explanation: try/catch keeps a batch job resilient and lets you track/report failures, turning crashes into recoverable events. It does not remove the need for testing — it just changes how failures are handled once they occur.
expert.concept: Workflow benefits of error handling in batch jobs

expert.question: Several of a lab’s shared scripts define nearly identical helper logic independently, copy-pasted with small tweaks each time. What environment-level change would most reduce this problem going forward?
options: Extract the shared logic into one common function file, kept in a shared folder that every relevant script’s path includes
Ask everyone to copy-paste more carefully
Rename all the duplicated code blocks to have unique variable names
Increase everyone’s font size for readability
expert.explanation: Consolidating duplicated logic into one shared function eliminates the divergence risk entirely — a fix at the codebase-organization level, not just careful copy-pasting.
optionExplanations: Correct — a single shared function removes the duplication itself.
Incorrect — "more carefully" doesn’t prevent the underlying structural problem.
Incorrect — unique variable names don’t address duplicated logic.
Incorrect — unrelated to the actual issue.
expert.concept: Consolidating duplicated logic

expert.question: Using dbstop if error causes MATLAB to automatically pause and enter debug mode at the exact line where an uncaught error occurs, rather than simply printing the error and stopping.
expert.explanation: True. dbstop if error tells MATLAB to break into the debugger right at the failing line whenever an uncaught error happens, so you can inspect the Workspace at the exact moment of failure.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is exactly what dbstop if error does.
Incorrect — this is a real, standard MATLAB debugging command.
expert.concept: dbstop if error

expert.question: A script processing ECG recordings throws an error deep inside a helper function three calls deep from the main script. What does the error message’s stack trace tell you?
options: The exact chain of function calls active when the error occurred, letting you trace from the main script down to the precise line that failed
Nothing useful — stack traces are only for advanced programmers
Which patient the data belongs to
How long the script has been running
expert.explanation: A stack trace lists every function call that was active at the moment of the error, from the outermost call down to where it actually failed — invaluable for tracing multi-level failures.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is precisely what a stack trace shows.
Incorrect — stack traces are useful at any experience level, including for beginners learning to read errors.
Incorrect — a stack trace has nothing to do with patient identity.
Incorrect — a stack trace doesn’t report execution duration.
expert.concept: Reading error stack traces

expert.question: Which of the following are legitimate reasons a script might behave correctly for one patient’s data file but error for another’s, even though the code itself never changed? Select all that apply.
options: The second file has an unexpected format (missing column, extra header row, different units) the code didn’t anticipate
The second file happens to trigger an edge case in the logic (e.g., a value of exactly zero causing a division by zero elsewhere)
MATLAB code always behaves identically regardless of input, so this cannot happen
The second file simply has a different filename
expert.explanation: Unexpected data formatting and edge-case-triggering values are genuine, common causes of input-dependent failures. Code behavior absolutely depends on its input, and a different filename alone (assuming it’s still found and loaded correctly) has no bearing on behavior.
expert.concept: Input-dependent failures

expert.question: You need to hand off a finished project — a main script, six helper functions across two subfolders, and a data folder — to a labmate. Which practice best ensures it runs correctly on their computer with minimal troubleshooting?
options: Share the entire project folder (not just the main script), with setup notes on any needed addpath calls — or add relative addpath calls to the top of the main script itself
Share only the main script file and let them figure out the rest
Rename all the helper functions to be shorter
Tell them to just guess the folder structure
expert.explanation: Sharing the complete, self-contained project (with either clear setup instructions or self-configuring relative addpath calls) is what actually lets someone else run it without extensive back-and-forth.
optionExplanations: Correct — a complete, documented (or self-configuring) project is the reliable handoff.
Incorrect — sharing only the main script omits its actual dependencies.
Incorrect — shorter names don’t address missing dependencies.
Incorrect — guessing wastes time and invites errors.
expert.concept: Handing off a multi-file project

expert.question: If a shared script needs a specific subfolder on the path every time it runs, adding an addpath call (relative to the script’s own location, not a hardcoded personal path) near the top of the script is more portable than requiring every user to manually configure their path first.
expert.explanation: True. A self-configuring, relative addpath call travels with the script and works on any machine, whereas requiring manual per-user setup is fragile and easy to forget.
optionExplanations: Correct — self-configuring, relative path setup is more portable.
Incorrect — requiring manual setup from every user is exactly the fragile approach this practice avoids.
expert.concept: Portable path configuration

expert.question: A code reviewer flags this function as a silent-error risk in a biomedical pipeline (e.g., normalizing a concentration by dividing by a baseline reading), even though it runs without error. Why?
options: Silently returning 0 when the denominator is 0 can be mathematically indistinguishable from a legitimate result of 0, hiding a real data problem instead of surfacing it
Division is not allowed inside MATLAB functions
The function is missing a semicolon
if/else is not valid inside a function
expert.explanation: A baseline reading of exactly 0 is almost certainly a data problem (a broken sensor, a missing measurement), not a legitimate value to divide by. Quietly returning 0 in that case hides the problem instead of surfacing it — a genuine error, warning, or NaN would be more honest here.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is exactly the kind of silent-failure design risk being flagged.
Incorrect — division is completely normal inside a function.
Incorrect — the missing-semicolon issue is unrelated to this specific concern.
Incorrect — if/else is fully valid inside functions.
expert.concept: Silent failure design risk

expert.question: analyze.m exists both on your Desktop and inside your shared project folder (which is on the path). You open the Desktop copy in the Editor and click Run. Which version actually executes, and why?
options: The Desktop copy — running from the Editor executes the specific open file you clicked Run on, regardless of what else with the same name exists on the path
The project folder copy, because path entries always take priority over open files
MATLAB refuses to run, due to the naming conflict
A merged combination of both files
expert.explanation: Clicking Run in the Editor runs the specific file that is open and active — it does not go searching the path for a same-named alternative.
optionExplanations: Correct — the explicitly opened and run file is what executes.
Incorrect — path-based resolution applies to calling a function/script BY NAME, not to directly running an open file.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not refuse to run due to a same-named file elsewhere.
Incorrect — MATLAB never merges two files together.
expert.concept: Running an open file vs. name-based path resolution

expert.question: You want a shared script’s behavior to be fully reproducible for a lab report — any labmate running it gets identical results. Which of these matter for that goal? Select all that apply.
options: Starting from a clean Workspace (e.g., clear at the top) so no leftover variables leak in
Not depending on any variable that must be manually set in the Command Window before running
Using consistent, version-controlled input data files rather than "whatever happens to be in the folder right now"
expert.explanation: A clean starting state, no hidden manual prerequisites, and stable, consistent inputs are all genuinely necessary for reproducibility. Variable naming aesthetics don’t affect whether results are reproducible.
expert.concept: Requirements for reproducible results

expert.question: A script that calls input() to ask the user for a value cannot be run unattended (e.g., in a batch job or scheduled task) without modification, because it will pause and wait for keyboard input that will never come.
expert.explanation: True. input() blocks execution until someone types a response — in an unattended/scheduled context with no one watching, that wait never ends, effectively hanging the job.
optionExplanations: Correct — input() genuinely blocks waiting for a keyboard response.
Incorrect — this blocking behavior is exactly why input() is incompatible with unattended runs as written.
expert.concept: input() and unattended/batch execution

expert.question: You’re finalizing a pipeline that will run nightly and unattended to process incoming patient monitor data, with no one watching the Command Window. Considering everything about scripts, functions, the Workspace, breakpoints, and error handling, what is the single most important property for this specific use case?
options: The pipeline must never pause waiting for interactive input (no input(), no active breakpoints) and must handle unexpected file/data problems gracefully (e.g., via try/catch and logging) rather than silently hanging or crashing the whole run
The pipeline should use the smallest possible font size
The pipeline should avoid using functions entirely
The pipeline should always be opened in the Editor and never run directly
expert.explanation: For an unattended, unsupervised run, the two properties that matter most are: nothing that can silently block waiting for a human, and graceful, logged handling of unexpected problems instead of a hard crash that no one is there to notice or fix.
optionExplanations: Correct — this synthesizes the key unattended-execution requirements from across the topic.
Incorrect — font size has no bearing on unattended execution.
Incorrect — avoiding functions entirely would make the pipeline harder to maintain, not more reliable.
Incorrect — an unattended job typically runs via a scheduler, not by someone manually opening the Editor.
expert.concept: Designing for unattended, unsupervised execution

beginner.question: Which of the following is a valid MATLAB variable name?
beginner.explanation: Variable names must start with a letter and may contain letters, digits, and underscores. "2ndValue" starts with a digit, "my-value" contains a hyphen (interpreted as minus), and "for" is a reserved keyword.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — variable names cannot start with a digit.
Correct — starts with a letter and uses only letters and an underscore.
Incorrect — the hyphen would be parsed as subtraction, not part of the name.
Incorrect — "for" is a reserved MATLAB keyword and cannot be used as a variable name.
commonMistakes: Trying to name a variable after a reserved word like for, if, or end.

beginner.question: What is displayed in the Command Window after this code runs?
beginner.explanation: The first two lines end in semicolons and produce no output. The third line has no semicolon, so MATLAB echoes the variable name and its value: "c = 7".
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB prints "c = 7" because the last line has no semicolon.
Incorrect — MATLAB shows the variable name and computed value, not the literal expression text.
Incorrect — MATLAB always echoes the variable name along with its value, not just the number.
Incorrect — only the first two lines are suppressed; the third is not.

beginner.question: In MATLAB, "%" begins a comment that continues to the end of the line.
beginner.explanation: True. Everything after a % on a line is ignored by MATLAB and treated as a comment.
optionExplanations: Correct — % marks the rest of the line as a comment.
Incorrect — % is exactly MATLAB’s single-line comment character.
