beginner.question: What does 3 + 4 * 2 evaluate to in MATLAB, using standard operator precedence?
beginner.explanation: Multiplication is evaluated before addition, so 4 * 2 = 8 is computed first, then 3 + 8 = 11.

beginner.question: MATLAB variable names are case-sensitive, so "Score" and "score" refer to two different variables.
beginner.explanation: True. MATLAB distinguishes uppercase and lowercase letters in identifiers, so Score and score are two completely separate variables.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB is case-sensitive.
Incorrect — case matters throughout MATLAB, including variable names.

beginner.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid MATLAB variable name?
beginner.explanation: Variable names must start with a letter, not an underscore. "_start" is invalid for that reason; the other three all start with a letter and use only letters, digits, and underscores.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — this is valid: starts with a letter, uses only letters, digits, and an underscore.
Correct — invalid, because a MATLAB name cannot start with an underscore.
Incorrect — this is valid: starts with a letter, mixes case and a digit.
Incorrect — a single letter is a perfectly valid name.

beginner.question: A MATLAB variable name can contain a space, such as "my var".
beginner.explanation: False. MATLAB variable names cannot contain spaces — use an underscore instead, e.g. my_var.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — a space is not a legal character in a MATLAB identifier.
Correct — spaces are not allowed in variable names; MATLAB would treat "my" and "var" as two separate tokens.

beginner.question: What is displayed after this code runs?
options: Error: must assign the result to a variable
beginner.explanation: When an expression is evaluated but not assigned to a variable, MATLAB automatically stores it in a built-in variable called ans and echoes it (since there is no semicolon).
optionExplanations: Correct — unassigned results are automatically stored in ans and displayed as "ans = 5".
Incorrect — MATLAB does not echo the literal expression text as a variable name.
Incorrect — MATLAB always shows the variable name (ans, in this case) along with the value.
Incorrect — no assignment is required; MATLAB happily evaluates and displays via ans.

beginner.question: What is displayed after typing just "pi" (with no semicolon) at the Command Window?
beginner.explanation: pi is a built-in MATLAB function that returns an approximation of π. Since it isn’t assigned to a variable, the result is stored in ans and displayed in the default format short style (4 decimal places): "ans = 3.1416".
optionExplanations: Correct — the unassigned result goes into ans, displayed with 4 decimal places by default.
Incorrect — the displayed name is ans, not pi, since pi itself was not reassigned.
Incorrect — pi is a valid, predefined MATLAB function.
Incorrect — this is format long precision, not the default format short display.

beginner.question: MATLAB has a built-in pi that returns an approximation of π; it is not a reserved keyword and can technically be overwritten by assigning your own value to it.
beginner.explanation: True. pi is an ordinary built-in function, not a protected keyword like for or end, so a script could legally (though inadvisably) reassign it with something like pi = 3;.
optionExplanations: Correct — pi behaves like any other function name and can be shadowed by a variable of the same name.
Incorrect — pi has no special protection against being overwritten.
beginner.concept: Built-in constants are not reserved words

beginner.question: What does 10 - 3 * 2 evaluate to in MATLAB?
beginner.explanation: Multiplication happens before subtraction: 3 * 2 = 6 is computed first, then 10 - 6 = 4.

beginner.question: Which pair of symbols marks a block (multi-line) comment in MATLAB?
beginner.explanation: %{ on its own line starts a block comment, and %} on its own line ends it — everything between is ignored, spanning multiple lines.
optionExplanations: Correct — %{ and %} (each alone on its own line) delimit a MATLAB block comment.
Incorrect — that is the block-comment syntax in C, Java, and similar languages, not MATLAB.
Incorrect — that is HTML comment syntax.
Incorrect — that is Python’s triple-quoted string convention, not a MATLAB comment.

beginner.question: Which of these correctly creates a variable holding the text "yes"?
beginner.explanation: Text must be enclosed in quotes to be treated as a character array; response = 'yes'; correctly assigns the text "yes" to response.
optionExplanations: Correct — the text is properly quoted and assigned.
Incorrect — without quotes, MATLAB treats yes as a variable name, not text, and would error if yes doesn’t already exist.
Incorrect — the closing quote is missing, which is a syntax error.
Incorrect — the variable name itself must not be quoted.

beginner.question: What does this code display?
beginner.explanation: y = x; copies the current value of x (7) into y. Later changing x to 99 does not retroactively change y — y keeps the value it was given, 7.
optionExplanations: Correct — y holds its own independent copy of the value 7.
Incorrect — y and x are not linked; changing x afterward has no effect on y.
Incorrect — y = x; is a valid assignment.
Incorrect — there is no arithmetic combining x and y here.
commonMistakes: Assuming y = x; creates a live link, so later changes to x automatically update y.

beginner.question: Which line correctly creates two separate variables, a and b, on a single line?
beginner.explanation: A semicolon (or comma) separates multiple statements written on the same line, so a = 1; b = 2; creates both variables correctly.
optionExplanations: Correct — the semicolon separates the two independent assignment statements.
Incorrect — with no separator, MATLAB cannot tell where the first statement ends.
Incorrect — this is not valid MATLAB multiple-assignment syntax.
Incorrect — & is a logical AND operator, not a statement separator.

beginner.question: A comma between two statements on the same line, like "a = 1, b = 2", still displays both results, unlike a semicolon.
beginner.explanation: True. A comma separates statements just like a semicolon does, but — unlike a semicolon — it does not suppress output, so both "a = 1" and "b = 2" get echoed.
optionExplanations: Correct — a comma separates statements without suppressing their output.
Incorrect — this is exactly the difference between a comma and a semicolon as statement separators.
beginner.concept: Comma vs. semicolon as statement separators

beginner.question: What does 2^3 evaluate to in MATLAB?
beginner.explanation: 2^3 means 2 raised to the power of 3, which is 8.

beginner.question: Which operator represents exponentiation (raising to a power) in MATLAB?
beginner.explanation: MATLAB uses the caret ^ for exponentiation, e.g. 2^3 for 2 cubed.
optionExplanations: Correct — ^ is MATLAB’s exponentiation operator.
Incorrect — ** is used in some other languages (like Python), not MATLAB.
Incorrect — pow is not a MATLAB operator (nor a standard function name for this).
Incorrect — not a MATLAB operator.

beginner.question: A MATLAB variable name cannot be the same as a reserved keyword, such as end or if.
beginner.explanation: True. Reserved keywords like if, for, while, and end cannot be used as variable names.
optionExplanations: Correct — reserved keywords are off-limits as variable names.
Incorrect — attempting to use a keyword like end as a variable name causes a syntax error.

beginner.question: What does this code display?
beginner.explanation: Text created with single quotes is stored as a char (character array), and class() reports that type name as "char".
optionExplanations: Correct — single-quoted text is of class char.
Incorrect — "string" is a different class, created with double quotes in newer MATLAB, not single quotes.
Incorrect — double is the class of numeric values, not text.
Incorrect — "text" is not a real MATLAB class name.

beginner.question: A line of code reads: x = 5; % set x to 5. What does MATLAB do with the text after the %?
options: Ignores it — it is a comment meant for human readers only
Executes it as a second statement
Displays it in the Command Window every time the line runs
beginner.explanation: Everything from % to the end of the line is a comment. MATLAB completely ignores it when running the code — it exists purely to help human readers.
optionExplanations: Correct — comments are never executed.
Incorrect — comment text is never treated as code.
Incorrect — a trailing comment after valid code is completely normal and error-free.
Incorrect — comments are never displayed at runtime; they only appear if you look at the source code itself.

beginner.question: Single-quoted text like 'abc' and double-quoted text like "abc" are always exactly the same underlying data type in MATLAB.
beginner.explanation: False. Single quotes create a char array (class char), while double quotes create a string object (class string) — two related but distinct data types.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — they look similar but are different classes under the hood.
Correct — 'abc' is class char, while "abc" is class string; they are not identical types.

beginner.question: What does 20 - 5 - 3 evaluate to, working left to right?
beginner.explanation: With two subtractions of equal precedence, MATLAB evaluates left to right: (20 - 5) = 15, then 15 - 3 = 12.

beginner.question: MATLAB evaluates 20 - 5 - 3 left to right (as (20 - 5) - 3) because subtraction is...
options: left-associative, like most arithmetic operators of equal precedence
beginner.explanation: Operators of the same precedence level (like + and -) are evaluated left to right — this is called left-associativity, and it is how MATLAB (and ordinary arithmetic) handles chained subtraction.
optionExplanations: Correct — equal-precedence operators like - are evaluated left to right.
Incorrect — that would mean 20 - (5 - 3) = 18, which is not how MATLAB evaluates it.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not evaluate arithmetic expressions in reverse.
Incorrect — MATLAB has a well-defined evaluation order even without extra parentheses.

beginner.question: Adding parentheses that make the intended order of operations explicit never changes the result of an already mathematically correct expression.
beginner.explanation: True. Parentheses that simply spell out the grouping an expression already follows (without changing which operations happen first) leave the computed result unchanged — they only add clarity for the reader.
optionExplanations: Correct — redundant, clarifying parentheses do not change a correct calculation.
Incorrect — adding parentheses that match the expression’s existing order of operations cannot change its value.

intermediate.question: What is displayed after this code runs?
intermediate.explanation: x / y performs standard division, giving 2.5. MATLAB’s default "format short" display shows non-integer doubles with four decimal digits, so it prints "z = 2.5000".
optionExplanations: Correct — format short displays 2.5 as 2.5000.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not silently truncate to an integer; "/" is true division, not integer division.
Incorrect — close, but MATLAB’s default display shows four decimal places, not the bare value.
Incorrect — "/" is a perfectly valid operator between two numeric scalars.
commonMistakes: Assuming "/" performs integer division like some other languages.

intermediate.question: What value does MATLAB return for mod(17, 5)?
intermediate.explanation: mod(17,5) returns the remainder after dividing 17 by 5: 17 = 3×5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.
intermediate.hint: mod(a,b) returns the remainder of a divided by b.

intermediate.question: Which operator tests whether two values are NOT equal in MATLAB?
intermediate.explanation: MATLAB uses ~= for “not equal to.” The other symbols shown are used in some other languages but are not valid MATLAB relational operators.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — not a MATLAB operator.
Incorrect — this is the “not equal” operator in languages like C or Python, not MATLAB.
Correct — ~= is MATLAB’s “not equal to” operator.
Incorrect — not a MATLAB operator.

intermediate.question: Write a single line of MATLAB code that assigns the value 42 to a variable named x AND suppresses the Command Window output.
intermediate.explanation: Assignment uses "=", and a trailing semicolon suppresses the echoed output — without it, MATLAB would print "x = 42".
intermediate.hint: You need both the assignment and the character that hides the printed result.
commonMistakes: Writing "x = 42" without the semicolon, which is a valid assignment but does not suppress output.

intermediate.question: What is displayed after this code runs?
intermediate.explanation: The right-hand side x + 5 is evaluated using the current value of x (10), giving 15, which is then reassigned to x.
optionExplanations: Correct — 10 + 5 = 15, reassigned to x.
Incorrect — this ignores the reassignment on line 2.
Incorrect — this is just the amount added, not the new value of x.
Incorrect — reassigning an existing variable is completely normal in MATLAB and does not error.
intermediate.concept: Reassignment using a variable’s current value

intermediate.question: What is displayed after this code runs?
intermediate.explanation: Exponentiation happens first: x^2 = 9, then 9 + 1 = 10.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — this is just x^2 without adding 1.
Incorrect — this would require (x+1)^2, which is not what the code computes.
Incorrect — this ignores the exponent entirely.

intermediate.question: Evaluate 2 + 3 * 4 - 6 / 2 using standard MATLAB operator precedence.
intermediate.explanation: Multiplication and division happen before addition/subtraction, left to right: 3*4=12 and 6/2=3, so the expression becomes 2 + 12 - 3 = 11.

intermediate.question: What does -3^2 evaluate to in MATLAB?
intermediate.explanation: Exponentiation binds more tightly than unary minus in MATLAB, so -3^2 is evaluated as -(3^2) = -9, not (-3)^2 = 9.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB computes 3^2 = 9 first, then applies the unary minus: -9.
Incorrect — that would be the result of (-3)^2, which is not what -3^2 means in MATLAB.
Incorrect — there is no multiplication here to produce -6.
Incorrect — MATLAB’s precedence rules make this unambiguous, even if it’s surprising at first.
commonMistakes: Assuming -3^2 means "negative 3, squared" (9), when MATLAB actually computes -(3^2) = -9.

intermediate.question: In MATLAB, -2^2 and (-2)^2 give the same result.
intermediate.explanation: False. -2^2 evaluates as -(2^2) = -4, because exponentiation binds tighter than unary minus, while (-2)^2 explicitly squares -2, giving 4. They differ.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — -2^2 = -4, while (-2)^2 = 4; these are not the same.
Correct — the parentheses in (-2)^2 change which value actually gets squared.

intermediate.question: Given P = 100; r = 0.05; n = 3; what does P * (1+r)^n evaluate to (tolerance 0.01)?
intermediate.explanation: The parenthesized sum is computed first (1 + 0.05 = 1.05), then raised to the power n=3 (1.157625), and finally multiplied by P: 100 * 1.157625 = 115.7625.

intermediate.question: What does this code display?
options: Error — characters cannot be combined with brackets
intermediate.explanation: Square brackets concatenate character arrays just like numeric arrays, placing them side by side into a single row: "xy".
optionExplanations: Correct — [a b] concatenates the two single characters into the two-character text "xy".
Incorrect — the variable names themselves are not displayed, only their concatenated contents.
Incorrect — bracket concatenation of char arrays is completely valid MATLAB syntax.
Incorrect — brackets here perform concatenation, not counting.

intermediate.question: What does this code display?
options: Error: cannot add a number to text
intermediate.explanation: Arithmetic on a character forces it to be treated as its underlying numeric code. 'a' has code 97, so 'a' + 1 produces the number 98 — a double, not a character.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'a' is treated as the number 97, and 97 + 1 = 98.
Incorrect — arithmetic on a char produces a number, not another character, even though 98 happens to be the code for 'b'.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not perform string-style concatenation with the + operator.
Incorrect — + on a char and a number is well-defined; it doesn't error.
commonMistakes: Expecting 'a' + 1 to produce the character 'b' instead of the number 98.

intermediate.question: Adding a number to a single character, like 'a' + 1, produces another character ('b'), not a number.
intermediate.explanation: False. 'a' + 1 produces the number 98 (a double), because arithmetic operators convert characters to their underlying numeric codes.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — the result is numeric (98), not the character 'b'.
Correct — character arithmetic in MATLAB yields a number, not another character.

intermediate.question: Which correctly converts the numeric character code 98 back into the character 'b'?
intermediate.explanation: char() converts a numeric code back into its corresponding character, so char(98) returns 'b'.
optionExplanations: Correct — char() converts a numeric code into the matching character.
Incorrect — str is not a MATLAB function for this purpose.
Incorrect — num2str(98) returns the text '98', not the character 'b'.
Incorrect — double() converts the other direction (character to number), and 98 is already numeric.

intermediate.question: What is rem(-7, 3) in MATLAB?
intermediate.explanation: rem() returns a remainder with the same sign as the dividend (the first argument). For rem(-7,3): -7 = 3×(-2) + (-1), so the remainder is -1.
intermediate.hint: rem takes the sign of the dividend (the first argument); mod takes the sign of the divisor.

intermediate.question: mod(-7, 3) and rem(-7, 3) always return the same value in MATLAB.
intermediate.explanation: False. mod(-7,3) = 2 (its sign follows the divisor, 3), while rem(-7,3) = -1 (its sign follows the dividend, -7). They agree when both inputs share the same sign, but differ here.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — mod and rem can disagree for mixed-sign inputs, as they do here (2 vs. -1).
Correct — mod follows the divisor’s sign and rem follows the dividend’s sign, so they diverge for -7 and 3.
intermediate.concept: mod() vs. rem() for negative inputs

intermediate.question: Which of these are valid MATLAB relational operators? Select all that apply.
intermediate.explanation: ==, <=, and ~= are all valid MATLAB relational operators. "=>" is not valid MATLAB syntax at all — the correct operator for "greater than or equal to" is >=, with the symbols in the opposite order.
commonMistakes: Writing => instead of >= for "greater than or equal to".

intermediate.question: Which is the correct MATLAB syntax for 'greater than or equal to'?
intermediate.explanation: MATLAB writes "greater than or equal to" as >=, with the greater-than symbol first.
optionExplanations: Correct — >= is the valid relational operator.
Incorrect — the symbols are in the wrong order; this is not valid MATLAB syntax.
Incorrect — not a valid MATLAB operator.
Incorrect — MATLAB source code uses ASCII operators, not the mathematical ≥ symbol.

intermediate.question: What does this code display?
intermediate.explanation: (x > 3) is true (1), and (x > 10) is false (0). Adding them numerically gives 1 + 0 = 1.
optionExplanations: Correct — true (1) plus false (0) equals 1.
Incorrect — only one of the two comparisons is true.
Incorrect — adding two logical values produces a number, not the word "true".
Incorrect — logical values can be added; they behave as 1 and 0 in arithmetic.
intermediate.concept: Logical values behave as numbers in arithmetic

intermediate.question: In MATLAB, the logical values true and false behave as 1 and 0 when used in arithmetic.
intermediate.explanation: True. Logical values are automatically treated as 1 (true) and 0 (false) whenever they’re used in a numeric expression, such as being added together.
optionExplanations: Correct — logical values numerically act as 1 and 0.
Incorrect — this numeric behavior is exactly how MATLAB treats logicals in arithmetic contexts.
intermediate.concept: Logical values behave as numbers in arithmetic

intermediate.question: Write a single MATLAB expression (no semicolon) that displays the result of raising 2 to the 10th power.
intermediate.explanation: The exponentiation operator ^ raises 2 to the 10th power; without a trailing semicolon, MATLAB displays the result (1024) via ans.
intermediate.hint: Use the caret operator between the base and the exponent.

intermediate.question: After running "format long", what happens when you display pi?
options: ans = 3.14159265358979 (many more digits than the default)
Error: format long is not a valid command
intermediate.explanation: format long switches the Command Window display to show roughly 15-16 significant digits for doubles, revealing much more of pi’s stored precision than the default format short.
optionExplanations: Correct — format long reveals many more digits than the default short format.
Incorrect — that’s the default format short display, before switching to format long.
Incorrect — 2 decimal places is even less precise than the default, not more.
Incorrect — format long is a valid, commonly used MATLAB command.

intermediate.question: format long and format short change how numbers are displayed, but do not change the actual precision stored internally.
intermediate.explanation: True. format only affects the Command Window display — the underlying stored value (a full double-precision number) is exactly the same regardless of which format is active.
optionExplanations: Correct — format is purely a display setting, not a change to stored precision.
Incorrect — the stored value never changes; only how many digits are shown changes.
intermediate.concept: format is a display setting only

intermediate.question: Match each operator to what it does.
matchOptions: Adds two values (or concatenates compatible arrays)
Subtracts one value from another
Raises each element to a power, element-wise
Left matrix division / solves a linear system
intermediate.explanation: Each operator has a distinct role: + adds, - subtracts, .^ raises elements to a power one at a time, and \ performs left (matrix) division, most notably used to solve Ax = b.

intermediate.question: Put these lines in the correct order to compute and display the area of a circle with radius r = 5, using pi.
intermediate.explanation: r must be defined before it can be used to compute area, and area must exist before disp() can display it.

advanced.question: A student expects this code to run silently and print only "11" once. Instead, MATLAB also prints "x = 10". What is the cause, and how should it be fixed?
options: MATLAB always displays every variable regardless of syntax; this cannot be prevented
The first line has no semicolon, so its value is echoed — add a semicolon after "x = 10"
disp() is broken and is echoing the wrong variable
The variable y should be renamed to something other than x + 1
advanced.explanation: The line "x = 10" has no trailing semicolon, so MATLAB echoes "x = 10" to the Command Window. Adding a semicolon after that line fixes the unwanted output while leaving the rest of the logic unchanged.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — output can always be suppressed with a semicolon; this is a very common and controllable behavior.
Correct — the missing semicolon on line 1 is the only source of the unwanted output.
Incorrect — disp(y) is functioning correctly; the extra output comes from line 1, not disp.
Incorrect — the variable name has nothing to do with output suppression.
commonMistakes: Blaming disp() for output that actually comes from an earlier unsuppressed assignment.

advanced.question: Because MATLAB is dynamically typed, the same variable can be reassigned from a number (e.g., x = 5) to text (e.g., x = 'hello') later in the same script without error.
advanced.explanation: True. MATLAB variables aren’t bound to a fixed type — reassigning x to a different class simply replaces its contents and type in the Workspace.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB variables can freely change type on reassignment.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not enforce a fixed type per variable name; this reassignment is perfectly legal.

advanced.question: Given a = 7; b = 2; what does "a - b^2" evaluate to, using standard MATLAB operator precedence (exponentiation before subtraction)?
advanced.explanation: Exponentiation binds tighter than subtraction, so b^2 = 4 is computed first, then a - 4 = 3.
commonMistakes: Evaluating left-to-right without respecting precedence and computing (a - b)^2 = 25 instead.
advanced.hint: Compute the exponent before the subtraction.

advanced.question: A student expects this to display 85, but it displays "Score" instead. Why?
options: MATLAB is case-sensitive, so Name and score are different variables — the student meant to write disp(score)
disp() always prints a variable’s name as a string, never its value
MATLAB ignores capitalization, so this is a display formatting bug
Score is a reserved MATLAB keyword and cannot be used this way
advanced.explanation: Name and score are two entirely separate variables because MATLAB is case-sensitive. disp(Name) correctly displays the string stored in Name ('Score'); the student needed disp(score) to see 85.
optionExplanations: Correct — the student is calling disp on the wrong (but validly separate) variable.
Incorrect — disp() prints a variable’s value, not its name.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not ignore capitalization; that’s exactly why this bug exists.
Incorrect — "Score" is not a reserved word; it’s just a string value here.
commonMistakes: Assuming two similarly-named but differently-cased variables are the same variable.

advanced.question: In the statement x = x + 1;, the right-hand side x is evaluated using its current (old) value before the assignment updates it.
advanced.explanation: True. MATLAB fully evaluates the right-hand side first, using whatever value x currently holds, and only afterward stores the result back into x. This is exactly how increment-style patterns (e.g., counters inside loops) work.
optionExplanations: Correct — the right side is computed with the old value before x is updated.
Incorrect — if this weren’t true, incrementing a counter in a loop would be impossible.

advanced.question: A pharmacist wants totalDose = doseWeight*doseRate + 10 (a flat 10 mg loading dose added afterward). They accidentally wrote the line below instead. For doseWeight=70, doseRate=2, what does totalDose actually equal, and why isn’t it the intended 150?
options: 145, because 10 / 2 is computed before the addition, adding only 5 instead of a flat 10
Error: cannot mix multiplication and division in one expression
advanced.explanation: Division happens before addition: doseWeight*doseRate = 140, and 10/2 = 5, giving 140 + 5 = 145 — not the intended flat +10.
optionExplanations: Correct — the accidental "/2" halves the intended loading dose due to operator precedence.
Incorrect — that would require the line to add a flat 10, not 10/2.
Incorrect — this doesn’t match the actual precedence-driven calculation.
Incorrect — MATLAB freely mixes * and / within one expression.
advanced.concept: Precedence bugs in real dosing formulas
commonMistakes: Typing a stray "/2" or similar and not noticing it silently changes the intended flat term.

advanced.question: A calibration formula converts a raw sensor value s = 40 to a temperature reading using T = -0.5*s^2 + 3*s + 10 (°C). Using MATLAB’s operator precedence, what is T (tolerance 0.01)?
advanced.explanation: s^2 = 1600 is computed first (exponent before the unary minus and multiplication). -0.5*1600 = -800, and 3*40 = 120, so T = -800 + 120 + 10 = -670.
advanced.concept: Precedence with unary minus, exponents, and multiplication together

advanced.question: weight_kg = 68; height_m = 1.75; bmi = weight_kg / height_m^2; What is bmi (tolerance 0.02)?
advanced.explanation: Exponentiation happens before division: height_m^2 = 3.0625 first, then 68 / 3.0625 ≈ 22.20. This line correctly implements the intended weight/height² formula — the precedence works in the formula’s favor here.
advanced.concept: When precedence naturally matches formula intent

advanced.question: Given systolic = 120; diastolic = 80;, which of these correctly compute Mean Arterial Pressure using MAP = diastolic + (systolic - diastolic)/3? Select all that apply.
advanced.explanation: The first three are all algebraically equivalent ways of writing the same correct formula (dividing by 3 vs. multiplying by 1/3, and reordering the addition, don’t change the result). The fourth drops the parentheses around (systolic - diastolic), producing a completely different — and wrong — value.
advanced.concept: Necessity of parentheses in a real formula
commonMistakes: Dropping the parentheses around (systolic - diastolic), turning a correct formula into a different calculation entirely.

advanced.question: For systolic = 120 and diastolic = 80, omitting the parentheses — writing diastolic + systolic - diastolic/3 instead of diastolic + (systolic - diastolic)/3 — changes the computed Mean Arterial Pressure.
advanced.explanation: True. The correct formula gives 80 + (40)/3 ≈ 93.33, while the unparenthesized version gives 80 + 120 - 80/3 ≈ 173.33 — a very different (and physiologically nonsensical) result.
optionExplanations: Correct — the two versions produce clearly different numeric results for these values.
Incorrect — the missing parentheses genuinely change what gets computed here.
advanced.concept: Necessity of parentheses in a real formula

advanced.question: What is the class and value of isRightTriangle after this code runs?
options: logical, value true (displays as 1) — because 9 + 16 equals 25
advanced.explanation: a^2+b^2 = 25 and c^2 = 25, so the == comparison is true. The result of any relational comparison in MATLAB is always of class logical, which displays as 1 but is not the same class as a plain double.
optionExplanations: Correct — 9+16=25=c^2, and relational operators always produce a logical result.
Incorrect — the value does display as 1, but its class is logical, not double.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not display logical results as the text "true".
Incorrect — == is a perfectly valid comparison between two numbers.

advanced.question: Given hr = 68; age = 30; using maxHR = 220 - age and percentage = hr/maxHR*100, what is percentage (tolerance 0.1)?
A script computes result = a + b / c;, intending (a+b)/c. For a=2, b=3, c=5, what does the code ACTUALLY compute (not the intended value)?
advanced.explanation: Division happens before addition: b/c = 3/5 = 0.6, then a + 0.6 = 2.6 — not the intended (2+3)/5 = 1.
advanced.concept: Precedence mismatches between code and intent

advanced.question: You are translating the Mosteller body surface area formula, BSA = sqrt(height_cm * weight_kg / 3600), into MATLAB. Which expression correctly matches the formula?
advanced.explanation: The formula takes the square root of the ENTIRE quantity (height×weight/3600); only the first option groups all three terms inside sqrt() as intended.
optionExplanations: Correct — height_cm*weight_kg/3600 is fully computed first, then the square root of that whole quantity is taken.
Incorrect — this only takes the square root of height_cm, not the full product divided by 3600.
Incorrect — this takes the square root of height×weight before dividing by 3600, which is a different formula.
Incorrect — this divides by the square root of 3600 rather than taking the square root of the whole expression.

advanced.question: Using the Mosteller formula BSA = sqrt(height_cm * weight_kg / 3600), for height_cm = 170 and weight_kg = 70, what is BSA in m² (tolerance 0.02)?
advanced.explanation: 170 * 70 = 11900, divided by 3600 gives ≈3.3056, and the square root of that is ≈1.818.

advanced.question: A student wants avg to be the average of x and y (i.e., (x+y)/2). For x=5, y=2, what does avg actually equal, and what is the fix?
options: avg = 6, because y/2 is computed first (1) and added to x (5); the fix is avg = (x + y) / 2;
avg = 7, because x and y are simply added
Error: cannot divide inside an addition expression
advanced.explanation: Division happens before addition: y/2 = 1, then x + 1 = 6. Wrapping (x + y) in parentheses before dividing by 2 fixes it to give the intended average, 3.5.
optionExplanations: Correct — precedence causes only y to be halved, not the sum; parentheses fix it.
Incorrect — 3.5 is the intended value, not what this specific code computes.
Incorrect — this ignores the division entirely.
Incorrect — dividing inside a larger expression is completely valid MATLAB syntax.
commonMistakes: Forgetting parentheses around a sum before dividing it, a very common "average" bug.

advanced.question: For a=10, b=4, c=2, which of these evaluate to the same value as (a - b) - c = 4? Select all that apply.
advanced.explanation: a - b - c evaluates left to right, same as (a-b)-c, giving 4. a - (b + c) = 10 - 6 = 4 also matches, coincidentally. a - (b - c) = 10 - 2 = 8 is different — grouping the subtraction the other way changes the result.

advanced.question: Subtraction in MATLAB is left-associative, meaning a - b - c is evaluated as (a - b) - c, not a - (b - c).
advanced.explanation: True. Chained subtraction (and addition) is always evaluated left to right in MATLAB.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is exactly MATLAB’s (and standard arithmetic’s) associativity rule for subtraction.
Incorrect — a - (b - c) would give a different result and is not how MATLAB evaluates chained subtraction.

advanced.question: What does this code display?
options: c = 2, and class(c) is double — arithmetic promotes logical values to double
c = true, and class(c) is logical
Error: cannot add logical values together
advanced.explanation: a + b + a = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. Whenever logical values are combined with an arithmetic operator like +, the result is promoted to class double, not left as logical.
optionExplanations: Correct — the sum is 2, and arithmetic converts the result to double.
Incorrect — the numeric value is right, but the class becomes double, not logical, once arithmetic is applied.
Incorrect — arithmetic combination does not preserve the logical class or produce the value "true".
Incorrect — logical values add together without error, producing a plain number.
advanced.concept: Arithmetic on logicals produces double, not logical

advanced.question: A 3-drug schedule computes total = dose1 + dose2*2 - dose3/2, with dose1=10, dose2=5, dose3=8. What is total?
advanced.explanation: dose2*2 = 10 and dose3/2 = 4 are computed first (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction), giving total = 10 + 10 - 4 = 16.

advanced.question: What does this code display for minutes, and is it correctly converting an IV infusion duration to minutes?
options: minutes = 240 — correct, and displayed because the last line has no semicolon
minutes = 4 — incorrect, the conversion to minutes is missing
Error: hours must be a whole number
minutes = 240, but nothing is displayed because of the missing semicolon
advanced.explanation: hours = 500/125 = 4, and minutes = 4*60 = 240. Since the last line has no trailing semicolon, MATLAB echoes "minutes = 240".
optionExplanations: Correct — the math is right (240 minutes), and it displays because of the missing semicolon.
Incorrect — the *60 conversion is present and correctly applied.
Incorrect — hours does not need to be a whole number in MATLAB.
Incorrect — a missing semicolon causes output to be shown, not hidden.
advanced.concept: Combining a real calculation with output suppression rules

advanced.question: Which of the following return a value equal to MATLAB’s pi (to full double precision)? Select all that apply.
advanced.explanation: pi and pi() are the same function call (parentheses are optional with no arguments) and both return the built-in double-precision approximation of π. 4*atan(1) also evaluates to exactly the same double-precision value, since atan(1) = π/4. 22/7 ≈ 3.142857 is only a coarse rational approximation of π, off by more than 0.001 — it does not match MATLAB’s pi.

advanced.question: MATLAB’s pi is best described as...
options: a double-precision floating-point approximation of π, accurate to about 15-16 significant digits
the mathematically exact value of π
advanced.explanation: Like all non-integer MATLAB numbers by default, pi is stored as a double-precision floating-point approximation — extremely precise, but not mathematically exact (π has infinitely many non-repeating digits).
optionExplanations: Correct — pi is a very precise, but ultimately finite-precision, floating-point approximation.
Incorrect — no finite-precision computer representation can be mathematically exact for an irrational number like π.
Incorrect — pi is numeric (a double), not text.
Incorrect — pi is clearly not an integer.

advanced.question: A drug half-life is estimated with t_half = 0.693 / k, where k = 0.05 (per hour). What is t_half in hours (tolerance 0.01)?
advanced.explanation: 0.693 (an approximation of ln 2) divided by 0.05 gives 13.86 hours.

advanced.question: You need C = (F - 32) * 5/9 to convert Fahrenheit to Celsius. A colleague instead wrote C = F - 32 * 5/9;. For F = 98.6 (normal body temperature), what does each version compute?
options: The colleague’s version gives ≈80.8 (nonsensical); the correct formula gives 37.0°C — normal body temperature. The missing parentheses around (F - 32) is the bug.
Both versions give the same correct result, 37.0°C.
The colleague’s version gives 37.0°C and the correct formula gives 80.8°C — they are reversed.
advanced.explanation: Correct: (98.6-32)*5/9 = 66.6*5/9 = 37.0°C. Buggy: 98.6 - 32*5/9 = 98.6 - 17.78 ≈ 80.82 — a physiologically meaningless result, revealing the missing parentheses.
optionExplanations: Correct — the numbers confirm the correct formula gives the expected 37.0°C, and the buggy one clearly does not.
Incorrect — the two versions give very different results here.
Incorrect — the values are not reversed; the buggy version’s output is simply wrong.
Incorrect — subtraction from F is valid; the issue is precedence, not a subtraction error.
advanced.concept: Missing parentheses in a real unit-conversion formula
commonMistakes: Forgetting parentheses around (F - 32) when translating the Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula.

expert.question: A sensor calibration converts a raw reading r = 250 to a physical value using value = r*c + o, where c = 0.02 and o = 1.5. What is value?
expert.explanation: Multiplication happens before addition: r*c = 250 * 0.02 = 5, then 5 + o = 5 + 1.5 = 6.5.
expert.concept: Operator precedence in a real calibration formula

expert.question: A researcher wants targetZone to represent the range from 50% to 85% of a measured heart rate, and writes this line. What is the bug?
expert.code:
heartRate = 72;
targetZone = heartRate * 0.5 - 0.85;
options: "*" and "-" combine into one number that isn’t a percentage range at all — the calculation needs two separate expressions, e.g. lower = heartRate*0.5; upper = heartRate*0.85;
heartRate should be written as a string
The semicolon at the end of the line is misplaced
MATLAB cannot multiply an integer by a decimal
expert.explanation: heartRate * 0.5 - 0.85 computes a single number (35.15) that doesn’t represent either bound of the intended 50%–85% range. Two separate expressions are needed — one for the lower bound and one for the upper bound.
optionExplanations: Correct — this line conflates two separate calculations (two bounds) into one meaningless expression.
Incorrect — heartRate is correctly used as a number here.
Incorrect — the semicolon placement is fine.
Incorrect — MATLAB freely mixes integers and decimals in arithmetic.
expert.concept: Translating a real-world range calculation into correct expressions
commonMistakes: Combining two separate quantities (a lower and an upper bound) into a single expression instead of computing them separately.

expert.question: Which of the following correctly compute a lower bound (50%) and upper bound (85%) of heartRate = 72 into two separate variables? Select all that apply.
expert.explanation: Options 1 and 3 both correctly compute a lower and an upper bound as two separate variables (multiplication is commutative, so the order of 72 and 0.5/0.85 doesn’t matter). Option 2 collapses everything into one meaningless number. Option 4 is invalid MATLAB syntax — you cannot unpack a plain numeric array into two output variables that way.
expert.concept: Computing a range as two separate values

expert.question: You are computing drug concentration decay with C = C0 * exp(-k*t). For t = 0, which best describes MATLAB’s behavior?
options: C = C0 * exp(-k*0), which correctly evaluates to C0, since exp(0) = 1
This causes a division error because t = 0 appears in the exponent
exp(0) returns NaN in MATLAB, so this expression fails at t = 0
t is not allowed to equal exactly 0 in a MATLAB expression
expert.explanation: exp(0) equals 1 in MATLAB (as it does mathematically), so at t = 0 the expression correctly reduces to C = C0 — exactly the expected physical behavior (the initial concentration).
optionExplanations: Correct — exp(0) = 1, so C = C0 exactly, as expected.
Incorrect — there’s no division anywhere in this expression.
Incorrect — exp(0) is a perfectly well-defined value (1), not NaN.
Incorrect — 0 is a completely valid numeric value for t.
expert.concept: Evaluating exponential decay expressions at a boundary value

expert.question: Because MATLAB uses double-precision floating point by default, an expression like 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 may evaluate to false, even though it’s true mathematically.
expert.explanation: True. Floating-point numbers can’t represent values like 0.1 or 0.2 exactly in binary, so tiny rounding differences accumulate — 0.1 + 0.2 actually comes out to something like 0.30000000000000004, which is not exactly equal to 0.3. The safe habit is comparing with a small tolerance (abs(a - b) < tol) instead of exact equality.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is a well-known floating-point representation quirk, not a MATLAB bug.
Incorrect — this specific comparison really can (and often does) evaluate to false in MATLAB.
expert.concept: Floating-point comparison
commonMistakes: Comparing computed floating-point results with == instead of a tolerance-based comparison.

expert.question: A one-compartment pharmacokinetic estimate uses C = (Dose/Vd) * exp(-k*t), with Dose=500 (mg), Vd=40 (L), k=0.1 (per hour), t=5 (hours). What is C in mg/L (tolerance 0.02)?
expert.concept: Multi-step pharmacokinetic formula evaluation

expert.question: Continuing the pharmacokinetic scenario (C ≈ 7.58, Dose/Vd = 12.5), this line was meant to compute the percentage of drug remaining, but the formula is inverted. What does it actually compute, and what is the fix?
expert.code: percentRemaining = Dose/Vd/C * 100;
options: It computes (Dose/Vd) divided by C, giving roughly 164.9% — nonsensical for a "percent remaining." The fix is percentRemaining = C/(Dose/Vd) * 100;, giving ≈60.65%.
It correctly computes 60.65%, exactly as intended
It computes exactly 100%, since Dose/Vd and C cancel out
expert.explanation: (Dose/Vd)/C = 12.5/7.58 ≈ 1.649, times 100 ≈ 164.9% — over 100%, an immediate red flag for a "percent remaining" quantity, which should be at most 100%. Swapping the division order to C/(Dose/Vd)*100 gives the correct ≈60.65%.
optionExplanations: Correct — the inverted division produces a value over 100%, which shouldn’t be possible for a percent-remaining calculation.
Incorrect — this is what the fixed version computes, not the code as actually written.
Incorrect — C is nonzero here, so no division-by-zero occurs.
Incorrect — Dose/Vd and C do not cancel; they’re divided, not multiplied and then divided by themselves.
expert.concept: Catching an inverted-ratio bug via a sanity check
commonMistakes: Writing a ratio "backwards" and not noticing the result is outside a physically sensible range (like a percentage exceeding 100%).

expert.question: A model computes stroke volume index SVI = SV / BSA, with SV = 70 (mL) and BSA = 1.82 (m²). Which of these correctly compute SVI? Select all that apply.
expert.explanation: SV/BSA, SV*(1/BSA), and 1/(BSA/SV) are all algebraically equivalent expressions of the same ratio. BSA/SV inverts the ratio and computes something entirely different (BSA per unit of SV, not SV per unit of BSA).
expert.concept: Recognizing algebraically equivalent expressions

expert.question: 1 / (BSA / SV) is algebraically equivalent to SV / BSA, for any nonzero BSA and SV.
expert.explanation: True. 1/(a/b) = b/a is a basic algebraic identity, so 1/(BSA/SV) = SV/BSA exactly.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is a standard, always-true algebraic identity for nonzero values.
Incorrect — the identity 1/(a/b) = b/a holds generally, not just in special cases.
expert.concept: Algebraic equivalence of ratio expressions

expert.question: A dosing protocol computes loadingDose = weight*5; maintenanceDose = weight*2*numDoses; totalDose = loadingDose + maintenanceDose;. For weight=68, numDoses=4, what is totalDose?
expert.explanation: loadingDose = 68*5 = 340. maintenanceDose = 68*2*4 = 544. totalDose = 340 + 544 = 884.
expert.concept: Multi-step formula evaluation

expert.question: Continuing the dosing scenario (totalDose = 884, numDoses = 4), this line computes avgPerDose, intended to be (totalDose/numDoses) plus a 1 mg buffer per dose. Is the code below actually correct, and what value does it produce?
expert.code: avgPerDose = totalDose / numDoses + 1
options: Yes, it is correct: division happens before addition, so this computes (884/4) + 1 = 222, exactly as intended
No, it is a bug: MATLAB adds 1 to numDoses first, giving 884/5 = 176.8
No, it is a bug: this displays "avgPerDose" as text, not a number
Yes, but only by coincidence — the formula happens to be ambiguous
expert.explanation: Division has higher precedence than addition, so totalDose/numDoses (=221) is computed first, then +1 gives 222 — precisely matching the intended "(totalDose/numDoses) plus a 1 mg buffer" meaning. This is a case where the straightforward code is already correct; not every suspicious-looking one-liner hides a bug.
optionExplanations: Correct — precedence here works in the formula’s favor, matching the intended calculation exactly.
Incorrect — addition never happens before division in MATLAB; numDoses is not modified before the division.
Incorrect — this is a numeric assignment and display, not a text operation.
Incorrect — MATLAB’s precedence rules make this expression completely unambiguous.
expert.concept: Verifying correctness rather than assuming a bug exists

expert.question: Continuing the dosing scenario (totalDose = 884), suppose the intended formula were actually totalDose / (numDoses + 1) instead — a common intent-vs-code mismatch. With numDoses = 4, what would avgPerDose be (tolerance 0.01)?
expert.concept: Comparing alternate intended formulas

expert.question: You need to compute cardiac output CO = heartRate * strokeVolume_mL / 1000 (converting mL to L), with heartRate=72, strokeVolume_mL=70. Which of these correctly compute CO? Select all that apply.
expert.explanation: The first three all use only multiplication and division, which are the same precedence and evaluated left to right — grouping them differently with parentheses doesn’t change the result (all give ≈5.04 L/min). The fourth swaps in addition, computing an entirely different (and meaningless) quantity.
expert.concept: Equivalent groupings for pure multiplication/division chains

expert.question: For an expression containing only multiplication and division (no addition or subtraction), the way the terms are grouped with parentheses does not affect the final numeric result.
expert.explanation: True. Because multiplication and division share the same precedence and are left-associative, any valid regrouping of a pure */ chain gives the same result (aside from potentially negligible floating-point rounding differences).
optionExplanations: Correct — regrouping a pure multiplication/division chain does not change its value.
Incorrect — this is a reliable property of chains using only * and /.
expert.concept: Equivalent groupings for pure multiplication/division chains

expert.question: You need adjustedDose = baseDose * (1 - reductionPct/100), with baseDose=200, reductionPct=15. A colleague instead wrote adjustedDose = baseDose * 1 - reductionPct/100; (missing parentheses). What is the DIFFERENCE between the buggy result and the correct result?
expert.concept: Missing parentheses in a percentage-reduction formula
commonMistakes: Writing value*1 - pct/100 instead of value*(1 - pct/100) for a percentage reduction.

expert.question: In the dosing scenario above (baseDose=200, reductionPct=15), omitting the parentheses in the percentage-reduction formula changes the computed adjustedDose.
expert.explanation: True, as shown by the 29.85-unit gap between the buggy (199.85) and correct (170) results for these specific values.
optionExplanations: Correct — for these values, the missing parentheses produce a clearly different result.
Incorrect — the two versions genuinely diverge here.
expert.concept: Missing parentheses in a percentage-reduction formula

expert.question: A ventilator setting uses TV = weight_kg * 6 (tidal volume, mL) and MV = TV * RR / 1000 (minute ventilation, L/min), with weight_kg=75, RR=14 (breaths/min). What is MV (tolerance 0.01)?
expert.concept: Multi-step formula evaluation

expert.question: Continuing the ventilator scenario, is this line’s computation for MV correct, given how MATLAB evaluates operators of equal precedence left to right?
options: Yes — TV*RR is computed first (left to right, since * and / share precedence), then divided by 1000, giving 6.3 L/min as intended
No — MATLAB divides RR by 1000 first, then multiplies by TV, giving a different result
No — this throws an error because * and / cannot be mixed in one expression
Yes, but only because weight_kg happens to be a multiple of 25
expert.explanation: TV*RR/1000 is evaluated left to right: TV*RR = 6300 first, then 6300/1000 = 6.3 — matching the intended calculation exactly. This is another case where the straightforward code turns out to already be correct.
optionExplanations: Correct — left-to-right evaluation of same-precedence * and / gives the intended result here.
Incorrect — MATLAB evaluates left to right, not right to left, for equal-precedence operators.
Incorrect — mixing * and / in one expression is completely valid MATLAB syntax.
Incorrect — this result doesn’t depend on weight_kg being any particular kind of number; the left-to-right evaluation always applies.
expert.concept: Verifying correctness rather than assuming a bug exists

expert.question: Which of the following are valid strategies for making a formula-translation script easier to verify against its source formula? Select all that apply.
options: Adding parentheses that mirror the formula’s mathematical grouping, even when not strictly required by precedence
Naming variables to match the formula’s terms (e.g., weight_kg instead of x)
Removing all spacing so the code takes up less room
Testing the code against a hand-calculated example with known values
expert.explanation: Clarifying parentheses, meaningful variable names, and testing against a known example all make it easier to trust and verify a formula translation. Removing spacing has no effect on correctness and only hurts readability.
expert.concept: Professional practices for reliable formula translation

expert.question: Adding parentheses that are mathematically redundant (they don’t change the computed result) but make the intended grouping visually explicit is considered good practice, not an error.
expert.explanation: True. Redundant, clarifying parentheses cost nothing computationally and make code far easier for a human to verify against the source formula.
optionExplanations: Correct — clarity-only parentheses are a recommended practice, not a mistake.
Incorrect — there is no downside to parentheses that don’t change the result but do improve readability.
expert.concept: Professional practices for reliable formula translation

expert.question: Put these steps in the correct order for safely translating and verifying a new formula in MATLAB.
options: Write out the formula’s intended order of operations on paper, adding your own grouping parentheses
Translate it into a MATLAB expression using variable names that match the formula’s terms
Test the expression with a simple example where you already know the correct answer by hand
Compare MATLAB’s output to your hand-calculated answer and investigate any mismatch
expert.explanation: Understanding the formula’s intended grouping comes first, then translating it into named MATLAB variables, then testing against a known example, and finally comparing and investigating any discrepancy.
expert.concept: A verification workflow for formula translation

expert.question: Given adjBMI = (weight_kg/height_m^2) * (1 + ageAdjust/100), with weight_kg=80, height_m=1.8, ageAdjust=5, what is adjBMI (tolerance 0.02)?
expert.concept: Multi-step formula evaluation

expert.question: Continuing the adjBMI scenario (intended value ≈25.926), a colleague drops both sets of parentheses, writing adjBMI = weight_kg/height_m^2 * 1 + ageAdjust/100;. What does this buggy version actually compute (tolerance 0.02)?
expert.explanation: weight_kg/height_m^2 = 24.691 (exponent before division), *1 leaves it unchanged, then + ageAdjust/100 = +0.05, giving 24.7414 — noticeably different from the intended 25.926.
expert.concept: Diagnosing a missing-parentheses bug

expert.question: You are asked to review a teammate’s MATLAB translation of a new formula before it is used on real patient data. Which review approach best catches operator-precedence bugs like the ones throughout this topic (missing parentheses, unary-minus-before-power surprises, left-to-right chains)?
options: Re-derive the formula from its original source, test the code against a hand-calculated example, and compare the results — rather than just reading the code and assuming it looks right
Assume the code is correct if it runs without throwing an error
Only check that variable names are spelled correctly
Trust that MATLAB automatically corrects any precedence mistakes
expert.explanation: Running without error only means the code is syntactically valid — it says nothing about whether it computes the intended formula. Independently verifying against a known correct example is the only reliable check.
optionExplanations: Correct — independent verification against a known result is the only reliable way to catch a semantic (precedence) bug.
Incorrect — precedence bugs are syntactically valid code; they never raise an error on their own.
Incorrect — correct spelling says nothing about whether the formula’s grouping is correct.
Incorrect — MATLAB never infers or corrects your intended order of operations; it only follows its fixed precedence rules.
expert.concept: Reviewing code for precedence correctness, not just syntax validity

expert.question: Because MATLAB never raises an error for a syntactically valid but operator-precedence-mismatched formula, the only reliable way to catch such bugs is to independently verify results against known correct values — not just checking that the code runs.
expert.explanation: True. A precedence mismatch produces a perfectly valid MATLAB expression that simply computes something other than what was intended — MATLAB has no way to know your intent, so only independent verification can catch it.
optionExplanations: Correct — precedence bugs are invisible to MATLAB’s error checking; only independent verification exposes them.
Incorrect — this is exactly why running without error is not sufficient evidence of correctness.
expert.concept: Reviewing code for precedence correctness, not just syntax validity

beginner.question: What does this code display?

beginner.question: Which command creates a row vector from 0 to 10 in steps of 2, using the colon operator?
beginner.explanation: The colon operator syntax is start:step:end, so 0:2:10 produces [0 2 4 6 8 10].
optionExplanations: Correct — start:step:end with start=0, step=2, end=10.
Incorrect — this would use a step of 10, producing only [0 10].
Incorrect — this creates a 3-element vector containing exactly 0, 10, and 2, not a range.
Incorrect — linspace(2,10,0) style args are wrong; linspace(a,b,n) specifies endpoints and a count, not a step.

beginner.question: In MATLAB, indexing begins at 0, just like in Python.
beginner.explanation: False. MATLAB indexing begins at 1 — the first element of any array is accessed with index 1, not 0.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — MATLAB is 1-indexed, unlike Python.
Correct — MATLAB arrays start at index 1.
commonMistakes: Carrying over 0-based indexing habits from Python or C and accidentally requesting element 0.

beginner.question: A 1×5 row vector and a 5×1 column vector containing the same five numbers are considered identical by MATLAB (size(a) == size(b)).
beginner.explanation: False. Orientation matters — a 1×5 row vector and a 5×1 column vector have different sizes, even if they contain the same numbers in the same order.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — MATLAB treats row and column vectors as different shapes.
Correct — size([1 2 3]) is [1 3], while size([1;2;3]) is [3 1]; these are not equal.

beginner.question: Which command creates a 2×2 matrix with rows [1 2] and [3 4]?
beginner.explanation: Semicolons separate rows, while spaces (or commas) separate columns within a row.
optionExplanations: Correct — semicolons separate rows, spaces (or commas) separate columns within a row.
Incorrect — with no row separator, this creates a single 1×4 row, not a 2×2 matrix.
Incorrect — with no row separator at all, this creates a single 1×4 row vector.
Incorrect — matrices are built with square brackets [ ], not parentheses.

beginner.question: What does this code display?

Incorrect — that is A(1,1).
Incorrect — that is A(2,1).

beginner.question: The command zeros(3) creates a 3×1 column vector of zeros.
beginner.explanation: False. A single argument to zeros creates a SQUARE matrix — zeros(3) creates a 3×3 matrix of zeros, not a 3×1 column.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — zeros(3) is a 3×3 square matrix, not a column vector.
Correct — a single argument to zeros produces a square n×n matrix; a 3×1 column needs zeros(3,1).
beginner.concept: zeros() with one vs. two arguments

beginner.question: Which of the following creates the column vector containing 1, 2, 3 in that order?
beginner.explanation: Semicolons stack values into a column, in the order given.
optionExplanations: Correct — semicolons stack values into a column, in the order given.
Incorrect — commas (or spaces) create a row vector, not a column.

beginner.question: How many elements does the vector produced by 1:2:9 contain?
beginner.explanation: 1:2:9 produces [1 3 5 7 9] — five elements, stepping by 2 from 1 up to (and including) 9.
beginner.concept: Counting elements in a colon range

beginner.question: The colon expression 5:1 (with no step specified) produces an empty result, since the default step is +1 and 5 is already greater than 1.
beginner.explanation: True. With the default step of 1, MATLAB would need to count up from 5 to reach 1, which never happens, so 5:1 produces an empty vector.
optionExplanations: Correct — the default ascending step can never go from 5 down to 1, so the result is empty.
Incorrect — 5:1 really does produce an empty vector, not an error or a descending sequence.
beginner.concept: Empty ranges from the colon operator
commonMistakes: Expecting a:b to automatically count downward when a > b — it does not, unless a negative step is specified.

beginner.question: Which function returns the total number of elements in an array, regardless of its shape?
beginner.explanation: numel always returns the total element count.

Incorrect — length returns only the size of the largest single dimension, not the total count for a matrix.
Incorrect — size returns the dimensions (e.g., [rows cols]), not a single total count.
Incorrect — count is not a MATLAB function for this purpose.

beginner.question: Which of the following create a 1×4 row vector containing 1, 2, 3, 4? Select all that apply.
beginner.explanation: [1 2 3 4], [1,2,3,4], and 1:4 all produce the same 1×4 row vector. [1;2;3;4] instead produces a 4×1 column vector.
beginner.concept: Equivalent ways to write a row vector

beginner.question: Write the MATLAB expression that creates a 2×3 matrix in which every element is 1.
beginner.explanation: ones(m,n) creates an m×n matrix of ones, so ones(2,3) gives the required 2×3 all-ones matrix.

beginner.question: What does the expression 3:3 produce?
options: A vector containing only the single value 3
An error, since start equals end

beginner.question: What is the value of the last element produced by 10:-2:2?
beginner.explanation: 10:-2:2 counts down by 2 from 10: 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 — the last value produced is 2.

beginner.question: In MATLAB, every row of a matrix literal must contain the same number of elements, or the definition is invalid.
beginner.explanation: True. For example, [1 2; 3] is invalid because the first row has 2 elements and the second has only 1 — MATLAB requires a rectangular, consistent shape.
optionExplanations: Correct — mismatched row lengths in a matrix literal cause an error.
Incorrect — MATLAB does enforce equal row lengths when building a matrix this way.

commonMistakes: Accidentally leaving out a value in one row of a matrix literal, causing a dimension error.

beginner.question: Write the MATLAB expression that creates a 2×3 matrix in which every element is 0.
beginner.explanation: zeros(m,n) creates an m×n matrix of zeros, so zeros(2,3) gives the required 2×3 all-zeros matrix.

beginner.question: What does this code display?

Incorrect — assigning (not just reading) beyond the current length is allowed and grows the vector rather than erroring.

beginner.question: Assigning to an index beyond a vector's current length, e.g. v(6) = 99 for a 3-element v, automatically grows the vector, filling any skipped positions with 0.
beginner.explanation: True. v(6) = 99 on a 3-element v grows v to 6 elements, with positions 4 and 5 automatically filled with 0.
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB pads any skipped positions with zero when auto-growing a vector this way.
Incorrect — this auto-grow-and-zero-fill behavior is real and commonly relied upon.
commonMistakes: Assuming skipped positions are left undefined rather than zero-filled.

beginner.question: Which of these produce a vector with exactly 3 elements? Select all that apply.
beginner.explanation: linspace(0,10,3) produces exactly 3 points by definition. 1:3 produces [1 2 3], 3 elements. zeros(1,3) produces 3 elements by definition. 0:5:20 instead produces [0 5 10 15 20] — 5 elements, not 3.
beginner.concept: Predicting element counts across vector-creation methods

beginner.question: How many elements are in the vector produced by linspace(1,10,4)?
beginner.explanation: linspace's third argument is a point count, not a step size — linspace(1,10,4) produces exactly 4 evenly spaced points.
commonMistakes: Confusing linspace’s third argument (a count) with a step size, unlike the colon operator.

intermediate.question: Given v = [4 8 15 16 23 42];, what is v(end)?
intermediate.explanation: end refers to the index of the last element of v, so v(end) is the last value, 42.

intermediate.question: Given A = [1 2; 3 4];, which of the following correctly compute the transpose of A? Select all that apply.
intermediate.explanation: A.', A', and transpose(A) all transpose A (for real-valued matrices, the plain transpose and complex-conjugate transpose are identical, so both A.' and A' work here). flip(A) reverses the order of elements along a dimension — it does not transpose the matrix.

intermediate.explanation: sum(A(:)) first linearizes A into a single column, then sums everything, giving 10. sum(sum(A)) sums each column first (giving [4 6]), then sums that result, also giving 10. sum(A) alone only gives the per-column sums [4 6] — a vector, not the grand total. numel(A) just counts elements (4), unrelated to summing them.

Incorrect — sum(A) genuinely returns per-column sums by default, not one grand total.

optionExplanations: Incorrect — ^ is matrix power, not element-wise power; the two operators behave very differently here.
Correct — v^2 errors for a non-square vector like this, while v.^2 correctly squares each element.

intermediate.question: Match each MATLAB expression to what it evaluates to, for A = [1 2; 3 4].
intermediate.explanation: size(A) = [2 2] (2 rows, 2 columns). numel(A) = 4 (total elements). length(A) = 2 (the largest dimension). A(:) stacks A’s columns top-to-bottom: column 1 is [1;3], column 2 is [2;4], giving [1;3;2;4].

intermediate.question: Which of the following correctly extract the last two elements of v = [10 20 30 40 50]? Select all that apply.

intermediate.explanation: Row 2 of A is [4 5 6]; column 3 of that row is 6.

intermediate.question: Concatenating two row vectors of different lengths with [A B] (e.g., A is 1×3 and B is 1×2) is valid and produces a 1×5 vector.

Incorrect — this concatenation is valid; only vertical concatenation ([A; B]) requires matching column counts.

intermediate.question: reshape(1:6, 3, 2) fills the new matrix column-by-column from the original vector’s order, not row-by-row.
intermediate.explanation: True. reshape strictly follows column-major order, so reshape(1:6,3,2) produces [1 4; 2 5; 3 6] — column 1 is [1;2;3], column 2 is [4;5;6].
optionExplanations: Correct — reshape strictly follows column-major order.
Incorrect — reshape does not fill row-by-row; that is a common misconception.
commonMistakes: Assuming reshape fills row-by-row, as in some other languages.

advanced.question: This code produces an error. Why?
options: A (1×3) and B (2×2) have incompatible dimensions for element-wise addition
MATLAB can never add a vector and a matrix, under any circumstance
C is used before it is defined
The lines are missing semicolons, which causes the error

advanced.question: You want to reverse the order of elements in vector v without typing each index by hand. Which command does this?

optionExplanations: Correct — A(:) stacks the columns of A, top to bottom, in order.
Incorrect — this is a well-defined and common operation in MATLAB.

Incorrect — transpose does not flatten a matrix into a vector; it swaps rows and columns.

advanced.question: You have two column vectors from an experiment, time (100×1) and pressure (100×1), and want a single 100×2 matrix with them as two side-by-side columns. Which command does this?
advanced.explanation: A comma inside brackets concatenates horizontally (side by side), producing a 100×2 matrix. A semicolon would stack them vertically into a 200×1 column instead.
