Incorrect — 'c' is the color cyan, not a marker.
Incorrect — MATLAB marker symbols are single characters, not words.
Incorrect — not a valid MATLAB marker symbol.

beginner.question: Which of the following are valid ways to plot a vector y = [3 6 9] with x-values 1, 2, 3? Select all that apply.
beginner.explanation: plot(y) implicitly uses the index (1,2,3) as x. plot(1:3, y) and plot([1 2 3], y) both explicitly supply the same x-values. plot(y, 1:3) swaps the arguments, plotting the index values against y instead — the opposite of what’s wanted.
beginner.concept: Equivalent ways to plot against an implicit or explicit index
commonMistakes: Swapping the order of arguments to plot(), reversing which vector becomes x and which becomes y.

beginner.question: Which function clears the contents of the current axes but leaves the figure window itself open?
beginner.explanation: cla ("clear axes") erases everything drawn on the current axes but keeps the figure window open, ready for new plotting.
optionExplanations: Correct — cla clears the axes contents only.
Incorrect — clf ("clear figure") clears the entire figure, including all its axes, but still keeps the window itself open.
Incorrect — close shuts the figure window entirely.
Incorrect — clc clears the Command Window display; it has nothing to do with plots.
commonMistakes: Confusing cla (clears axes), clf (clears whole figure), and close (closes the window) — they are three different levels of "clearing."

beginner.question: xlabel and ylabel can be called in either order after plot() — the result looks the same either way.
beginner.explanation: True. xlabel sets the x-axis label and ylabel sets the y-axis label; since they affect different, independent parts of the axes, calling them in either order produces the same final plot.
optionExplanations: Correct — the two calls are independent of each other.
Incorrect — there is no ordering requirement between xlabel and ylabel.

beginner.question: Which function saves the currently active figure to an image file?
beginner.explanation: saveas(gcf, filename) saves the figure referred to by gcf ("get current figure") to the given file. (print can also save figures, but requires additional format flags to reliably control the output — saveas is the simplest beginner-level tool.)
optionExplanations: Correct — saveas(gcf, filename) is the standard beginner-level way to save a figure to an image file.
Incorrect — savefig saves a figure in MATLAB’s own .fig format for reopening in MATLAB, not a general image file by itself with just a filename like this.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — print can save figures, but calling it with just a filename and no format flag does not reliably produce the intended image file.
beginner.concept: Saving a figure to a file

beginner.question: After this code runs, which subplot cell has the title "Cell Two"?
beginner.code:
subplot(1,2,1)
plot(1:5)
subplot(1,2,2)
plot(5:-1:1)
title('Cell Two')
options: Neither — title() only works on a full figure, not a subplot
beginner.explanation: title() always applies to whichever axes are currently active — here, subplot(1,2,2) was called immediately before title(), making the second (right) cell the current axes.
optionExplanations: Correct — the most recently selected subplot (the second cell) is the current axes when title() runs.
Incorrect — the first cell was current earlier, but subplot(1,2,2) switched the current axes to the second cell before title() was called.
Incorrect — title() only affects the single currently active set of axes, not every subplot in the figure.
Incorrect — title() works perfectly well on an individual subplot’s axes.
beginner.concept: title() applies to the current axes

beginner.question: What is the difference between "close" and "close all"?
options: close closes only the current figure window; close all closes every open figure window
close closes every figure; close all closes only the current one
They are exactly the same command
close deletes the figure’s data; close all only hides the window
beginner.explanation: close (with no arguments) closes just the current figure (gcf); close all closes every figure window that is currently open.
optionExplanations: Correct — close is single-figure, close all is every figure.
Incorrect — this reverses their actual behavior.
Incorrect — they behave differently, as described above.
Incorrect — both simply close the window(s); there is no distinction like this in MATLAB.

beginner.question: When using legend, the number and order of labels given should match the number and order of lines that were plotted.
beginner.explanation: True. legend assigns each label, in the order given, to the corresponding line in the order it was added to the axes — mismatched counts or order will mislabel the lines.
optionExplanations: Correct — labels are matched to lines in plotting order.
Incorrect — mismatched or misordered labels will incorrectly label the lines.
commonMistakes: Listing legend labels in a different order than the lines were actually plotted.

beginner.question: Which single function call sets BOTH the x-axis and y-axis display ranges at once?
beginner.explanation: axis([xmin xmax ymin ymax]) sets both axis ranges in a single call, as an alternative to calling xlim and ylim separately.
optionExplanations: Correct — axis() with a 4-element vector sets both ranges at once.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
beginner.concept: Setting both axis ranges at once

beginner.question: Which line correctly completes this code to add gridlines to the plot?
beginner.explanation: grid on is the correct, complete command to turn on gridlines for the current axes.
optionExplanations: Correct — grid on turns on gridlines.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — grid is not a valid argument to pass inside a plot() call.

beginner.question: A plot’s title can be set with title(...) either before or after the plot() call, and the final displayed title looks the same either way.
beginner.explanation: True. title() sets the text of the current axes’ title regardless of when it’s called relative to plot() (as long as it’s not later overwritten or the axes cleared) — the end result is the same title either way.
optionExplanations: Correct — the order relative to plot() does not change the final title text shown.
Incorrect — title text placement does not depend on call order relative to plot().

beginner.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid MATLAB line-style symbol?
beginner.explanation: MATLAB's valid line styles are '-' (solid), '--' (dashed), ':' (dotted), and '-.' (dash-dot). '==' is not a recognized line-style symbol.
optionExplanations: Correct — "==" is not a valid MATLAB line-style symbol.
Incorrect — "--" is a valid dashed line style.
Incorrect — ":" is a valid dotted line style.
Incorrect — "-." is a valid dash-dot line style.

beginner.question: subplot(2,3,5) divides the current figure into a grid with how many total subplot cells?
beginner.explanation: subplot(m,n,p) divides the figure into an m-by-n grid. Here m=2 and n=3, so the grid has 2 × 3 = 6 total cells (this particular call selects cell 5 of those 6).

beginner.question: Which of the following functions are used to add text annotations to a plot (title, axis labels, or legend)? Select all that apply.
beginner.explanation: title, xlabel, and legend all add descriptive text to a plot. plot() itself draws the data — it doesn’t add any text annotation on its own.
beginner.concept: Annotation functions vs. the plotting function itself

intermediate.question: Which line correctly completes this code to plot y versus x?
intermediate.explanation: plot(x, y) plots the y-values against the corresponding x-values, which is what "y versus x" means.
optionExplanations: Correct — plots y as a function of x, in the conventional order.
Incorrect — this would plot x as a function of y, swapping the intended axes.
Incorrect — plot(x) alone plots x against its own index, not against y.
Incorrect — "sin" by itself is a function handle-like reference, not the computed data; this is not valid usage here.
commonMistakes: Swapping the x and y arguments to plot().

intermediate.question: What is the purpose of "hold on" in MATLAB plotting?
options: It keeps the current plot in place so later plot() calls are added to the same axes instead of replacing it
It pauses script execution until a key is pressed
It saves the current figure to disk
intermediate.explanation: hold on prevents a new plot() call from erasing the existing plot, so multiple lines can be layered onto the same axes.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is exactly what hold on does.
Incorrect — that describes pause, not hold on.
Incorrect — that describes saveas or print, not hold on.
Incorrect — that describes clf or cla, the opposite behavior of hold on.

intermediate.question: legend('a','b') labels the plot's axes rather than the plotted lines.
intermediate.explanation: False. legend labels the individual data series (lines/markers) shown in a plot; xlabel and ylabel label the axes.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — legend labels series, not axes.
Correct — legend identifies which line is which; axis labels come from xlabel/ylabel.
commonMistakes: Confusing legend() with xlabel()/ylabel().

intermediate.question: Which function sets the visible range of the x-axis on the current plot?
intermediate.explanation: xlim([a b]) sets the x-axis display range to [a b]. (ylim does the same for the y-axis.)
optionExplanations: Correct — xlim is the standard function for setting x-axis limits.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not valid axis() syntax.

intermediate.question: Which line correctly completes the missing x-axis label?
intermediate.explanation: xlabel('Time') sets the x-axis label. The parallel function ylabel('Position') is already shown labeling the y-axis.
optionExplanations: Correct — xlabel sets the x-axis label text.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — axis() controls axis limits/scaling, not label text.

intermediate.question: What does this code display in the legend?
intermediate.code:
t = 0:0.1:10;
plot(t, sin(t))
hold on
plot(t, cos(t))
legend('sin(t)', 'cos(t)')
options: Two entries: "sin(t)" labeling the first line, "cos(t)" labeling the second
Only "cos(t)", since it was plotted last
Only "sin(t)", since it was plotted first
An error, because legend needs exactly one label per plot() call, not two labels for one call
intermediate.explanation: Because hold on kept both lines on the axes, legend correctly assigns "sin(t)" to the first line added and "cos(t)" to the second, in the order given.
optionExplanations: Correct — both lines remain, and legend labels them in plotting order.
Incorrect — hold on preserved the first line too, so it still gets its own legend entry.
Incorrect — the second line is also present and labeled.
Incorrect — legend accepts one label per line total, not per plot() call; two labels for two lines is exactly correct here.

intermediate.question: Without specifying any colors, what happens when you plot() two lines on the same axes using hold on?
options: MATLAB automatically cycles through a default sequence of colors, so the two lines appear in different colors
Both lines are plotted in black, since no color was specified
MATLAB throws an error — a color must always be specified explicitly
The second line is invisible until a color is manually assigned
intermediate.explanation: MATLAB automatically assigns each new line a different color from a default color order, cycling through it as more lines are added — you don’t need to specify colors manually for lines to be visually distinguishable.
optionExplanations: Correct — automatic color cycling is MATLAB’s default plotting behavior.
Incorrect — lines are not all black by default; each gets a distinct default color.
Incorrect — color is optional; plot() works fine without it.
Incorrect — every plotted line is visible by default, just in a different automatically-assigned color.

intermediate.question: Which line correctly completes this code to plot a green, thick line?
intermediate.explanation: plot(x, y, 'g', 'LineWidth', 2) sets the line color to green via the line-spec string and increases the line width via the 'LineWidth' name-value pair.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'g' sets color, and the 'LineWidth' name-value pair sets thickness.
Incorrect — not a valid MATLAB line-spec string.
Incorrect — the Color property expects a color name/RGB value, not a plain-English description like this.
Incorrect — LineWidth(2) is not valid syntax; it should be the string 'LineWidth' followed by the numeric value 2.
intermediate.concept: Line-spec strings combined with name-value pairs

intermediate.question: axis equal forces the same scale on the x-axis and y-axis, so, for example, a circle is displayed as a circle rather than an ellipse.
intermediate.explanation: True. axis equal makes one unit along the x-axis represent the same physical length on screen as one unit along the y-axis, preventing shape distortion.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is exactly the purpose of axis equal.
Incorrect — axis equal specifically exists to prevent this kind of distortion.

intermediate.question: Which of the following would correctly set the y-axis range to run from 0 to 100? Select all that apply.
intermediate.explanation: ylim([0 100]) directly sets the y-range. axis([xlim 0 100]) reuses the current x-limits (via xlim, which returns the current [xmin xmax]) and sets y to [0 100]. axis([-inf inf 0 100]) leaves x auto-scaled (using -inf/inf as placeholders) while fixing y to [0 100]. ylim(0, 100) is invalid — ylim expects a single 2-element vector argument, not two separate numeric arguments.
intermediate.concept: Different valid ways to set y-axis limits
commonMistakes: Passing two separate numeric arguments to ylim/xlim instead of one 2-element vector.

intermediate.question: What does this code display?
options: Two lines on the same axes in a single plot() call — a solid blue line for y1 and a dashed red line for y2
Only the second pair (x, y2) is plotted; the first pair is ignored
An error, because plot() only accepts one x-y pair at a time
Two separate figure windows, one per line
intermediate.explanation: plot() accepts multiple x-y-linespec triplets in a single call, plotting each as its own line on the same axes — no hold on is needed when they’re all given to one plot() call like this.
optionExplanations: Correct — a single plot() call can plot multiple line pairs at once.
Incorrect — both pairs are plotted; nothing is ignored.
Incorrect — plot() explicitly supports multiple x-y pairs (with optional line specs) in one call.
Incorrect — this produces one figure with two lines, not two separate figures.
intermediate.concept: Multiple line pairs in a single plot() call

intermediate.question: Which function call places the text "Peak" directly on the plot at the data coordinates (5, 20)?
intermediate.explanation: text(x, y, 'string') places the given text string at the data coordinates (x, y) on the current axes.
optionExplanations: Correct — text(x, y, string) is the standard function for this.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB function.
Incorrect — not the correct function name/argument order for this task.
Incorrect — title() only sets the axes title text; it does not accept coordinates to place text elsewhere on the plot.
intermediate.concept: Placing text annotations on a plot

intermediate.question: subplot(2,2,1) and subplot(221) (a single three-digit number) refer to the same subplot cell.
intermediate.explanation: True. When rows, columns, and index are each single digits, MATLAB allows the shorthand of combining them into one number — subplot(221) means the same thing as subplot(2,2,1).
optionExplanations: Correct — this compact three-digit shorthand is valid MATLAB syntax for single-digit grid dimensions.
Incorrect — this shorthand is genuinely equivalent, not a different cell.

intermediate.question: Which line correctly completes this code to give the legend a location in the upper-left of the axes?
intermediate.code:
plot(t, hr); hold on; plot(t, bp);
_____
intermediate.explanation: legend accepts a 'Location' name-value pair, and 'northwest' is a valid named location corresponding to the upper-left corner of the axes.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'Location', 'northwest' is valid legend positioning syntax.
Incorrect — legend does not accept a bare positional string like 'upper-left'; it needs the 'Location' name-value pair.
Incorrect — position() is not how legend placement is set.
Incorrect — 'Position' with a raw [0 0] coordinate is not the correct way to request a named corner location like this.

intermediate.question: A figure is divided using subplot(3,2,p) for a 3-row, 2-column grid. Reading left-to-right, top-to-bottom, what value of p refers to the cell in the second row, second column?
intermediate.explanation: Cells are numbered left-to-right, then top-to-bottom: row 1 is p=1,2; row 2 is p=3,4; row 3 is p=5,6. The second row, second column is p=4.

intermediate.question: Match each plotting-related function to what it controls.
matchOptions: Whether new plot() calls replace or add to the current axes
The visible range of the x-axis
Whether gridlines are shown
Text labels identifying each plotted line
intermediate.explanation: xlim controls the x-axis range, grid controls gridline visibility, legend labels each series, and hold controls whether plot() replaces or accumulates on the current axes.

intermediate.question: Put these commands in a correct order to produce a figure with a labeled, gridded, titled plot of y versus x.
intermediate.explanation: x must be defined before y (which depends on it), y must exist before plot() can use it, and plot() must be called before any axes-decorating commands (labels, title, grid) can act on the resulting axes.

intermediate.question: Write a single line of MATLAB code that sets the x-axis range to [0, 10].
intermediate.explanation: xlim takes a single 2-element vector [xmin xmax] specifying the new x-axis range.

intermediate.question: A single plot() call can accept multiple x-y pairs, each with its own line-spec string, without needing hold on.
intermediate.explanation: True. hold on is only needed to accumulate lines across SEPARATE plot() calls; a single plot() call already supports multiple x-y-linespec triplets that all appear together.
optionExplanations: Correct — multiple line pairs in one plot() call don’t require hold on.
Incorrect — hold on is unnecessary within a single plot() call; it only matters between separate calls.
intermediate.concept: When hold on is (and isn’t) needed

intermediate.question: Which of the following correctly plot y = x.^2 with red circular markers connected by NO line (markers only)? Select all that apply.
intermediate.explanation: 'ro' combines the color 'r' and marker 'o' with no line-style character, which MATLAB interprets as markers-only with no connecting line — same effect as explicitly setting Color/Marker/LineStyle name-value pairs with LineStyle set to 'none'. 'r', 'o' as two separate string arguments is not valid line-spec syntax. 'r-o' includes a solid line style ('-') plus markers, so it draws a connected line WITH markers, not markers alone.
commonMistakes: Including a line-style character alongside a marker when only markers (no connecting line) were intended.

intermediate.question: What happens when this code runs?
options: Only the third plot (the square-root curve) ends up visible, because hold off was called before it
All three curves remain visible together
The first two curves stay, and the third is added as well
An error occurs at hold off
intermediate.explanation: hold off restores the default replace behavior. The third plot() call, made after hold off, replaces the axes contents entirely, leaving only the square-root curve visible.
optionExplanations: Correct — hold off means the next plot() call replaces everything before it.
Incorrect — hold off specifically ends the "keep adding lines" behavior.
Incorrect — the third plot() call replaces the first two rather than adding to them.
Incorrect — hold off is valid, ordinary MATLAB syntax and does not error.
intermediate.concept: hold off resets plot() to replace mode

intermediate.question: Which axis option automatically sets the axis limits tightly around the actual range of the plotted data, with no extra padding?
intermediate.explanation: axis tight sets the axis limits to exactly the range of the data, removing MATLAB’s default extra padding around the edges.
optionExplanations: Correct — axis tight removes the default padding around the data range.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB axis option.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB axis option.
Incorrect — not a real MATLAB axis option.

intermediate.question: Write a single line of MATLAB code that plots y versus x using a solid blue line with square markers.
intermediate.explanation: The line-spec string combines a color letter ('b'), a marker symbol ('s' for square), and a line style ('-' for solid), in any order.
intermediate.concept: Combining color, marker, and line style in one line-spec string
intermediate.hint: You need a color letter, a marker symbol, and a line-style symbol all in one short string.

intermediate.question: Calling xlim('auto') tells MATLAB to go back to automatically choosing the x-axis range based on the plotted data.
intermediate.explanation: True. Passing 'auto' to xlim (or ylim) restores MATLAB's automatic limit-selection behavior, undoing any manually set fixed range.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'auto' restores automatic axis-limit selection.
Incorrect — this is exactly what 'auto' does.

intermediate.question: Which of the following are valid reasons a plotted line might not be visible in the current axes view? Select all that apply.
options: The line was plotted, but its y-values fall entirely outside the currently set ylim range
hold off was called and a later plot() call replaced it
The line’s color happens to be white on a white plot background
The vector passed to plot() had zero elements
intermediate.explanation: All four are genuine reasons a line can end up invisible: it can be plotted outside the visible axis range, replaced by a later plot() call without hold on, colored the same as the background, or simply contain no data to draw in the first place.

advanced.question: You call plot(x, y) where x has 100 elements and y has 80 elements. What happens?
options: MATLAB throws an error, because x and y must have the same number of elements
MATLAB automatically truncates the longer vector to match the shorter one
MATLAB interpolates the shorter vector up to 100 points
MATLAB plots only the x vector against its own index
advanced.explanation: plot(x,y) requires x and y to have the same length, since each point (x(i), y(i)) must be paired. A mismatch raises a dimension error rather than being silently "fixed."
optionExplanations: Correct — MATLAB requires matching lengths and errors otherwise.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not silently truncate data; that would risk hiding a real bug.
Incorrect — plot() does not perform interpolation to reconcile mismatched lengths.
Incorrect — with two explicit arguments, MATLAB attempts to pair them, not fall back to a single-vector plot.
commonMistakes: Not checking that computed x and y vectors ended up the same length before plotting.

advanced.question: The student wanted both sin(t) and cos(t) to appear on the same axes, but only cos(t) shows up. What line is missing, and where?
options: "hold on" is missing, right after the first plot(t,y) call
"clf" is missing, right before the first plot(t,y) call
"legend" is missing, right after the first plot(t,y) call
"figure" is missing, right before the second plot call
advanced.explanation: Without hold on, the second plot(t, cos(t)) call replaces the axes contents instead of adding to them, so only the cosine curve remains visible. Adding hold on after the first plot keeps both curves.
optionExplanations: Correct — hold on prevents the second plot() call from erasing the first curve.
Incorrect — clf clears a figure; it wouldn’t solve the “only one curve shows” problem, and isn’t needed here.
Incorrect — legend would only label the curves, not make both of them appear.
Incorrect — adding figure before the second plot would put cos(t) in a separate window, not overlay it on the same axes as requested.
commonMistakes: Forgetting hold on and being surprised when only the most recent plot() call is visible.

advanced.question: Using subplot(2,1,1) and subplot(2,1,2) allows two separate plots to appear in one figure window, stacked vertically.
advanced.explanation: True. subplot(m,n,p) divides the current figure into an m-by-n grid of axes; subplot(2,1,1) and subplot(2,1,2) select the top and bottom cells of a 2-row, 1-column grid.
optionExplanations: Correct — this creates a 2×1 grid with two stacked plot areas in a single figure.
Incorrect — subplot is exactly designed to place multiple plots within one figure.

advanced.question: This code throws an error. Why?
options: x has 5 elements and y has 4 — plot(x, y) requires them to be the same length
plot cannot accept a range like 1:5 as an argument
y must be defined before x
Missing semicolons cause plot() to error
advanced.explanation: plot(x, y) pairs up x(i) with y(i) for every point, so x and y must have the same number of elements. Here x has 5 and y has 4, which MATLAB rejects with a dimension-mismatch error.
optionExplanations: Correct — mismatched lengths are exactly the problem.
Incorrect — 1:5 produces a perfectly normal numeric vector, which plot accepts.
Incorrect — variable definition order here is fine; x is used correctly after being defined.
Incorrect — semicolons only control output display, not whether code runs.

advanced.question: You want to compare systolic and diastolic blood pressure trends over time on the SAME axes, each as its own labeled line, with a legend distinguishing them. Which sequence of commands does this correctly?
options: plot(t, systolic); hold on; plot(t, diastolic); legend('Systolic', 'Diastolic')
advanced.explanation: hold on keeps the first line on the axes while the second plot() call adds the second line, and legend labels them in the order the lines were added.
optionExplanations: Correct — hold on plus a legend call is exactly how to overlay and label two series.
Incorrect — plot(t, systolic, diastolic) is not valid syntax for plotting two separate series this way.
Incorrect — without hold on, the second plot() call erases the first, leaving only diastolic visible, and there’s no legend.
Incorrect — subplot() creates a grid of separate axes; it doesn’t take data arguments like this.

advanced.question: A student wants a scatter-style plot (markers only, no connecting line) of ages vs. cholesterol, but this code draws a connected line with markers instead. What’s the fix?
advanced.code: plot(age, chol, 'ro-')
options: Remove the '-' from the line-spec string, leaving just 'ro' (color + marker, no line style)
Replace plot with scatter — plot() can never omit the connecting line
Add hold on before the plot() call
The code is already correct as written
advanced.explanation: 'ro-' explicitly includes the solid line style ('-'), so a connecting line IS drawn. Dropping the '-' (using just 'ro') keeps the red circle markers but removes the connecting line.
optionExplanations: Correct — the line-style character is what’s causing the connecting line; removing it fixes the issue.
Incorrect — plot() can absolutely produce markers-only output; scatter() isn’t required, just a different line-spec.
Incorrect — hold on controls whether new plots replace old ones; it doesn’t affect line style.
Incorrect — as written, this line-spec explicitly requests a connecting line.
advanced.concept: Removing the connecting line from a line-spec
commonMistakes: Including a line-style character in the line-spec when a markers-only appearance was intended.

advanced.question: You plot three ECG channels using three separate plot() calls with hold on, but all three end up in the same color because you keep manually specifying 'b' for every call. What is the simplest fix?
options: Remove the manual color argument entirely and let MATLAB’s default color cycling assign each line a distinct color automatically
Call figure before each plot() call
Call hold on three times, once per line
Use subplot instead of hold on
advanced.explanation: MATLAB automatically cycles through distinct default colors for successive lines added to the same axes — manually forcing every line to 'b' overrides that and defeats the automatic distinction. Simply omitting the color argument restores the automatic cycling.
optionExplanations: Correct — letting MATLAB choose colors automatically is the simplest fix here.
Incorrect — separate figures would put each channel in its own window, not overlay them for comparison.
Incorrect — hold on only needs to be called once; calling it repeatedly changes nothing about color.
Incorrect — subplot would separate the channels into different axes rather than overlay them as requested.
advanced.concept: Letting automatic color cycling do its job
commonMistakes: Manually hardcoding the same color for every line in a loop or sequence of plot() calls, defeating automatic color cycling.

advanced.question: The student wants both subplots to have gridlines, but only the bottom one does. What’s wrong?
advanced.code:
subplot(2,1,1)
plot(t, hr)
subplot(2,1,2)
plot(t, spo2)
grid on
options: grid on was only called once, after the second subplot() call, so it only affects the currently active (bottom) axes — a separate grid on is needed for each subplot
grid on can only ever apply to the very first subplot in a figure
plot() automatically disables gridlines on all but the last subplot
grid on needs to be called before any plot() commands, not after
advanced.explanation: Each subplot has its own independent axes, and grid on only affects the CURRENT axes at the time it’s called. Since it was called only once, after switching to the second subplot, only that subplot gets gridlines.
optionExplanations: Correct — grid on needs to be called once per subplot to affect that subplot’s axes.
Incorrect — grid on can be applied to any subplot’s axes, not just the first.
Incorrect — plot() has no such automatic gridline-disabling behavior.
Incorrect — grid on works whether called before or after plot(); the real issue is it was only called for one of the two subplots.
advanced.concept: Per-axes scope of grid on in subplots
commonMistakes: Calling an axes-affecting command like grid on only once, expecting it to apply to every subplot in the figure.

advanced.question: Calling cla instead of clf between two unrelated plots in the same figure keeps any subplot layout in place while clearing what was drawn.
advanced.explanation: True. cla clears the contents of the current axes but leaves the axes object (and any subplot layout) in place, whereas clf would remove the axes themselves, destroying the subplot layout too.
optionExplanations: Correct — cla preserves the axes/subplot structure, only removing what was drawn inside it.
Incorrect — this is exactly the distinction between cla and clf.
advanced.concept: cla vs. clf and subplot layout

advanced.question: You want to compare oxygen saturation curves from Trial A and Trial B, plotting each on its own dedicated axes so a reader can inspect either independently, without them visually overlapping. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: subplot(2,1,1) for Trial A and subplot(2,1,2) for Trial B, in one figure
plot both curves with hold on, in the same axes
Use two separate legend() calls in the same axes
Use two separate xlabel() calls in the same axes
advanced.explanation: subplot gives each trial its own separate axes, stacked in one figure — appropriate when curves should be independently inspectable rather than directly overlaid. hold on would overlay them on the same axes, which is the opposite of what’s being asked for here.
optionExplanations: Correct — subplot creates genuinely separate axes for independent inspection.
Incorrect — hold on overlays both curves on the SAME axes, which is not what was requested.
Incorrect — legend labels lines; it doesn’t create separate axes.
Incorrect — xlabel sets an axis label; it doesn’t create separate axes either.
advanced.concept: Choosing subplot vs. hold on based on the comparison being made

advanced.question: A student insists this code has a bug because the resulting figure shows only scattered markers with no connecting line between them, and they expected a "real plot." Is there actually a bug here?
options: No — 'ko' (black color + circle marker, with no line-style character) is deliberate markers-only syntax; a scatter of unconnected markers is exactly what it should produce
Yes — 'ko' is invalid syntax and should throw an error
Yes — plot() requires a line-style character to be present or it silently fails
Yes — the ages vector must be sorted in increasing order before plot() will accept it
advanced.explanation: 'ko' combines a color letter and a marker symbol with no line-style character, which MATLAB correctly renders as unconnected markers — there is nothing to fix. This is a case where the code is right and the student's expectation (that a "plot" must always include a connecting line) is the misconception.
optionExplanations: Correct — 'ko' is genuinely correct, deliberate markers-only syntax; nothing here is broken.
Incorrect — 'ko' is valid MATLAB line-spec syntax and does not throw an error.
Incorrect — plot() works perfectly well with no line-style character; it just means "no connecting line," not "invalid."
Incorrect — plot() accepts x-values in any order; it never requires sorted input.
advanced.concept: Distinguishing a real bug from a mistaken expectation about markers-only styling
commonMistakes: Assuming every plot() call must include a connecting line, and treating deliberate markers-only output as if it were broken.

advanced.question: A figure needs to show drug concentration on a scale spanning several orders of magnitude (0.01 to 1000) over time. Which of the following would help make the trend legible? Select all that apply.
options: Using a log-scaled y-axis (beyond plain plot(), MATLAB offers semilogy for exactly this) so widely-varying values are all visible at once
Adding a descriptive title and axis labels with units
Leaving the y-axis on a plain linear scale, which shows every value with equal precision regardless of magnitude
Adding a legend if more than one concentration curve is shown
advanced.explanation: A log-scaled y-axis (semilogy — beyond this topic’s core plot()/hold()/subplot() material, mentioned here as a preview) is specifically suited to data spanning orders of magnitude; without it, small values become visually indistinguishable near zero on a linear scale. A title, labeled axes, and a legend remain good practice regardless. A plain linear y-axis is actually the opposite of helpful here — small values would be compressed near the bottom.
advanced.concept: Choosing an appropriate axis scale for wide-ranging data

advanced.question: Calling subplot a second time with the SAME (rows, cols, index) arguments makes that subplot the current axes again, without erasing what was already plotted there.
advanced.explanation: True. Re-selecting an existing subplot with the same coordinates just makes it the current axes again for further commands (like adding another line with hold on) — it does not clear what’s already there.
optionExplanations: Correct — re-selecting a subplot does not clear its existing contents.
Incorrect — subplot() by itself does not erase existing content; only something like cla/clf would.

advanced.question: A student wants gridlines on a subplot grid of 4 patient plots but only wrote grid on once, at the very end. What is the most efficient fix, avoiding four nearly-identical blocks of repeated code?
advanced.code:
for p = 1:4
    subplot(2,2,p)
    plot(t, data(p,:))
end
grid on
options: Move grid on inside the loop, right after each plot() call, so it runs once per subplot
Call grid on four separate times outside the loop, once per subplot index
Replace the for loop with four separate hold on calls
grid on is a figure-wide setting and this code is already correct
advanced.explanation: Since grid on only affects the current axes, and the loop is already iterating over each subplot, the cleanest fix is to move grid on inside the loop body so it executes once per subplot — no repeated code blocks needed.
optionExplanations: Correct — this reuses the existing loop instead of hand-repeating code.
Incorrect — this works but throws away the benefit of the loop, requiring four near-duplicate lines instead of one moved line.
Incorrect — hold on controls whether plots accumulate; it has nothing to do with gridlines.
Incorrect — grid on is per-axes, not figure-wide, which is exactly why it currently only affects the last subplot.
advanced.concept: Applying an axes-level command inside a loop over subplots

advanced.question: A researcher lays out 12 patients’ plots in a grid using subplot(3,4,p) inside a loop for p = 1:12. How many rows does this grid have?
advanced.explanation: subplot(rows, cols, index) — here rows = 3 (the first argument), so the grid has 3 rows (and 4 columns, holding all 12 patients).

advanced.question: You need to visually compare gait cycle joint-angle curves from 5 trials, all on one shared set of axes with a shared, meaningful color per trial and a legend. Which combination of commands sets this up correctly?
options: A loop over the 5 trials calling plot() with hold on already active, followed by a single legend() call listing all 5 trial names after the loop
A loop calling figure and plot() for each trial, then one shared legend() call at the end
A single plot() call listing all 5 trials as separate arguments with no line specs, and no legend
subplot(5,1,trial) inside the loop, then one shared legend() call at the end
advanced.explanation: hold on (set once, before the loop) keeps every trial’s line on the same shared axes, and one legend() call after the loop, with all 5 names in plotting order, correctly labels every line.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is the standard pattern for accumulating and labeling multiple series on one shared axes.
Incorrect — calling figure inside the loop would put each trial in its own separate window, defeating the "one shared set of axes" goal.
Incorrect — a bare plot() call like this isn’t valid for combining five independent trial datasets this way, and there’s no legend to identify them.
Incorrect — subplot would give each trial its own separate axes, which is the opposite of the shared-axes comparison requested.
advanced.concept: Correctly overlaying and labeling multiple series from a loop

advanced.question: Which of the following would cause a legend to show the WRONG label next to a line? Select all that apply.
options: Listing the legend labels in a different order than the lines were plotted
Adding an extra line to the axes after legend() was already called, without updating the legend
Using a longer, more descriptive label text than the original variable name
Calling legend with the exact same number of labels as lines, in matching order
advanced.explanation: Mismatched order directly causes wrong labels. Adding a new line after legend() was called also leaves the legend showing only its original entries, effectively mislabeling the plot relative to what’s now shown. Longer, more descriptive labels are perfectly fine — legend text doesn’t need to match variable names. Matching count and order in the correct sequence is exactly the correct usage, not a source of error.
commonMistakes: Calling legend() before all lines have been added, so later lines end up unlabeled or the legend becomes stale.

advanced.question: If you call legend() BEFORE plotting all of your lines, lines added afterward will not automatically appear in the legend.
advanced.explanation: True. legend() captures the lines present in the axes (and the labels you give it) at the moment it’s called; lines added to the axes afterward are not automatically added to an already-created legend.
optionExplanations: Correct — a legend does not automatically track lines added after it was created.
Incorrect — later-added lines are not automatically picked up by an already-existing legend.
commonMistakes: Calling legend() too early, before every line that should be labeled has actually been plotted.

advanced.question: The student expects a 2x2 grid of 4 subplots but gets an error. What is wrong?
advanced.code:
for p = 1:5
    subplot(2,2,p)
    plot(t, data(p,:))
end
options: The loop runs p up to 5, but a 2×2 grid only has 4 valid subplot indices (1–4) — subplot(2,2,5) is out of range
subplot cannot be called inside a for loop
plot() cannot be called more than 4 times in a script
The grid should have been declared with a separate grid() function before the loop
advanced.explanation: A 2×2 grid has exactly 4 cells, indexed 1 through 4. Looping p from 1 to 5 attempts subplot(2,2,5), which has no valid cell to select, producing an error. Either the grid needs to be bigger (e.g., subplot(3,2,p) for up to 6 cells) or the loop should only run to 4.
optionExplanations: Correct — index 5 doesn’t exist in a 2×2 (4-cell) grid.
Incorrect — subplot is commonly and correctly used inside loops.
Incorrect — there’s no such limit on how many times plot() can be called in a script.
Incorrect — grid() (gridlines) is unrelated to declaring a subplot layout; subplot() itself defines the grid.
advanced.concept: subplot() index must not exceed the grid size
commonMistakes: Looping a subplot index past the total number of cells the grid actually has.

advanced.question: You want each of 4 subplots (one per patient) to share the exact same y-axis range so visual comparisons between patients aren’t misleading. What is the most direct way to enforce this?
options: Compute one shared [ymin ymax] range from all the data up front, then call ylim([ymin ymax]) once inside the loop, after selecting each subplot
Let each subplot auto-scale independently, since MATLAB always keeps y-ranges consistent across subplots by default
Call ylim only once, before the loop starts, and let it apply retroactively to all future subplots
Use different line colors for each subplot instead
advanced.explanation: MATLAB does NOT automatically keep y-axis ranges consistent across separate subplots — each auto-scales to its own data by default. Explicitly computing a shared range and calling ylim() for each subplot (after selecting it) is the direct way to force a fair, comparable scale.
optionExplanations: Correct — explicitly setting the same ylim for every subplot enforces a fair comparison.
Incorrect — subplots do NOT automatically share a y-range; each auto-scales independently by default.
Incorrect — ylim only affects the currently active axes at the moment it’s called, not axes created afterward.
Incorrect — line color doesn’t affect the y-axis scale at all, and isn’t relevant to fixing this comparison problem.
advanced.concept: Synchronizing axis ranges across subplots for fair comparison
commonMistakes: Assuming MATLAB automatically keeps y-axis ranges consistent across separate subplots.

advanced.question: Three lines are plotted but the legend only ends up showing two entries. What is the problem?
advanced.code:
plot(t, y1); hold on; plot(t, y2); plot(t, y3);
legend('Signal 1', 'Signal 2')
options: Only 2 labels were given to legend for 3 plotted lines, so the third line has no corresponding legend entry — a third label needs to be added
legend() automatically invents a label for any line it wasn't given a name for, using the variable name
MATLAB always throws an error whenever the label count doesn't match the number of plotted lines
This code is correct as written, since legend() only ever labels the two most recently plotted lines
advanced.explanation: legend needs one label per line you want identified. With only 2 labels supplied for 3 plotted lines, the third line ends up without a matching legend entry — add a third label string to cover it.
optionExplanations: Correct — the label count needs to match the number of lines that should be identified.
Incorrect — legend does not invent labels from variable names; it only uses the label strings you explicitly provide.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not require the counts to match and will not throw an error over this; it simply leaves extra lines unlabeled.
Incorrect — legend labels lines in the order they were plotted, starting from the first, not just the two most recent.
advanced.concept: Legend label count must match the number of lines to be identified
commonMistakes: Supplying fewer legend labels than the number of lines actually plotted on the axes.

advanced.question: A line's thickness can be set with the 'LineWidth' name-value pair even when a color is also specified through a line-spec string in the same plot() call.
advanced.explanation: True. A line-spec string (like 'r--') and name-value pairs (like 'LineWidth', 2) can be freely combined in the same plot() call — for example, plot(x, y, 'r--', 'LineWidth', 2).
optionExplanations: Correct — line-spec strings and name-value pairs can be combined in one call.
Incorrect — combining them is standard, valid MATLAB syntax.
advanced.concept: Combining line-spec strings with name-value pairs

advanced.question: A figure lays out sensor channels using subplot(4,3,p) (4 rows, 3 columns). How many total subplot cells does this grid provide?
advanced.explanation: subplot(rows, cols, index) creates a grid with rows × cols total cells: 4 × 3 = 12.

advanced.question: You have a 2×2 grid of subplots and want ONE title describing the whole figure, not a separate title per subplot. Calling title() after the last subplot() only labels that last subplot. What is the correct approach?
options: Use sgtitle(...) — a MATLAB function specifically for a single title spanning an entire grid of subplots (beyond this topic’s core material, but useful to know exists)
Call title() before the first subplot() call instead of after the last one
Manually call title() once for every individual subplot with the exact same text
It is not possible to add a single title covering an entire subplot grid in MATLAB
advanced.explanation: sgtitle(...) is designed specifically to place one title spanning an entire figure of subplots, unlike title(), which is always tied to whichever individual axes are currently active.
optionExplanations: Correct — sgtitle exists precisely for this whole-figure-title use case.
Incorrect — title() always applies to the currently active axes regardless of when it’s called; calling it earlier doesn’t make it figure-wide.
Incorrect — this would work but requires repeating the same text across every subplot rather than a single clean call.
Incorrect — MATLAB does support a single title spanning a subplot grid, via sgtitle.
advanced.concept: A single title spanning an entire subplot grid

advanced.question: A legend shows the correct NUMBER of entries, but each label sits next to the wrong line. Which of the following would actually fix this? Select all that apply.
options: Reorder the legend() label arguments to match the order the lines were actually plotted in
Re-check the actual plotting order and correct the label list to match it exactly
Increase the font size of the legend text
Move the legend box to a different corner of the plot
advanced.explanation: A label/line mismatch is fixed by correcting the ORDER of the labels to match plotting order — options 1 and 2 both describe doing that. Font size and legend position are purely cosmetic and don’t change which label is associated with which line.
advanced.concept: Fixing a legend label/line order mismatch

expert.question: You are plotting oxygen saturation (SpO2) for 3 patients on the same axes, generated inside a loop over for p = 1:3, and want each patient’s line correctly labeled in a legend. What is the key requirement?
options: Call hold on before the loop so all three plot() calls accumulate on the same axes, then call legend once after the loop with all three labels in the order the lines were plotted
Call legend inside the loop, immediately after every plot() call
Use a separate figure for each patient, so hold on is never needed
MATLAB automatically labels each line using the loop variable p
expert.explanation: hold on before the loop keeps every plot() call on the same axes instead of replacing the previous line. legend is then called once, after the loop, with labels listed in the same order the lines were added.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is the standard pattern for overlaying multiple series from a loop with one legend.
Incorrect — calling legend repeatedly inside the loop is unnecessary and typically only the final call’s labels remain relevant.
Incorrect — separate figures would prevent the requested side-by-side comparison on one set of axes.
Incorrect — MATLAB never auto-generates legend text from a loop variable.
expert.concept: Overlaying multiple series generated in a loop

expert.question: A student expects three separate colored lines but sees only one, and the legend labels don’t match. What is missing?
expert.code:
figure
for p = 1:3
    plot(t, spo2(p,:))
end
legend('Patient 1','Patient 2','Patient 3')
options: hold on before the loop — without it, each plot() call inside the loop erases the previous one, so only the last patient’s line remains
legend must be called inside the loop instead of after it
figure must be called on every iteration of the loop
plot cannot be used inside a for loop
expert.explanation: Without hold on, every plot() call inside the loop replaces the axes contents, so by the time the loop finishes, only patient 3’s line is left — but the legend still lists all three names, mismatched against the single visible line.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is precisely why only one line survives the loop.
Incorrect — a single legend call after the loop, with labels in order, is the standard (and simpler) approach.
Incorrect — calling figure every iteration would open 3 separate windows, defeating the goal of one combined plot.
Incorrect — plot() works perfectly well inside loops; that’s a common, valid pattern.
expert.concept: hold on inside a plotting loop
commonMistakes: Forgetting hold on before a loop of plot() calls and being surprised only the last line appears.

expert.question: Using subplot(3,1,p) inside a for p = 1:3 loop is a reasonable way to give each of 3 patients’ data its own stacked set of axes within a single figure.
expert.explanation: True. subplot(3,1,p) selects the p-th cell of a 3-row, 1-column grid of axes, so looping p from 1 to 3 places each patient’s plot into its own stacked panel within one figure.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is a standard, idiomatic use of subplot inside a loop.
Incorrect — this is a valid and commonly used pattern.
expert.concept: subplot inside a loop

expert.question: Which of the following genuinely make a multi-line physiological plot (e.g., 3 patients’ heart rate over time) easier to interpret? Select all that apply.
options: Axis labels with units, e.g. xlabel('Time (min)'), ylabel('Heart Rate (bpm)')
Removing all color so every line is plotted in black
expert.explanation: A legend, labeled axes with units, and a descriptive title all help a reader correctly interpret the plot. Removing color from a multi-line plot makes the individual lines harder, not easier, to tell apart.
expert.concept: Effective plot annotation

expert.question: Put these steps in the correct order — each line strictly depends on the one before it — to compute a smoothed peak value and use it in a plot title.
expert.explanation: raw must exist before movmean can smooth it; smoothed must exist before max() can find its peak; and peakValue must exist before it can be inserted into the title string. movmean is a MATLAB function beyond Unit 0’s core material — introduced here as a preview of the kind of pipeline later units build on.
expert.concept: Sequential data-to-plot pipelines

expert.question: You need to produce a figure comparing drug concentration decay curves for 6 different dosing regimens, on a y-axis spanning 3 orders of magnitude, each curve distinctly colored, with a legend and a shared title. Which combination of techniques is most appropriate?
options: A loop with hold on accumulating all 6 curves via semilogy (log-scaled y-axis), followed by one legend() call and one title() call
Six separate figure windows, one per regimen, each with its own linear-scale plot() and no legend needed
subplot(6,1,r) for each regimen on a linear scale, with no shared axis range
A single plot() call listing all 6 y-vectors with no color specs and no legend
expert.explanation: A shared log-scaled axis (semilogy) is appropriate for data spanning orders of magnitude, hold on accumulates all curves on one shared axes for direct comparison, and one legend() plus one title() call (after all curves are plotted) correctly labels everything once.
optionExplanations: Correct — this combination directly addresses the wide data range, the need for direct comparison, and correct labeling.
Incorrect — separate windows prevent the direct visual comparison that was the whole point, and a legend is still useful even split across figures if comparison across them is ever needed.
Incorrect — a linear scale would compress the visual differences given a 3-order-of-magnitude range, and separate subplots don’t give a single shared-axes comparison.
Incorrect — with no color specs or legend, the 6 curves would be indistinguishable from one another.
expert.concept: Combining log scaling, overlay, and labeling for a demanding comparison

expert.question: A student building a grid of 4 patient subplots wants each to share the y-axis label "Heart Rate (bpm)" but only wrote ylabel once, after the loop, and now only the last subplot has a label. Identify the fix that avoids four nearly-duplicated ylabel lines scattered through the code.
expert.code:
for p = 1:4
    subplot(2,2,p)
    plot(t, hr(p,:))
end
ylabel('Heart Rate (bpm)')
options: Move the ylabel call inside the loop body, right after each plot() call
ylabel() can only be called once per figure, so this limitation cannot be worked around
Replace ylabel with title, which labels every subplot in a figure at once
Call figure before the loop starts so ylabel applies figure-wide
expert.explanation: Like grid on and other axes-level commands, ylabel only affects the currently active axes when it runs. Moving it inside the existing loop (right after each subplot’s plot() call) reuses the loop structure that’s already iterating over every subplot, with no duplicated code blocks.
optionExplanations: Correct — reusing the existing loop structure is the appropriate fix, exactly as with grid on in a similar case.
Incorrect — ylabel can be called as many times as needed, once per axes.
Incorrect — title() is also a per-axes command, not a figure-wide one; it would have exactly the same one-subplot-only issue.
Incorrect — figure() creates a new window; it doesn’t change which axes ylabel applies to, and there’s no such thing as a figure-wide ylabel.
expert.concept: Per-axes labeling commands inside a subplot loop
commonMistakes: Calling a per-axes command once, outside a loop over subplots, expecting it to apply everywhere.

expert.question: You’re preparing a figure for a manuscript comparing pre- and post-treatment EMG amplitude across 8 subjects. Which of the following choices would genuinely improve clarity and correctness of the figure? Select all that apply.
options: Using consistent line colors/styles across subplots to represent the same condition (e.g., always blue for "pre," always red for "post")
Setting a shared y-axis range across all subplots so amplitude differences are visually comparable
Randomizing which color represents "pre" vs. "post" in each subplot to keep the figure visually varied
Including a legend or clear labeling scheme so a reader doesn’t have to guess what each color means
expert.explanation: Consistent encoding of conditions, a shared comparable axis range, and clear labeling are all genuine best practices for a comparison figure. Randomizing color meaning across subplots actively harms interpretability — a reader would have to re-learn the color coding for every subplot.
expert.concept: Design choices for a scientifically honest comparison figure

expert.question: Put these steps in the correct order — each strictly depends on the one before it — to build a 2×1 subplot figure comparing raw and smoothed sensor data, with a shared title-like annotation.
expert.explanation: raw must be defined before it can be smoothed; smoothed must exist before it can be plotted in the second subplot; and typically the raw-signal subplot is set up before the smoothed one, though the two subplot blocks could in principle be swapped — what strictly cannot change is that both raw and smoothed must be computed before either is plotted. movmean is beyond Unit 0’s core material, introduced here as a preview.
expert.concept: Sequencing a data-processing-then-plotting pipeline across subplots

expert.question: Two figures with identical data but different y-axis ranges (one auto-scaled, one manually fixed) can visually suggest very different conclusions about how much a value changed, even though the underlying numbers are the same.
expert.explanation: True. A tightly auto-scaled axis can make a small change look dramatic, while a wide fixed range can make the same change look negligible — axis range is a real, easily-overlooked source of potentially misleading visual interpretation, which is exactly why deliberately choosing (and reporting) axis ranges matters in scientific figures.
optionExplanations: Correct — identical data can look very different depending on the chosen axis range.
Incorrect — axis range genuinely changes the visual impression of the same underlying data.
expert.concept: Axis range as a source of visual (mis)interpretation

expert.question: A student’s script produces 3 overlapping figures instead of one figure with 3 overlaid lines, because they misunderstood the difference between two similarly-behaving commands. What did they most likely do?
expert.code:
for trial = 1:3
    figure
    plot(t, data(trial,:))
end
options: Called figure inside the loop, which always opens a brand-new window, instead of calling hold on once before the loop to accumulate lines on one shared set of axes
Forgot to preallocate the data matrix before the loop
Used a for loop instead of a while loop
expert.explanation: figure always opens a new window when called — placing it inside the loop guarantees 3 separate figures. Removing the figure call and instead calling hold on once, before the loop, would keep all 3 lines together on one shared set of axes.
optionExplanations: Correct — figure() inside a loop is exactly what produces separate windows.
Incorrect — plot() is the correct function to draw each line; the issue is the repeated figure() call, not plot() itself.
Incorrect — preallocation is a performance concern, unrelated to how many figure windows appear.
Incorrect — the loop type (for vs. while) has no bearing on how many figure windows get created.
expert.concept: figure() inside a loop vs. hold on before a loop
commonMistakes: Calling figure() inside a loop when the goal was actually to overlay lines with hold on.

expert.question: A researcher builds a subplot grid for 10 patients using subplot(m, 3, p) inside a loop for p = 1:10, choosing the smallest number of rows m that still fits all 10 patients in a 3-column grid. What is m?
expert.explanation: With 3 columns, 3 rows only provide 9 cells (not enough for 10 patients); 4 rows provide 12 cells, which is the smallest number of rows that fits all 10 (with 2 cells left empty).
expert.concept: Sizing a subplot grid to fit a given number of items

expert.question: A colleague’s script produces one figure per patient in a loop, and they now want to instead produce ONE figure with all patients on separate stacked subplots. Which changes are necessary? Select all that apply.
options: Replace each loop iteration’s figure call with a single figure call placed before the loop
Add a subplot(n,1,p) call inside the loop, selecting the correct cell for each patient
Remove the plot() calls entirely, since subplot() draws the data automatically
Adjust the subplot() row count n to match the total number of patients
expert.explanation: Moving figure() outside the loop ensures only one window is created; adding subplot() inside the loop routes each patient into its own cell of that one figure; and n must match the patient count so every patient has a valid cell. plot() calls are still required — subplot() only selects/creates axes, it does not draw any data itself.
expert.concept: Refactoring "one figure per item" into "one figure with a subplot grid"

expert.question: You are asked to build a single figure that: (1) shows raw and filtered EMG signals overlaid on one set of axes, (2) shows a separate subplot with the corresponding force output over the same time axis, and (3) clearly labels both. Which overall structure achieves this?
options: subplot(2,1,1): plot raw, hold on, plot filtered, add legend and title. subplot(2,1,2): plot force, add labels and title.
Plot all three signals (raw EMG, filtered EMG, force) on one single set of axes with hold on, and skip subplot entirely
Use three separate figure windows, one per signal
subplot(3,1,p) for each of the three signals separately, with no hold on used anywhere
expert.explanation: This structure correctly groups the two EMG traces together (since they share the same physical quantity and benefit from direct overlay comparison) in one subplot, while giving force its own separate subplot (since it’s a different physical quantity, better shown on its own axes) — matching exactly what was asked for.
optionExplanations: Correct — this matches the requested grouping: EMG traces overlaid together, force on its own subplot.
Incorrect — putting force on the same axes as EMG signals (likely very different units/scales) would make the plot hard to interpret and doesn’t match the requested separate subplot for force.
Incorrect — three separate windows would prevent the requested overlay of raw and filtered EMG on one set of axes.
Incorrect — this would give raw EMG and filtered EMG each their own separate axes rather than overlaying them as requested.
expert.concept: Structuring a figure that mixes overlay and separate-subplot requirements

expert.question: Manually setting identical, fixed axis limits (via xlim/ylim) across every subplot in a multi-patient comparison figure removes a real (if often overlooked) source of misleading visual comparison, at the cost of extra code to compute the shared range up front.
expert.explanation: True. Since MATLAB auto-scales each subplot independently by default, patients with a narrower data range would otherwise appear to have "more dramatic" changes purely due to a tighter auto-scaled axis — fixing a shared range removes that artifact, at the modest cost of computing the shared min/max beforehand.
optionExplanations: Correct — this trade-off (extra setup code for a fairer, non-misleading comparison) is a genuine and worthwhile one.
Incorrect — independent auto-scaling across subplots is a real source of potentially misleading comparison, not a non-issue.
expert.concept: Trade-offs of enforcing shared axis ranges across subplots

expert.question: A student’s loop is meant to plot 5 patients’ curves in 5 different, clearly distinguishable colors, but ends up with all 5 curves in the same default blue. What is the most likely cause?
expert.code:
hold on
for p = 1:5
    plot(t, data(p,:), 'Color', 'b')
end
options: The 'Color', 'b' name-value pair explicitly forces every line to blue, overriding automatic color cycling — removing it lets MATLAB assign a distinct color to each line automatically
hold on prevents color cycling from working
for loops always plot every line in the same color, regardless of any color argument
plot() ignores Color name-value pairs inside a loop
expert.explanation: Explicitly specifying 'Color', 'b' on every call forces every line to blue — exactly the same underlying issue as an earlier "everything is one color" question, but here dressed up in name-value-pair syntax instead of a line-spec string. Removing the explicit color argument restores MATLAB’s automatic per-line color cycling.
optionExplanations: Correct — the explicit blue color argument is what’s overriding automatic color cycling.
Incorrect — hold on is what enables multiple lines to coexist on the axes at all; it doesn’t interfere with color cycling.
Incorrect — for loops have no inherent effect on plot colors; the color comes entirely from what’s passed to plot().
Incorrect — plot() honors Color name-value pairs everywhere, loop or not — that’s precisely why every line here is forced blue.
expert.concept: Explicit color arguments overriding automatic color cycling (name-value pair form)
commonMistakes: Hardcoding the same explicit color for every line generated in a loop.

expert.question: Before sharing a multi-panel figure with a research team, which of the following checks are worth doing? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm every subplot that should have a title, axis labels, and (if applicable) a legend actually has one — not just the last one touched
Confirm axis ranges are either consistently shared (if comparison is intended) or clearly justified if they differ
Confirm the figure still displays correctly with hold on left permanently on for any axes that shouldn’t keep accumulating lines
Assume that because the code ran without throwing an error, the figure must be correct
expert.explanation: Because axes-level commands like title/xlabel/legend/grid only affect the currently active axes, it’s easy to accidentally leave one subplot unlabeled — worth explicitly checking. Consistent (or justified) axis ranges and correctly-scoped hold on state are both real, common sources of subtly wrong-looking figures that still run without any error. Running without an error says nothing about whether the figure is visually correct — MATLAB doesn’t know what you intended it to look like.
expert.concept: Pre-sharing sanity checks for multi-panel figures

expert.question: A figure lays out 7 sensor channels using subplot(4,2,p) for p = 1:7 (4 rows, 2 columns). How many of the 8 available grid cells are left empty?
expert.explanation: A 4×2 grid has 4 × 2 = 8 total cells. Only 7 are used (p = 1 to 7), leaving 8 − 7 = 1 cell empty.
expert.concept: Computing unused cells in a subplot grid

expert.question: You need a figure showing 4 subjects’ dose-response curves that (a) share one legend since the same 4 subjects appear on 2 separate subplots showing different outcome measures, and (b) each line must be the same color for the same subject across both subplots. What is the most reliable strategy?
options: Explicitly assign and reuse a fixed line-spec (e.g., a specific color) per subject in both subplots, rather than relying on each subplot’s own independent automatic color cycling
Rely entirely on automatic color cycling in both subplots, since MATLAB is guaranteed to assign the same colors in the same order in every subplot
Use a single legend() call before any plotting begins
Plot all 4 subjects’ data for both outcome measures on one shared set of axes instead of two subplots
expert.explanation: Each subplot has its own independent axes and its own independent automatic color cycling — there is no built-in guarantee that "subject 1" gets the same automatic color in both subplots. Explicitly assigning and reusing a specific color per subject in both subplots is the reliable way to keep the color coding consistent across them.
optionExplanations: Correct — explicit, reused color assignment is the only reliable way to guarantee consistency across independently-cycling subplots.
Incorrect — automatic color cycling is independent per set of axes; there’s no guarantee it lines up the same way across two different subplots.
Incorrect — legend() needs the actual lines to exist (with their final labels) before it can correctly capture them; calling it before any plotting is premature.
Incorrect — combining two different outcome measures onto one shared axes conflates unrelated quantities and doesn’t match the two-subplot structure requested.
expert.concept: Ensuring consistent color coding across independent subplot color cycles

expert.question: It is possible to write a script that runs from top to bottom without any error, yet still produces a figure that visually misrepresents the underlying data (e.g., through a misleading axis range or inconsistent color coding).
expert.explanation: True. MATLAB only checks that code is syntactically valid and that function calls are used correctly — it has no concept of whether the resulting figure is a faithful, non-misleading representation of the data. That judgment call is entirely the author’s responsibility.
optionExplanations: Correct — error-free execution says nothing about whether a figure is visually honest or well-designed.
Incorrect — plenty of misleading-but-valid figures are entirely possible; MATLAB has no way to catch that kind of problem.
expert.concept: Error-free code vs. a correct, honest figure

expert.question: Only the last subplot ends up with a (misleading) title, and the other three remain untitled. What is the bug?
expert.code:
figure
for p = 1:4
    subplot(2,2,p)
    plot(t, data(p,:))
end
title(sprintf('Patient %d', p))
options: title() runs only once, after the loop ends, so it only affects the last subplot (p=4) — the sprintf/title call needs to move inside the loop so it runs once per subplot
sprintf cannot be used inside a title() call
The loop variable p is automatically deleted as soon as the loop finishes, so title() actually throws an error
title() automatically applies retroactively to every subplot that was visited during the loop
expert.explanation: title() only ever affects the currently active axes at the moment it runs. Called once after the loop, it only labels whichever subplot was selected last (p=4) — and since p still holds its final loop value (4), every implied reference to "Patient" would be wrong for the other three subplots anyway. Moving the title/sprintf call inside the loop, right after each subplot() call, fixes both problems at once.
optionExplanations: Correct — moving title() inside the loop makes it run once per subplot, using the correct p each time.
Incorrect — sprintf works perfectly well as an argument to title().
Incorrect — MATLAB for-loop variables are NOT deleted when the loop ends; they retain their final value as an ordinary variable.
Incorrect — title() never applies retroactively; it only affects the axes that are current at the exact moment it is called.
expert.concept: Per-axes title() combined with a loop variable used in sprintf
commonMistakes: Calling title() with a loop-variable-based string outside the loop, so every intended distinct title collapses into one, applied to only the last axes.

expert.question: With p = 4, which of the following correctly build the exact string 'Patient 4' (with the space)? Select all that apply.
expert.explanation: sprintf('Patient %d', p) and ['Patient ' num2str(p)] (bracket concatenation of a char array that already includes the trailing space, with the number-as-text) both correctly produce 'Patient 4'. 'Patient ' + p performs numeric addition on the character codes of 'Patient ' plus the number p — it does not build a text string at all. ['Patient' num2str(p)] is missing the space in the literal text ('Patient' with no trailing space), so it produces 'Patient4', not 'Patient 4'.
expert.concept: Building dynamic title/label strings correctly
commonMistakes: Using + to combine text and a number, which performs numeric addition on character codes instead of building a string.
Forgetting to include a literal space when concatenating text and a number-as-text.

expert.question: After 'for p = 1:4 ... end' finishes running, the variable p still exists in the Workspace and holds its final value (4), unless it is explicitly cleared or reassigned afterward.
expert.explanation: True. A for-loop variable in MATLAB is an ordinary variable — it is not automatically removed when the loop ends, and it retains whatever value it held on the last completed iteration.
optionExplanations: Correct — the loop variable persists in the Workspace with its final value.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not automatically clear loop variables when a loop finishes.
expert.concept: Loop variables persist after the loop ends

expert.question: You need a 2×3 grid of 6 subplots where every subplot has BOTH its own unique title AND a shared x-axis label "Time (s)". What is the correct, efficient way to add both to every subplot?
options: Inside the same loop that already builds each subplot, call both the unique title() and the shared xlabel() once per subplot, right after each plot() call
MATLAB automatically shares one xlabel across every subplot in a grid, so only the title needs to be added per subplot
Call xlabel once after the loop finishes; it retroactively applies to every subplot that was created
It is not possible for every subplot in a grid to have its own individual x-axis label
expert.explanation: Both title and xlabel are per-axes commands, exactly like grid on and ylabel in earlier scenarios — reusing the existing subplot loop to call both once per subplot (with the shared "Time (s)" text for xlabel and a unique string for title) correctly labels all 6 subplots in one pass.
optionExplanations: Correct — both per-axes commands belong inside the existing loop.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not automatically share an xlabel across separate subplots; each is independent.
Incorrect — a command run once after the loop only ever affects whichever axes happen to be current at that moment, not every subplot created earlier.
Incorrect — every individual subplot absolutely can have its own xlabel; it just requires calling xlabel once per subplot.
expert.concept: Combining a unique per-subplot title with a shared per-subplot axis label

expert.question: A researcher needs to fit 9 patients into a grid with exactly 2 rows, using subplot(2, n, p). What is the smallest number of columns n that provides enough cells for all 9 patients?
expert.explanation: With 2 rows, the grid holds 2n cells. 2×4 = 8 is not enough for 9 patients; 2×5 = 10 is the smallest multiple of 2 that reaches at least 9, so n = 5 (with 1 cell left empty).

intermediate.concept: Correctly testing a range with two comparisons

intermediate.question: Because && requires scalar operands, writing "if v1 > 0 && v2 > 0" where v1 and v2 are multi-element vectors produces an error rather than silently doing something unexpected.
intermediate.explanation: True. && (and ||) require both operands to be convertible to a scalar logical value. If v1 > 0 produces a vector of multiple true/false values, MATLAB raises an error rather than guessing what you meant.
optionExplanations: Correct — && genuinely requires scalar operands and errors on arrays.
Incorrect — this does error; MATLAB does not silently handle non-scalar && operands.

intermediate.question: n = 4; if mod(n,2) == 0, if n > 2, y = 100; else, y = 200; end; else, y = 300; end — what is y?
intermediate.explanation: mod(4,2) = 0, so the outer if is true, entering the nested if. n > 2 (4 > 2) is also true, so y = 100.

intermediate.question: Which of the following are valid reasons to use & instead of && in a piece of code? Select all that apply.
options: The operands are non-scalar arrays and an element-wise result is wanted
Both sides must always be evaluated (no short-circuiting), even if the first is false
intermediate.explanation: & is the right choice for element-wise operations on arrays, or when you specifically need both sides evaluated regardless of short-circuiting. There is no general performance advantage to &, and "difficulty levels" is not a real property of either operator.

intermediate.question: What is the value of result?
intermediate.code:
a = true; b = false; c = true;
result = a || b && c;
options: true, because && evaluates before ||, making this a || (b && c)
true, because operators always evaluate strictly left to right
Error: cannot mix && and || in one expression
intermediate.explanation: && has higher precedence than ||, so this parses as a || (b && c). b && c is false && true = false. a || false is true || false = true.
optionExplanations: Correct — && binds tighter than ||, just like * binds tighter than + in arithmetic.
Incorrect — a is true, so the overall || result is true regardless of the && part.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not evaluate mixed && / || strictly left to right; precedence applies.
Incorrect — mixing && and || in one expression is valid MATLAB syntax.

intermediate.question: Match each logical operator to its behavior.
matchOptions: Short-circuit AND (scalar operands only)
Short-circuit OR (scalar operands only)
Element-wise AND (works on arrays)
Logical NOT
intermediate.explanation: && and || are the short-circuit, scalar-only logical operators typically used in if conditions. & performs element-wise AND and works on arrays. ~ negates a logical value.

intermediate.question: Put these lines in the correct order to classify heart rate hr into 'Low', 'Normal', or 'High', checking the low bound first.
intermediate.explanation: hr must be defined before it is tested; the if/elseif/else chain then checks the low bound first, the normal range next, and falls back to High otherwise, closed by end.

intermediate.question: Write a single MATLAB condition expression (just the expression, no "if" keyword, no "end") that is true exactly when x is less than 0 OR greater than 100.
intermediate.explanation: Two comparisons joined by || correctly express "either of these is true."

intermediate.question: Write the MATLAB expression (not a full if statement) that tests whether bp is NOT equal to 120.
intermediate.explanation: The ~= operator directly expresses "not equal to."

intermediate.question: What is displayed?

    case 'A'
        disp(1)
    case 'B'

    case 'C'

end

Incorrect — disp(2) is what runs, not disp(x).
Incorrect — the matched case runs disp(2), not disp of the switch expression.
