intermediate.question: Which of the following if-conditions correctly detect that a vector v has AT LEAST ONE negative element? Select all that apply.
intermediate.explanation: any(v < 0) is the direct, idiomatic way to test "at least one." ~isempty(find(v < 0)) also works, if awkwardly. Using v < 0 directly as an if-condition requires EVERY element to be true (MATLAB’s if applies all() semantics to array conditions), which is not "at least one." all(v < 0) tests the opposite — every element negative.
intermediate.concept: Testing "at least one" element of a vector

intermediate.question: When you write "if v" where v is a vector (not a scalar), MATLAB treats the condition as true only if EVERY element of v is nonzero.
intermediate.explanation: True. For a non-scalar array condition, MATLAB’s if (and while) require every element to be nonzero — equivalent to applying all() to the array.
optionExplanations: Correct — if on an array condition requires all elements to be nonzero.
Incorrect — this is precisely how MATLAB evaluates a non-scalar if-condition.
intermediate.concept: if condition semantics for non-scalar arrays

advanced.question: What does this code display, and why is the "otherwise" branch not triggered?
advanced.code:

switch x
    case 1
        disp('one')
    case 5
        disp('five')
    otherwise
        disp('other')
end
advanced.explanation: switch compares x against each case in order and executes the first match. x = 5 matches "case 5", so "five" is displayed and otherwise is never reached.
optionExplanations: Correct — x matches case 5 directly, so that branch runs and switch exits.
Incorrect — otherwise only runs when no case matches; here, case 5 matches.
Incorrect — case 1 is checked first but does not match x = 5, so it’s skipped.
Incorrect — MATLAB’s switch works fine with numeric values, not just strings.

advanced.question: You want to flag hypertension only when a diastolic reading is above 90 mmHg AND a systolic reading is above 140 mmHg — both conditions must hold. Which logical operator combines them correctly?
advanced.explanation: && is logical AND — the combined condition is only true when both the diastolic and systolic checks are true, matching “both must hold.”
optionExplanations: Correct — && requires both conditions to be true simultaneously.
Incorrect — | is logical OR; it would flag hypertension if only ONE condition were true, which is not what’s required.
Incorrect — xor is true only when exactly one condition holds, the opposite of “both must hold.”
Incorrect — ~ is logical NOT, a negation operator, not a way to combine two conditions.

advanced.question: In an if / elseif / else chain, MATLAB evaluates the conditions in order and executes only the first block whose condition is true.
advanced.explanation: True. As soon as one condition evaluates to true, its block runs and the rest of the chain (including any later elseif or else) is skipped entirely.
optionExplanations: Correct — the chain short-circuits at the first true condition.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not evaluate every condition and does not run multiple blocks in a single if/elseif/else chain.

advanced.question: For bp = 145, what does this code display, and why don’t the later elseif branches also run?

    disp('Stage 2 Hypertension')
elseif bp > 130
    disp('Stage 1 Hypertension')

    disp('Elevated')

    disp('Normal')

options: 'Stage 2 Hypertension' — once the first true condition is found, MATLAB runs that block and skips the rest of the chain
'Normal' — because 145 fails the final else condition
All four messages are displayed, one per branch
Nothing — bp must be a string for comparisons like this to work
advanced.explanation: bp > 140 is true for bp = 145, so MATLAB runs that block and immediately exits the entire if/elseif/else chain — the remaining elseif and else branches are never even evaluated.
optionExplanations: Correct — the first true condition wins, and the rest of the chain is skipped.
Incorrect — else only runs when every preceding condition is false, which isn’t the case here.
Incorrect — an if/elseif/else chain runs at most one block, never all of them.
Incorrect — bp is a perfectly valid number for numeric comparisons; no string conversion is needed.

advanced.question: If none of the conditions in an if/elseif chain with no else are true, MATLAB throws an error because it expects some branch to execute.
advanced.explanation: False. If no condition is true and there’s no else, MATLAB simply runs none of the branches and continues on with the rest of the script — no error occurs.
optionExplanations: Incorrect — MATLAB does not require some branch to run; skipping all of them is perfectly valid.
Correct — the chain simply does nothing if no condition matches and there’s no else.

advanced.question: What does this code display for o2 = 91 (blood oxygen saturation %)?

    disp('Critical')

    disp('Low')
else
    disp('Normal')

Incorrect — 91 is not below the Critical threshold of 90.
Incorrect — o2 < 95 matches before the else is ever reached.
Incorrect — this is valid, error-free syntax.
advanced.concept: Tracing an elseif chain with SpO2 thresholds

advanced.question: This code fails to run at all (a parse/syntax error). What is the bug?
advanced.code:
hr = 45;
if hr > 100
    disp('Tachycardia')
else if hr < 60
    disp('Bradycardia')
else
    disp('Normal')
end
options: Writing "else if" as two words starts a NESTED if inside the else block, which needs its own end — but only one end is provided for both the outer and nested if
This correctly prints Bradycardia for hr=45, exactly as intended
This prints both Tachycardia and Bradycardia
MATLAB automatically treats "else if" as "elseif" so this runs fine
advanced.explanation: MATLAB parses "else if" as two words as: else, followed by a brand-new nested if statement — which needs its own end before the outer if's end. With only one end total, the block structure is unbalanced and MATLAB reports a parse error.
optionExplanations: Correct — "else if" as two words nests a nested if, requiring an extra end that is missing here.
Incorrect — this code does not run successfully; it is a parse error.
Incorrect — a parse error prevents the code from running at all.
Incorrect — MATLAB does not silently rewrite "else if" into "elseif"; they parse very differently.
advanced.concept: "else if" (two words) creates a nested block requiring its own end
commonMistakes: Writing "else if" as two words, intending elseif behavior, without realizing it creates a nested if requiring an additional end.

advanced.question: You want to flag a lab value v as abnormal if it is either below lowLim OR above highLim. Which condition correctly implements "outside the reference range"?
advanced.explanation: v cannot be both below lowLim AND above highLim simultaneously, so the && version is always false. The chained "lowLim < v < highLim" is the classic pitfall — it does not test a range. Comparing only against the two limit values with ~= misses everything strictly between them.
optionExplanations: Correct — either bound being violated correctly flags "outside the range."
Incorrect — a value can never satisfy both conditions at once, so this is always false.
Incorrect — this chained comparison does not test a range in MATLAB.
Incorrect — this only excludes the exact limit values, not the whole abnormal range.
advanced.concept: Correctly expressing "outside a range" with OR

advanced.question: glucose = 145; if glucose >= 200, flag = 3; elseif glucose >= 140, flag = 2; elseif glucose >= 100, flag = 1; else, flag = 0; end — what is flag?
advanced.explanation: glucose = 145 fails glucose >= 200 but satisfies glucose >= 140, so flag = 2.

advanced.question: A script uses "if isfield(patientData,'weight') && patientData.weight > 0". Which statements about why && matters here are correct? Select all that apply.
options: If isfield returns false, && short-circuits and never evaluates patientData.weight, avoiding an error from accessing a nonexistent field
Using & instead of && would always still work identically here, with no risk
If & were used instead, MATLAB would attempt to evaluate patientData.weight even when the field does not exist, which could error
&& only works with numeric inputs, never with the output of isfield
advanced.explanation: && short-circuits, so once isfield returns false, patientData.weight is never evaluated. & does not short-circuit — it would attempt to evaluate both sides regardless, risking an error when the field is missing. isfield returns a logical value, which && handles perfectly well.

advanced.question: What does this code display?

    otherwise
        disp('other')
end
advanced.explanation: switch performs an exact numeric equality match. 2.0 and 2 are the same double-precision value, so case 2 matches and "two" is displayed.
optionExplanations: Correct — 2.0 and 2 are numerically identical.
Incorrect — 2.0 does match case 2 exactly.
Incorrect — this is valid, error-free syntax.
Incorrect — the matching case produces output.
advanced.concept: switch numeric matching uses exact equality

advanced.question: This code produces a syntax error. Why?
advanced.code:
flag = true;
if flag = false
    disp('off')
end
options: A single = is assignment, not comparison — if requires ==, and MATLAB does not allow a bare assignment as an if-condition expression
flag cannot be declared using true/false in MATLAB
if cannot be combined with logical variables
advanced.explanation: MATLAB does not support inline assignment-as-expression the way some C-family languages do. "flag = false" inside an if-condition is not a valid expression, so this is a parse error — the fix is "if flag == false" (or simply "if ~flag").
optionExplanations: Correct — assignment is not a valid if-condition expression in MATLAB.
Incorrect — true and false are valid ways to create logical values.
Incorrect — if works perfectly well with logical variables (that is the intended fix here, using ==).
Incorrect — disp() is written correctly; the error is in the if-condition.
advanced.concept: Assignment (=) is not valid inside an if-condition
commonMistakes: Writing = instead of == inside a condition, expecting MATLAB to interpret it as a comparison.

advanced.question: In "if x == 5", where x is an ordinary scalar variable (technically a 1x1 array under the hood), the comparison behaves exactly the same as comparing two plain numbers.
advanced.explanation: True. Nearly all "plain numbers" in MATLAB are, technically, 1x1 (scalar) arrays. Comparisons between them behave exactly like ordinary numeric comparisons — the array machinery is invisible for the scalar case.
optionExplanations: Correct — scalar arrays behave just like ordinary numbers for comparisons.
Incorrect — there is no special or different behavior for scalar comparisons in MATLAB.

        disp('Bradycardia')
    otherwise
        disp('Normal')

Incorrect — high without quotes would be interpreted as an undefined variable, not the text 'high'.
Incorrect — if is not valid syntax inside a switch block.
Incorrect — a colon after case is not valid MATLAB syntax.

advanced.question: A researcher writes "if patientAge > 65 & patientAge < 18" intending to flag ambiguous ages. Which statements about this code are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The condition can never be true, since no age is simultaneously greater than 65 and less than 18 — this is a logic bug regardless of & vs &&
Using & instead of && here is itself the bug
The researcher likely meant || (OR) instead of & (AND)
This code will throw a runtime error
advanced.explanation: The real bug is the logical operator choice (AND vs. OR) — no age can be both over 65 and under 18 at once, so the condition is always false. Switching & to && would not fix this; the AND itself is the problem, and the researcher almost certainly meant OR. Neither version throws an error — it just silently never triggers.
advanced.concept: Distinguishing a logic bug from an operator-choice bug

advanced.question: n1 = 5; n2 = 15; if n1 > 0 && n2 > 0, total = n1 + n2; elseif n1 > 0 || n2 > 0, total = max(n1,n2); else, total = 0; end — what is total?
advanced.explanation: Both n1 and n2 are positive, so the first condition (n1 > 0 && n2 > 0) is true, and total = n1 + n2 = 5 + 15 = 20.

Incorrect — that would require y > 0.

advanced.question: A switch statement can be used with no otherwise clause; if no case matches, execution simply continues after the switch block with no error.
advanced.explanation: True. Just like an if with no else, a switch with no otherwise (and no matching case) simply does nothing and moves on — no error is raised.
optionExplanations: Correct — otherwise is optional and a non-match with none present is not an error.
Incorrect — this is completely valid, error-free MATLAB behavior.

advanced.question: For status = 'Normal' (capital N), this displays 'Check' instead of the expected 'OK'. Why?

optionExplanations: Correct — the capitalization mismatch means no case matches.
Incorrect — switch supports string/char comparisons perfectly well, just case-sensitively.
Incorrect — otherwise only runs when no case matches, which happens here because of the case mismatch, not automatically.

advanced.question: Which of the following would fix the case-sensitivity bug from the previous question, without changing how status itself is generated? Select all that apply.

Compare using switch lower(status), with case 'normal'
Use strcmpi(status,'normal') inside an if statement instead of switch
Nothing can fix this; switch can never be used with strings that vary in case
advanced.explanation: Matching the case label exactly, lower-casing the switch expression before comparing, or switching to a case-insensitive comparison function (strcmpi) inside an if statement all correctly resolve the mismatch.

advanced.question: Put these lines in order to build a nested if/else classifying v as 'positive-even', 'positive-odd', or 'non-positive'.
advanced.explanation: The outer if is checked first; if true, a nested if further classifies even vs. odd, closed with its own end, before the outer else and final end.

advanced.question: Match each MATLAB construct to the situation it is best suited for.
matchOptions: Testing numeric ranges or combining several different kinds of conditions
Comparing one variable against a short list of discrete exact values
Combining two scalar conditions with short-circuit evaluation
Combining conditions element-wise across an entire array
advanced.explanation: Each construct has a distinct sweet spot: range/combined-condition logic favors if/elseif; discrete-value matching favors switch; scalar short-circuit logic favors && / ||; array-wide element-wise logic favors & / |.
advanced.concept: Choosing the right control-flow / logical construct

advanced.question: Write the MATLAB switch case label (just the "case ..." line, no body) that matches when a variable equals 1, 2, or 3.

advanced.question: What is the value of result? (Hint: ~ has higher precedence than relational operators, so this is (~x) > 3, not ~(x > 3).)
advanced.code:
x = 5;
result = ~x > 3;
options: 0 (false) — ~x is evaluated first, giving false (0 — since x is nonzero, ~x negates it to false), and 0 > 3 is false
Error: cannot apply ~ to a non-logical number
advanced.explanation: MATLAB’s ~ (logical NOT) binds tighter than relational operators. x = 5 is nonzero, so ~x is false (0). Then 0 > 3 is false, so result = 0 (false).
optionExplanations: Correct — ~x evaluates first, then the result is compared to 3.
Incorrect — this would only be true if ~(x > 3) were computed instead, which is not how MATLAB parses this expression.
Incorrect — ~ negates x rather than passing it through unchanged.
Incorrect — ~ can be applied to any numeric value; nonzero values are treated as true and negated to false.
advanced.concept: Operator precedence: ~ binds tighter than relational operators

advanced.question: You need to EXCLUDE a subject from a study if age < 18, OR age > 75, OR their BMI is unknown (NaN). Which condition correctly captures this?
advanced.explanation: Any one of the three conditions should trigger exclusion, so they must be combined with ||, and isnan(bmi) is the correct way to detect a missing BMI (bmi == NaN never works, since NaN never equals anything). The && version requires all three simultaneously, which is far too strict. The last option is a convoluted, incorrect attempt at negation.
optionExplanations: Correct — any one condition should trigger exclusion, correctly combined with ||, using isnan for the missing-value check.
Incorrect — requiring all three at once excludes almost no one.
Incorrect — bmi == NaN is always false; NaN never equals anything, even itself.
Incorrect — this negated expression does not correctly represent the intended exclusion logic.

expert.question: You need to classify a patient’s BMI into categories: Underweight (<18.5), Normal (18.5–24.9), Overweight (25–29.9), Obese (≥30). Which control structure is most appropriate, and why?
options: if/elseif/else, because the category depends on ranges of a continuous value, which switch/case cannot test directly
switch/case, because there are exactly four categories to choose between
A for loop over the four category names
expert.explanation: switch/case matches a variable against exact, discrete values (or short lists of them) — not numeric ranges. Classifying a continuous value like BMI into ranges requires relational comparisons, which is exactly what if/elseif/else is for.
optionExplanations: Correct — range-based classification needs relational comparisons, not exact-value matching.
Incorrect — having exactly four outcomes doesn’t make switch appropriate; what matters is that the input is a continuous range, not a discrete value.
Incorrect — while loops repeat until a condition changes; they don’t naturally express a one-time classification.
Incorrect — looping over category names doesn’t determine which category the BMI actually falls into.
expert.concept: Choosing if/elseif over switch for range-based logic

expert.question: This code does not correctly classify BMI. What’s wrong with using switch here?

bmi = 27;
switch bmi
    case bmi < 18.5
        disp('Underweight')
    case bmi >= 18.5 && bmi < 25
        disp('Normal')
    otherwise
        disp('Other')
end
options: switch compares bmi against the exact VALUE each case expression evaluates to (0 or 1, a logical value) — not against a range — so this almost always falls through to otherwise
The case expressions need semicolons at the end
bmi must be converted to a string for switch to work
otherwise must be listed first, before any case
expert.explanation: case bmi < 18.5 evaluates the expression bmi < 18.5 to 0 or 1 first, and switch then compares bmi (27) directly against that 0-or-1 value — which it will essentially never equal. This is exactly why range-based classification uses if/elseif instead of switch.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is precisely the mismatch between what switch compares and what the author intended.
Incorrect — semicolons don’t affect switch/case matching logic.
Incorrect — switch works with numeric values directly; no string conversion is needed.
Incorrect — otherwise is a catch-all and is conventionally listed last, not first.
expert.concept: Why switch/case cannot express range conditions directly
commonMistakes: Writing a relational expression as a case value, expecting switch to evaluate it as a condition rather than compare against its 0/1 result.

expert.question: Which of the following are legitimate reasons to prefer if/elseif/else over switch/case in MATLAB? Select all that apply.
options: Testing numeric ranges (e.g., bp > 140) rather than exact discrete values
Combining multiple independent conditions with && or ||
Comparing a variable against a short list of exact string labels like 'low', 'medium', 'high'
Testing more than two conditions in general
expert.explanation: Range tests and combined logical conditions genuinely require if/elseif (switch can’t express either directly). Matching a variable against a short list of exact labels is actually a case where switch is well suited, not a reason to avoid it. And "more than two conditions" alone isn’t a meaningful reason either way — switch handles many cases just fine.

expert.question: Given x = 8; if mod(x,2) == 0 && x > 5, y = x^2; else, y = 0; end — what is y?

expert.question: Short-circuit operators (&&, ||) can prevent an error in a condition like if isfield(s,'x') && s.x > 0, because the second condition is never evaluated when the first is false.
expert.explanation: True. && stops evaluating as soon as the overall result is determined — if isfield(s,'x') is false, MATLAB never evaluates s.x > 0, avoiding an error from accessing a field that doesn't exist. The non-short-circuit & would evaluate both sides regardless and could error here.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is exactly what makes && (and ||) useful for guarding against errors in later conditions.
Incorrect — short-circuit evaluation is a real and important MATLAB behavior.
expert.concept: Short-circuit evaluation as an error guard

expert.question: A triage classifier must flag 'Critical' if (HR > 120 OR HR < 40) OR (O2 < 90) OR (SBP < 90). Which single boolean expression correctly implements this?
expert.explanation: The correct expression combines every individual danger condition with ||. Option 2 requires HR to be simultaneously above 120 AND below 40, which is impossible. Option 3 has an operator-precedence bug: && binds tighter than ||, so it parses as hr>120 || hr<40 || (o2<90 && sbp<90), wrongly requiring BOTH o2 and sbp to be abnormal together. Option 4 attempts a De Morgan negation but uses strict inequalities that don’t correctly match the boundary values in the original (non-strict) thresholds, making it subtly non-equivalent.
optionExplanations: Correct — every danger condition is combined with OR, exactly as required.
Incorrect — AND between hr>120 and hr<40 can never be true simultaneously.
Incorrect — && binds tighter than ||, incorrectly requiring both o2 and sbp to be abnormal together.
Incorrect — the boundary (strict vs. non-strict inequality) does not correctly mirror the original thresholds.
expert.concept: Combining multiple OR-connected danger conditions correctly

expert.question: Calling classify(85) produces an error. Why?

MATLAB functions cannot use if/elseif inside them
85 is not a valid numeric value in MATLAB
disp() cannot display strings returned from functions
expert.explanation: bp = 85 fails both bp > 140 and bp > 90, and there is no else, so result is never assigned inside the function. MATLAB then errors because the function is expected to return a value in result but didn’t — "Output argument 'result' ... not assigned."
optionExplanations: Correct — an unassigned output variable is the source of the error.
Incorrect — if/elseif inside functions is completely standard and supported.
Incorrect — 85 is an ordinary valid number.
Incorrect — disp() works fine on strings; the error happens before disp() is even reached.
expert.concept: Unassigned output variable when no branch executes
commonMistakes: Writing an if/elseif chain with no else inside a function that must assign an output variable, leaving it undefined for some inputs.

expert.question: In a MATLAB function, you write "if nargin < 2, thresh = 50; end" at the top. What does this accomplish?
options: Sets a default value for thresh only when the caller did not supply that input argument
Always overwrites thresh to 50, regardless of what the caller passed in
Counts how many outputs the function returns
expert.explanation: nargin reports how many input arguments were actually supplied when the function was called. If fewer than 2 were given, thresh has not been set by the caller, so this idiom provides a sensible default only in that case.
optionExplanations: Correct — this is the standard idiom for providing a default argument value.
Incorrect — the if only runs when fewer than 2 arguments were supplied.
Incorrect — nargin counts supplied arguments, it does not inspect a value for sign.
Incorrect — that would be nargout, not nargin.
expert.concept: Using nargin with if to provide default argument values

expert.question: Which of the following are legitimate reasons a switch statement might unexpectedly fall into otherwise when working with sensor readings? Select all that apply.
options: Comparing a computed floating-point value against an exact case value like case 98.6, when tiny floating-point rounding makes them not exactly equal
